# Bellevue Home Values & Market Report | Updated October 2026

Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/market-reports/bellevue/
Updated: October 2026. Data window: July to September 2026 (rolling 3 months, single family homes). Source: Redfin Data Center.

Bellevue's median single family sale price was $1.84 million for July to September 2026, up 2.3% from the same months last year. 266 single family homes sold (15.6% fewer than a year ago), and the median home spent 20 days on the market.

| Metric | Jul to Sep 2026 | Last month's window | Last year | Change vs last year |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Median sale price | $1,841,766 | $1,775,000 | $1,799,950 | Up 2.3% |
| Homes sold | 266 | 303 | 315 | Down 15.6% |
| Median days on market | 20 days | 16 days | 8 days | Up 12 days |
| Average sale to list price | 97.4% | 97.8% | 98.8% | Down 1.4 pts |
| Months of supply | 3.1 | 2.8 | 1.8 | Up 1.3 |

## What this means if you're selling

At 3.1 months of supply, buyers have some choice but not a lot. Homes that are prepared and priced right still move; homes priced on hope tend to sit. Sellers averaged 97.4% of list price, so buyers are negotiating. Pricing right from day one protects you from a string of reductions. Homes are taking longer to sell than a year ago (20 days at the median versus 8), so build that into your timeline.

## What this means if you're buying

At 3.1 months of supply you have some room to look. That's more choice than a year ago, but well priced homes in the best locations draw competition. Homes averaged 97.4% of list price, so there is room to negotiate, especially on homes that have been on the market a while. Prices are higher than a year ago, so waiting has not been cheaper lately.

# Bellevue Farmers Market: What to Know Before You Go

> A practical guide to the Bellevue Farmers Market from a local who actually goes. What to expect, when to arrive, and what makes it worth the trip.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 23, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/bellevue-farmers-market-guide/

People ask me about the Bellevue Farmers Market more than you might expect. It comes up in buyer consultations surprisingly often, usually from someone moving from Seattle or another city where a weekly farmers market was part of their routine. They want to know if Bellevue has that. The short answer is yes, and it's genuinely good.

## Where It Is and When It Runs

The market runs on Thursday afternoons, and for 2026 the regular season is May 21 through October 1, in the parking lot of Bellevue Presbyterian Church at 1717 Bellevue Way NE, just north of downtown. Hours are 3 to 7:30 p.m. through August and 3 to 7 p.m. in September, though the vendors with the most popular items tend to sell out before the closing bell, especially if it's a warm summer Thursday.

The location is easy to get to from most of Bellevue, and parking is simple: there's free parking right on site in the church lot, and the market is on nearby bus routes.

## What You'll Actually Find There

This is a producer only market, which matters. It means the vendors are the people who actually grew or made the product, not resellers buying from a warehouse and marking it up. The Bellevue Farmers Market, a nonprofit, requires it of every vendor, and everything sold there comes from within Washington State, and you can tell the difference when you're there. When you ask a vendor how something was grown or what variety an apple is, they know the answer.

The produce selection is strongest in midsummer through early fall. Stone fruits from eastern Washington show up in July and August, corn and tomatoes peak around August, and fall brings winter squash, potatoes, and the best of the apple crop. In May and June, expect more greens, radishes, spring onions, and early strawberries.

Beyond produce, the market has a solid mix of:

* Bread and baked goods from a handful of regular vendors who rotate through the season

* Flowers, particularly dahlias later in the summer, which this region grows exceptionally well

* Eggs, honey, and small batch preserves

* A few prepared food stalls with hot options for eating on site

* Occasionally mushrooms, which tend to attract a line

It's not the biggest market in the region. The University District Farmers Market in Seattle runs year round and has more vendors. But for Bellevue residents, the Thursday afternoon timing and the Bellevue Way location make it genuinely convenient, and the quality is consistently high.

## The Thursday Timing: A Real Consideration

It's worth being honest that this is a weekday market, but the afternoon and early evening hours help a lot. If you work from home or have a flexible schedule, you can go early in the afternoon, and if you're commuting to Seattle or working a traditional office schedule, you can usually still make it after work if you head straight there.

The regular season is Thursdays only, but for 2026 the market has also scheduled two Saturday fall markets, on October 31 and November 21, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

## How It Fits Into the Neighborhood

The market itself isn't in Old Bellevue, but Old Bellevue's stretch of Main Street, with good coffee, a mix of restaurants, and a few independent shops, is a short drive south if you want to extend the outing. It doesn't feel like an outdoor mall the way some parts of Bellevue do. Old Bellevue has a more relaxed, neighborhood scale feel than the Bellevue Square corridor a few blocks away.

For buyers looking at homes in the 98004 zip code, which covers much of this area, proximity to the farmers market is something that actually comes up as a selling point, and reasonably so. Being able to walk or bike to the market on a Thursday afternoon is a real lifestyle feature, not just a talking point.

## A Few Practical Tips

Bring cash. Most vendors take cards now, but a few still prefer cash, and if you're buying from multiple stalls, cash moves faster and avoids the occasional connectivity issues you get with mobile readers at outdoor events.

Bring bags. Reusable bags or a sturdy tote make a real difference, especially if you're picking up both produce and flowers.

Come early if there's something specific you want. The vendors with artisan bread, popular flower arrangements, or specialty mushrooms can get picked over as the afternoon goes on. If you arrive in the last hour on a nice day, you'll still find plenty, but the selection won't be what it was right after the 3 p.m. opening.

The market has free parking right on site in the church lot, so you don't need a garage or street parking strategy.

## Is There Anything Missing?

A few things the market doesn't have, at least not consistently: a full winter season. The regular Thursday season wraps up in early October, and after that there are only a couple of Saturday fall markets. The market does list fresh meats and seafood among what its vendors sell, but if you want more vendors or a market that runs every week of the year, the University District Farmers Market in Seattle is open Saturdays year round.

None of that is a reason to skip it. It just means it works best as one part of how you shop rather than a single stop for everything.

## Common Questions

### Is the Bellevue Farmers Market open year round?

No. For 2026 the regular season runs Thursdays from May 21 through October 1, plus two Saturday fall markets on October 31 and November 21. There's no regular winter season, so if you want a year round option, the University District Farmers Market in Seattle operates every Saturday regardless of season.

### Is this a producer only market, or do vendors resell other farms' products?

It is a producer only market, which means vendors are required to sell what they grew, raised, or made themselves. The Bellevue Farmers Market, a nonprofit, requires it, and everything sold there comes from within Washington State. In practice it means better quality and more knowledgeable vendors, since you're talking directly to the grower.

### Can you walk to the market from the Bellevue downtown core?

The market is at 1717 Bellevue Way NE, north of Bellevue Square, so it's walkable from the north end of downtown and a longer walk from Main Street and Old Bellevue. If you drive, there's free parking on site. From neighborhoods like Medina or Clyde Hill, most people drive.

### What time of year has the best produce selection?

August through early October is the strongest window. That's when eastern Washington stone fruits are winding down, corn and tomatoes are peaking, and the early apple varieties start appearing. Dahlias are also at their best in late summer, if flowers are what you're after.

### Is there food you can eat on site, or is everything meant to be taken home?

There are usually a few prepared food vendors with hot items, enough to make a meal of it if you want to eat while you browse. The surrounding Old Bellevue restaurants are also a natural extension of the visit if you want a proper sit down meal after shopping.

# The Best Coffee Shops in Bellevue, WA Worth Knowing

> A local real estate agent's honest guide to the best coffee shops in Bellevue, WA, by neighborhood, from downtown to Crossroads and beyond.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 16, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/best-coffee-shops-in-bellevue-wa/

People moving to Bellevue almost always ask about coffee at some point, usually framed around whether they'll need to drive into Seattle to find something good. The short answer is no. The longer answer is that Bellevue's coffee scene has filled in considerably over the past decade, and where you land in the city actually shapes which shops become part of your regular routine.

I'm not a coffee reviewer, but I spend a lot of time in these neighborhoods and I pay attention to where people actually go, not just what shows up on a list. Here's what I know.

## Downtown Bellevue

The downtown core is dense enough now that you have real options within a few blocks of each other. **Caffe Ladro** has a location at 333 108th Avenue NE, a short walk from the Bellevue Transit Center, and draws a mix of office workers and people just off the Bellevue Transit Center. It's a Pacific Northwest small chain with consistent quality and a calm enough atmosphere that you can actually sit and work without feeling like you need to clear out.

**Mercurys Coffee** opened a downtown shop at City Center Bellevue on 108th Avenue NE in late 2024. It's an Eastside company that roasts its own coffee, and it opens early on weekdays, which makes it an easy stop before work.

There are also plenty of Starbucks locations and various hotel lobby options, but those are more about convenience than experience.

## Crossroads and the Eastside Middle Belt

Crossroads is one of the more interesting parts of Bellevue to watch right now. The neighborhood has a lot of cultural and culinary diversity that downtown doesn't quite have, and the coffee reflects that. Chain options are there, but locals tend to gravitate toward smaller spots.

Crossroads' smaller spots change often, so it's worth walking the shopping center and the nearby plazas to see what's open now rather than relying on an old list.

If you're in the Crossroads area regularly, the Crossroads Shopping Center itself has changed a lot and draws a community crowd in a way that the downtown mall doesn't. Coffee there tends to be tied to errands and social time rather than a destination visit.

## Bellevue's Quieter Pockets: Somerset, Factoria, and Points South

This is where the chain dependence is most noticeable. Somerset and the Factoria area are primarily residential, and the coffee options are mostly tied to grocery store plazas and drive throughs. There are Starbucks locations and similar chain options. If you live in this part of Bellevue and want something more independent, you're generally driving north toward downtown or east toward Issaquah.

That's not a knock on the area. It's just a real thing to know if your morning coffee routine matters to you.

## The Newport Hills and Eastgate Area

Similar story here. It's convenient to I 90 and has solid suburban infrastructure, but independent coffee is sparse. The closest genuinely good options tend to be back toward downtown or over toward Issaquah.

## What's Worth the Short Drive Out of Bellevue

A few shops just outside Bellevue's city limits get used by Bellevue residents regularly enough that they deserve a mention.

**Zoka Coffee** has a Kirkland location on Central Way that draws people from the south end of Kirkland and occasionally from north Bellevue. Their roasting operation is taken seriously and it shows in the cup.

**Mercurys Coffee** has multiple Eastside locations, including two in Bellevue itself (a roastery and bakery on NE 20th Street and the downtown City Center shop) plus several in Redmond and Kirkland, and it's a locally grown chain that actually maintains quality across its stores. It fills a useful middle ground between the pure independents and the national brands.

**Herkimer Coffee** is a Seattle roaster worth knowing about, but all of its cafes are in Seattle (Phinney Ridge, Ravenna, and downtown), so it's a trip across the lake rather than a neighborhood stop.

## A Note on How This Connects to Neighborhood Choice

This comes up in conversations about where to buy more than you might expect. Someone who works from home and starts their day at a coffee shop with good wifi needs to think about this differently than someone commuting into Seattle who just needs a drive through on the way to the freeway. Downtown Bellevue or the area around Bellevue Way gives you walkable options. The further south and east you go, the more car dependent your coffee routine becomes.

It's a small thing on paper, but small daily routines add up. It's worth thinking about alongside the commute and the school question.

## Common Questions

### Is there a good independent coffee shop walkable from downtown Bellevue?

Yes. Mercurys at City Center Bellevue and Caffe Ladro on 108th Avenue NE are both walkable from the core of downtown. If you live or work near Bellevue Way or Main Street, you're in reasonable reach of both without needing to drive.

### Does Bellevue have any locally roasted coffee options?

A few. Mercurys has a roastery and bakery right in Bellevue on NE 20th Street. Zoka based in Seattle with a Kirkland location nearby, is a legitimate roaster worth knowing. Mercurys is Eastside grown and roasts in house. You're not limited to what comes off a national supply chain.

### What parts of Bellevue have the fewest coffee options within walking distance?

The southern and southeastern parts of the city, including Factoria, Somerset, and the Eastgate corridor near I 90, have mostly drive through chains and grocery plaza options. If a neighborhood coffee shop is part of your daily rhythm, those areas require more driving.

### How does Bellevue compare to Seattle for coffee?

Seattle has more density of independent shops, especially in neighborhoods like Capitol Hill, Fremont, and Columbia City. Bellevue has good options but they're more spread out and less concentrated. You won't be stuck with just Starbucks, but you may need to be intentional about where you live relative to the shops you actually want to use.

### Are there coffee shops in Bellevue with good space for remote work?

Caffe Ladro and the downtown Mercurys are the independent options to try first, but check the seating before planning a long work session. Some of the chain locations have more square footage but less atmosphere. The independent shops on the Eastside tend to be smaller, so arriving at an off peak time helps if you need reliable seating.

# Bellevue vs Kirkland: Which Eastside City Fits You?

> Comparing Bellevue and Kirkland as places to live on the Eastside. Real differences in housing, commute, feel, and tradeoffs to help you decide.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 26, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Kirkland, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/bellevue-vs-kirkland-which-eastside-city-is-right-for-you/

This is probably the most common question I get from buyers relocating to the Eastside who have done some initial research and narrowed things down to two cities. Both are good. Both are expensive. And they are different enough that the choice genuinely matters depending on what you actually want out of where you live.

Let me walk through the real differences, not the chamber of commerce version.

## The Feel of Each City

Bellevue has changed dramatically in the last fifteen years. Downtown Bellevue is a real urban core now, with high rise condos, a growing office market, and the kind of density that would have seemed improbable when I was growing up here. If you want walkable access to restaurants, shopping at Bellevue Square, and light rail via the East Link extension, that downtown corridor delivers it. Outside of downtown, though, most of Bellevue is still quiet residential neighborhoods on larger lots, and the contrast between those two versions of the city can be jarring if you have not spent much time here.

Kirkland has a different character. It is more horizontal, more consistently residential, and the waterfront along Lake Washington gives the city a genuine sense of place that does not depend on new construction. Downtown Kirkland around Lake Street is walkable in the way a small town is walkable: coffee shops, restaurants, a Wednesday farmers market at Marina Park in summer, and access to the water. It has not developed a high rise core, and most long term Kirkland residents seem to prefer it that way.

Neither of these is better. They are answering different questions about how you want to live.

## Housing Stock and What Your Budget Gets You

Both cities are expensive, but they are not priced identically. Bellevue tends to command a premium, particularly in neighborhoods like West Bellevue, Medina adjacent areas, and Somerset. You are paying for school district reputation, proximity to major employers, and in some cases, lot size and views. New construction in Bellevue has also pushed prices up across the board, because even older homes get compared against what new product is selling for nearby.

Kirkland gives you more variety. Totem Lake in the north end is priced more accessibly than downtown Kirkland or the waterfront neighborhoods. Finn Hill and Juanita have a mix of older ranches and split levels alongside newer construction, and you can often find more square footage for the same money than you would in comparable Bellevue neighborhoods. The tradeoff is that Kirkland does not have the same concentration of prestige neighborhoods that Bellevue does, so if you are buying partly as a long term investment in one of the most competitive zip codes on the Eastside, Bellevue has historically held that edge.

That said, both cities have appreciated significantly over the past decade, and I would not make a purchase decision based on speculation about which one will appreciate faster.

## Commute and Getting Around

If you are working in Seattle, the math is different for each city. From Bellevue, you have I 90 and SR 520 as options, and East Link light rail now adds a car free alternative that was not there before. Bellevue to downtown Seattle by train is genuinely fast if you live or work near a station.

Kirkland does not have light rail access yet, and the cross lake commute from Kirkland relies on SR 520. Traffic on 520 heading into Seattle in the morning can be significant, and the SR 520 bridge is tolled, which adds real cost if you drive it every day. If you are commuting to Seattle every day and do not want to drive, Bellevue is the cleaner option right now.

If you are working somewhere on the Eastside, the calculus shifts. Kirkland is centrally located for getting to Redmond, Bellevue, or Bothell without fighting as much traffic, and the drive times to major tech campuses in Redmond are often quite manageable depending on exactly where you land.

## The Waterfront Question

This comes up constantly, so it is worth addressing directly. Both cities have Lake Washington frontage, but Kirkland's relationship with the lake is fundamentally different from Bellevue's. In Kirkland, the waterfront is integrated into daily life in a way it simply is not in Bellevue. Waverly Beach Park, Juanita Beach, Marina Park, the path along the water near downtown: these are places people actually use regularly, not just on holidays.

Bellevue has Meydenbauer Bay Park and some waterfront access, but the lakefront in Bellevue is largely private and residential. Waterfront homes in Bellevue are exceptional and extraordinarily expensive. For most buyers, the practical lake access in Kirkland is more relevant to daily quality of life than what Bellevue offers.

## Schools

Bellevue School District has one of the strongest reputations in the state, and it is a real driver of demand in Bellevue neighborhoods. That reputation is earned: test scores, program offerings, and college placement results are consistently strong. Buyers with school age kids often have Bellevue SD circled before they even look at a single house.

Lake Washington School District, which serves most of Kirkland, is also a strong district. It is not an afterthought. Individual schools within both districts vary, and I would encourage any buyer with kids to look at the specific schools serving a given address rather than treating the district name as the whole story.

One nuance worth knowing: Lake Washington School District covers almost all of Kirkland, including schools on Finn Hill, but district lines do not always follow city limits. If school district matters to your decision, verify which district covers the specific neighborhood you are considering.

## Who Each City Tends to Suit

Bellevue tends to be a stronger fit if you want access to a real urban core without living in Seattle, if the school district is a primary factor, if you are working in or near downtown Bellevue, or if you want the densest concentration of amenities and services on the Eastside.

Kirkland tends to suit people who want a less dense, more outdoorsy lifestyle, who value walkable waterfront access as part of everyday life, who are working in Redmond or somewhere in the north Eastside, or who want more home for their budget without going as far out as Sammamish or Issaquah.

There is also a personality dimension that is hard to quantify but real. Kirkland has historically attracted people who prioritize lifestyle over prestige. Bellevue attracts people who want both and are willing to pay for it. Neither orientation is wrong.

## The Honest Tradeoffs

Choosing Bellevue over Kirkland usually means paying more for a comparable home, getting better school district name recognition, and gaining access to more urban amenities and transit. You may be trading some neighborhood character and waterfront access to do it.

Choosing Kirkland usually means a more relaxed pace, genuine proximity to the lake in daily life, and slightly more buying power. The commute to Seattle is a real consideration, and you should think honestly about how often you will make that trip and how you feel about driving versus transit.

Most people who ask me this question already know, at some level, which city fits them better. The research phase usually confirms what they already sensed from spending time in both places.

## Common Questions

### Does Kirkland have light rail access?

Not currently. The 2 Line serves Bellevue and Redmond but not Kirkland. Sound Transit's longer term plans include a South Kirkland to Issaquah light rail line with a 2041 target, and a Stride bus rapid transit station at NE 85th and I 405 in Kirkland is under construction, but for now, commuting from Kirkland to Seattle means driving or taking a bus, and most people drive via SR 520.

### Is Bellevue School District really that much better than Lake Washington School District?

Both are strong districts by any objective measure. Bellevue SD has a slightly stronger brand and some specific programs, like the International School, that are genuinely distinctive. Lake Washington SD consistently performs well and is not a step down in any meaningful sense. If you have a child with specific academic needs or interests, it is worth comparing the particular programs available rather than just the district names.

### Which city has better access to outdoor recreation?

They are different rather than one being better. Kirkland has easier, more integrated lake access and a good trail network including the Cross Kirkland Corridor, which runs through the middle of the city on a former rail line. Bellevue has Bellevue Downtown Park, Mercer Slough, and proximity to Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park. If lake swimming and kayaking are important to your daily life, Kirkland is the clearer choice.

### Can you get more house for your money in Kirkland compared to Bellevue?

Generally yes, though it depends heavily on the specific neighborhoods you are comparing. Parts of Kirkland like Totem Lake and Finn Hill tend to offer more square footage per dollar than comparable Bellevue neighborhoods. However, Kirkland waterfront and prime downtown Kirkland properties are not cheap by any standard, and the gap narrows in those areas.

### Are there parts of Bellevue that feel more like Kirkland, or vice versa?

Yes. The residential neighborhoods in east Bellevue, like Lake Hills and Crossroads, feel quieter and more suburban than downtown Bellevue, and they are priced more accessibly. Totem Lake in north Kirkland is more commercial and less charming than downtown Kirkland or Juanita. Both cities have internal variety, so it is worth spending time in the specific neighborhoods you are considering rather than forming an impression from the city center alone.

# Newport Hills Bellevue: What Buyers Should Know

> A real look at Newport Hills in Bellevue for buyers. Housing stock, commute, schools, tradeoffs, and what makes this neighborhood different from nearby areas.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 19, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/newport-hills-bellevue-neighborhood-guide-for-buyers/

## Where Newport Hills Sits and Why It Gets Overlooked

Newport Hills occupies a stretch of south Bellevue that a lot of buyers drive through without really stopping to think about. It sits south of Factoria and I 90, with I 405 along its western edge, Coal Creek Parkway wrapping around its north and east sides, and its southern edge near SE 69th Street. It is close enough to downtown Bellevue to matter but far enough away that prices have historically stayed a step below what you see in Bellevue's more talked about neighborhoods.

That positioning is both the appeal and the thing buyers need to think through honestly before committing.

## What the Housing Stock Actually Looks Like

Most of Newport Hills was built in the 1960s and 1970s, with some pockets of infill from later decades. You are looking primarily at single story and split level homes on decent sized lots, though lot size varies quite a bit from street to street. Garages are almost always attached. Yards tend to be usable rather than just decorative.

The architectural style is pretty understated. These are not the craftsman bungalows you find in Kirkland's older neighborhoods or the newer construction you see in Issaquah Highlands. They are solidly built midcentury homes that have been updated to varying degrees. Some have been renovated extensively. Others are still on their original kitchens and bathrooms and represent a project for the right buyer.

Lot sizes and the age of the homes mean buyers should pay attention to a few things: roofs, plumbing, electrical panels, and insulation. A lot of these homes are at or past the point where major systems need attention. A thorough inspection matters more here than it would in a neighborhood full of newer construction.

## The Commute Reality

This is where Newport Hills genuinely earns points. I 90 access is fast from most parts of the neighborhood, which makes this one of the better positioned areas in Bellevue for people who commute toward Seattle or toward the Eastside tech campuses. The Newport Hills Park and Ride sits right by I 405, and South Bellevue Station on the 2 Line is a short drive away, which means if you are a transit commuter you have real options.

Getting to downtown Bellevue by car takes around 10 to 15 minutes depending on traffic and exactly where in the neighborhood you start. Mercer Island is just across the bridge, which matters if you have connections there. Renton is accessible without going back to a freeway.

The one thing to be aware of is that surface street traffic on Coal Creek Parkway during peak hours can back up noticeably. If your daily route depends on that corridor, it is worth driving it at rush hour before you decide.

## Schools in Newport Hills

Newport Hills feeds into the Bellevue School District, which is one of the strongest public school districts in Washington state. The elementary school in the neighborhood is Newport Heights Elementary, and Newport High School serves Newport Hills. Middle school assignments vary, so confirm the exact address with the district's school locator.

Newport High School has a solid reputation and a long history in south Bellevue. If schools are a primary decision factor for your family, the district overall is a significant draw for this area.

## Walkability and Day to Day Life

Newport Hills has a small commercial core, the Newport Hills Shopping Center at 119th Avenue SE and SE 60th Street, with a handful of local businesses. For a suburban neighborhood, that is genuinely useful. Being able to walk to a few local businesses is not something every Bellevue neighborhood can claim.

Beyond that core, the neighborhood is not particularly walkable in the way that someone coming from an urban background might hope. You will drive to most restaurants, most errands beyond the basics, and most of what Bellevue's broader retail and dining scene has to offer. That is worth being honest about.

The trail connections are a real bright spot though. The Coal Creek Trail runs through the area and connects into a broader network that gets you to Bellevue's trail system without needing a car. If you are a runner or someone who bikes recreationally, this is a meaningful quality of life feature.

## How Newport Hills Compares to Nearby Neighborhoods

The most useful comparison is probably with Somerset, which sits just to the east. Somerset tends to have slightly newer homes and sits at higher elevation with better views in some parts, and prices reflect that. Newport Hills generally comes in a bit lower for comparable square footage, though the gap narrows or widens depending on what has been updated.

Factoria and the areas just north around I 90 have more of a commercial feel. Newport Hills is more purely residential. If you are comparing against West Bellevue or Medina, you are looking at a completely different price bracket and a different kind of buyer profile.

Compared to similar vintage homes in Renton just over the border, Newport Hills commands a premium because of the Bellevue School District and the Bellevue address. Whether that premium is worth it depends on how much those factors matter to you specifically.

## What Buyers Tend to Get Right and Wrong About This Neighborhood

The buyers who do well here are usually the ones who want a stable, quiet residential neighborhood with good schools and reasonable freeway access, and who are not expecting the lot or the house to be turnkey without some investment. They are also typically comfortable with the tradeoff of being in south Bellevue rather than closer to the city's center.

Where buyers sometimes get it wrong is in underestimating renovation costs on the older homes, or in assuming that because this is Bellevue, everything comes at Bellevue's higher price points. Newport Hills is generally more accessible than most of the city, but the homes do require due diligence and sometimes real money to bring up to modern standards.

The other thing that catches some buyers off guard is the topography. Parts of Newport Hills are hilly enough that lot usability varies quite a bit from one home to the next. A flat, fully usable backyard is worth looking for specifically if that matters to your household.

## A Realistic Summary

Newport Hills is a neighborhood that rewards buyers who do their homework. Good school district, reasonable commute options, some walkability, established tree canopy, and a price point that is typically lower than Bellevue's most competitive areas. The housing stock is older and requires attention. The neighborhood is quiet in a way that some people love and others find a bit sleepy. There is no waterfront, no skyline view, and nothing flashy about it.

For the right buyer, that is exactly the point.

## Common Questions

### What school district serves Newport Hills in Bellevue?

Newport Hills is in the Bellevue School District. The elementary school in the neighborhood is Newport Heights Elementary, and Newport High School serves Newport Hills. Confirm the exact address with the district's school locator, especially for middle school.

### How old are most homes in Newport Hills?

The majority of Newport Hills homes were built in the 1960s and 1970s. Some have been significantly updated; others are closer to original condition. Given the age, buyers should pay close attention to major systems like roofing, electrical, and plumbing during inspection.

### Is Newport Hills walkable?

Partially. The Newport Hills Shopping Center has a handful of local businesses within walking distance for many residents, which is genuinely useful. Beyond that, most errands and dining require a car. The Coal Creek Trail access is a strong point for outdoor recreation without needing to drive.

### How does Newport Hills compare in price to other Bellevue neighborhoods?

Newport Hills is generally priced below Bellevue's more prominent neighborhoods like West Bellevue, Enatai, or Somerset, while still carrying a premium over comparable homes just across the border in Renton due to the Bellevue School District and Bellevue address. The exact gap shifts with the market and what has been updated in a given home.

### What is the commute like from Newport Hills?

I 90 access is one of the neighborhood's genuine strengths. Seattle, Mercer Island, and the Eastside tech corridors are all reasonably accessible. The Newport Hills Park and Ride by I 405 is nearby for transit commuters, and South Bellevue Station on the 2 Line is a short drive away. Coal Creek Parkway can back up during peak hours, so it is worth checking your specific route at rush hour.

# West Bellevue Neighborhoods: What Buyers Should Know

> A local agent's honest guide to West Bellevue homes, neighborhoods, price ranges, schools, and what buyers often get wrong about this part of the city.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 17, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/west-bellevue-homes-for-sale-neighborhood-guide/

## West Bellevue Is Not One Thing

When people say they want to buy in West Bellevue, I always ask what they actually mean by that. The area west of I 405 covers a lot of ground, and the neighborhoods inside it feel genuinely different from each other. Medina and Clyde Hill are old money, large lots, lake access. Beaux Arts is a tiny incorporated village. Enatai and the streets around it feel more like a mix of original ramblers and newer teardown rebuilds. Knowing which pocket you are actually targeting matters a lot, both for what you will pay and what you will get.

This guide focuses on the broader West Bellevue area, which most buyers and agents loosely define as Bellevue west of I 405 and south of SR 520. That includes neighborhoods like Enatai, parts of Vuecrest, and streets that border Medina and Clyde Hill without quite being in them.

## What the Housing Stock Actually Looks Like

West Bellevue has more variety than people expect. You will find mid century ramblers from the 1950s and 60s sitting next to homes built in the 2010s on lots where the original house was torn down. Lot sizes tend to be larger than in central or East Bellevue, which is one reason the area attracts buyers who want space without leaving the city.

The ramblers are interesting because they give buyers a real choice. Some are well maintained and have been updated over the decades. Others are essentially land plays, where the structure has minimal value and a builder or a family willing to start over is the likely buyer. If you are looking at one of those and planning to live in it while you save up to rebuild, make sure you understand what deferred maintenance looks like in a 60 year old house, especially the roof, electrical, and any polybutylene plumbing that might still be in place.

Newer construction in this area tends toward larger square footage and modern finishes, but the lot sizes shrink compared to what original owners had. That is a tradeoff worth thinking about depending on whether you care more about the house or the yard.

## Schools and How Buyers Usually Think About Them

West Bellevue falls within the Bellevue School District, which is consistently one of the strongest in the state. Most families moving here with kids are aware of that before they call me. What they ask about more specifically is feeder school assignments, since those vary by exact address. Bellevue High School serves most of West Bellevue, and Enatai Elementary serves the Enatai area, but elementary and middle school assignments vary by address. The reputation of the elementary schools draws a lot of families to specific streets.

I would just flag that school assignments can change, and with the growth happening in the area, boundaries occasionally get redrawn. If a specific school assignment is the deciding factor for you, verify it directly with the Bellevue School District before you close, not just at the start of your search.

## Commute and Getting Around

One of West Bellevue's practical advantages is access. You can reach downtown Bellevue in under ten minutes from most of the neighborhood. SR 520 is close enough to make Seattle commutes manageable on non peak hours, though anyone who has driven 520 into Seattle between 7:30 and 9am knows that manageable is relative.

I 90 is not far either, which makes the Eastside feel connected in a way that neighborhoods further north do not always have. Redmond and Kirkland are reasonable drives. The Microsoft campus in Redmond is maybe 20 to 25 minutes depending on where in West Bellevue you start.

Walkability is lower than downtown Bellevue or Kirkland's waterfront area. Most errands require a car. Bellevue Square and the Lincoln Square area are close, but the streets in West Bellevue itself are residential and not set up for walking to coffee or groceries the way some buyers hope for. If walkability is high on your list, you should weigh that honestly.

## What Buyers Often Get Wrong About This Area

The biggest misconception I run into is that West Bellevue is all one price point. People see Medina and Clyde Hill on a map and assume everything nearby carries the same premium. It does not. There are streets in West Bellevue where homes sell in the low to mid $2 million range, and there are streets a mile away with a Medina address where prices typically run far higher. The label matters less than the specific street and lot.

The second thing buyers get wrong is assuming that a larger lot automatically means more flexibility to build or expand. West Bellevue has some meaningful setback requirements and critical area ordinances, particularly near the lake and around natural drainage features. If you are buying with a plan to add an ADU, expand the footprint, or rebuild entirely, get a conversation started with a local land use consultant or architect before you are in a committed position on a specific property. Finding out after closing that the lot has constraints you did not expect is an expensive surprise.

## Who West Bellevue Tends to Suit Well

Families with school age kids who want to stay in Bellevue proper but prefer a quieter street than you find in some of the denser neighborhoods closer to downtown. Buyers who want a larger lot and are willing to either update an existing home or take on a rebuild. People who need quick access to both Seattle and the Eastside tech corridor and do not want to pick one side or the other.

It is less of a fit for buyers who want walkable urban life, or who are looking for the kind of newer construction you find in master planned communities like Issaquah Highlands or some of the newer Redmond neighborhoods. The character here is more established and residential, and the pace reflects that.

## A Note on Pricing

West Bellevue is one of the higher priced parts of the Eastside, and the range is wide. Entry level for a livable single family home in this area has been well above $1.5 million in recent years, and that buys you something that probably needs updating. Move in ready homes with good lot size and updated finishes push into the $2 to $3 million range in many pockets. Waterfront or partial lake view properties are their own category entirely.

The market here tends to be less volatile than some other Eastside areas because the buyer pool is made up heavily of people with significant equity or cash, which creates a floor. That also means it does not swing as dramatically in either direction when rates move. It is a relatively illiquid market, meaning fewer transactions, which can make pricing comparisons harder. Two homes a block apart can sell for meaningfully different prices based on lot orientation, view, condition, or simply when they came to market.

## Common Questions

### What neighborhoods are included in West Bellevue?

West Bellevue generally refers to the area west of I 405 and south of SR 520. That includes Enatai, areas bordering Medina and Clyde Hill, and Vuecrest. Medina and Clyde Hill are technically separate cities, though many buyers lump them together with West Bellevue when they are searching.

### What schools serve West Bellevue?

Most of West Bellevue is served by the Bellevue School District. Bellevue High School serves most of West Bellevue, and Enatai Elementary serves the Enatai area, though exact elementary and middle school assignments depend on your specific address. School boundaries do occasionally change, so confirm directly with the district.

### Is West Bellevue walkable?

Not particularly, by urban standards. It is a residential area and most daily errands require a car. Bellevue Square and Lincoln Square are nearby, but within the neighborhood itself there is not much to walk to. That is a real consideration if walkability matters to you.

### What is the price range for homes in West Bellevue?

Entry level single family homes that are livable but need work have generally been above $1.5 million. Updated homes with good lot size in desirable streets run $2 to $3 million or more. Waterfront and view properties are priced well above that. The range is wide and depends heavily on the specific street, lot, and condition.

### Are there teardown or land opportunities in West Bellevue?

Yes, particularly among the original mid century homes from the 1950s and 60s. Some of these are priced essentially as land plays. If you are considering a teardown or major rebuild, check setback requirements and any critical area designations on the lot before getting too far into the process. Some lots have constraints that limit what you can build.

# Somerset Bellevue Homes for Sale: Neighborhood Guide

> Thinking about buying a home in Somerset Bellevue? Jack Macdonald shares what makes this neighborhood stand out, from the schools to the views to the streets.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 11, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/somerset-bellevue-homes-for-sale-neighborhood-guide/

## Somerset Bellevue: What It's Actually Like to Live Here

Somerset sits on the southeast side of Bellevue, up in the hills above I 90, and it has a character that's hard to replicate closer to downtown. The lots are generous. The tree cover is real, not decorative. And on a clear day, the views from the upper streets reach across Lake Washington toward Seattle in a way that stops people mid sentence when they first see it.

I've been through these neighborhoods more times than I can count, and Somerset is the kind of place where people tend to stay. You don't see a lot of quick flips here. When a home comes available, neighbors notice, because turnover is low enough that new listings actually mean something.

## The Homes in Somerset

The housing stock in Somerset leans toward homes built from the early 1960s through the late 1970s, with a mix of split levels, traditional two story homes, and some more contemporary builds that have come in on the larger lots over the past decade or so. Lot sizes tend to be bigger than what you find in neighborhoods closer to downtown Bellevue, which is part of the draw for families who want space for a yard, a garden, or just some separation between themselves and their neighbors.

Many of the homes have been updated over the years, but the neighborhood still has a settled, established feel rather than the freshly constructed look you get in newer Issaquah or Sammamish developments. If you're coming from somewhere like Redmond or Kirkland and want more square footage without crossing into the far east suburbs, Somerset is often worth a serious look.

## Parks, Greenbelts, and Getting Outside

The city greenbelts around Somerset, including the Somerset Greenbelts, Forest Hill Park, and the nearby Coal Creek Natural Area, are the anchor green space for the neighborhood, and they get real use. The trails connect into a broader network that lets you get out on foot without jumping in a car, which matters more than people give it credit for when they're deciding where to live. On weekends you'll find families with kids, people walking dogs, and the occasional runner who figured out that the elevation here makes for a harder workout than it looks on a map.

The parks and trail access, combined with the views, are the two things I hear people mention most when they describe why they moved to Somerset and why they've stayed.

## Schools in the Somerset Area

Somerset falls within the Bellevue School District, which is one of the stronger public school districts in the state. Families moving to Bellevue consistently ask about schools first, and this part of the city holds up well under that scrutiny. I'd encourage anyone with specific questions about current school boundaries or programs to verify directly with the district, since boundaries and offerings do change, but the district reputation is something I hear reinforced regularly from the families I work with across Bellevue.

## Getting Around from Somerset

The location on the southeast side of Bellevue puts you close to I 90, which is a real practical advantage. Seattle is accessible without having to thread through downtown Bellevue traffic. Eastgate and the broader Bellevue grid are nearby, and Issaquah is a reasonable drive east if you need it. The tradeoff is that this part of Bellevue is more car dependent than neighborhoods closer to the Spring District or downtown core. That's worth knowing going in rather than discovering later.

## What the Somerset Real Estate Market Looks Like

Somerset doesn't produce a huge volume of listings at any given time, which means when something comes up that fits, the window to act is usually shorter than buyers expect. Homes here compete on views, lot size, and school district access, and well priced properties tend to move. If you're tracking this neighborhood, it helps to be ready rather than getting ready after you find something you like.

Pricing varies significantly based on whether the home has views, how much the interior has been updated, and lot size. I don't think it serves anyone well to quote a number here that might be stale by the time someone reads it. What I can say is that Somerset consistently holds its value relative to comparable Bellevue neighborhoods, and the people I've helped buy here have not regretted the decision.

## Thinking About Buying or Selling in Somerset?

I grew up watching this part of Bellevue develop, and I still track it closely. If you're thinking about buying in Somerset or wondering what your home there might be worth in this market, I'd rather have a real conversation about your specific situation than send you a generic report. Reach out to me directly at Macdonald Group and Compass. I return calls quickly, and I'll give you a straight answer.

## Common Questions

### What makes Somerset different from other Bellevue neighborhoods?

Somerset sits up in the hills on the southeast side of Bellevue, which gives it larger lots, more tree cover, and views that many flatter neighborhoods simply don't have. It also tends to have lower turnover than neighborhoods closer to downtown, which reflects how much people like living there once they settle in.

### Is Somerset a good neighborhood for families?

It's one of the more popular choices for families in Bellevue. The Bellevue School District is a consistent draw, the parks and trails give kids somewhere to actually go, and the lots are large enough that homes feel like homes rather than townhomes with grass.

### How often do homes come up for sale in Somerset Bellevue?

Somerset has relatively low turnover compared to newer developments in Sammamish or Issaquah. That means fewer listings at any given time, and the ones that do come available tend to attract real interest quickly. If you're serious about this neighborhood, being financially prepared before you start looking matters.

### What schools serve the Somerset neighborhood?

Somerset falls within the Bellevue School District. I recommend verifying current school boundaries directly with the district since assignments can change, but the district overall is one of the stronger public school systems in Washington State.

### How is the commute from Somerset to Seattle?

Access to I 90 is one of Somerset's practical strengths. Seattle is reachable without fighting through downtown Bellevue. That said, this part of Bellevue is car dependent, so public transit options are more limited than you'd find near downtown Bellevue or the Spring District.

# Living in Bridle Trails, Bellevue: A Neighborhood Guide

> Thinking about living in Bridle Trails? Discover what makes this Bellevue neighborhood special, from forested trails to top schools and the local real estate market.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 11, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/living-in-bridle-trails-a-neighborhood-guide/

## What Makes Bridle Trails One of Bellevue's Most Distinctive Neighborhoods

If you've driven through Bridle Trails and felt like you'd somehow left the city behind without actually going anywhere, you're not imagining things. This pocket of Bellevue, bordered by Kirkland to the north and Redmond to the east, has a character that's genuinely hard to find this close to the tech corridor. We're talking wooded lots, equestrian properties, winding streets that feel intentionally unhurried, and a community that takes its green space seriously.

For buyers looking at the Eastside, Bridle Trails often comes up as a surprise. It doesn't have the same name recognition as Bellevue's downtown adjacent neighborhoods, but once people find it, they tend to stay.

## The Bridle Trails State Park Factor

The anchor of the neighborhood, and honestly the reason it feels the way it does, is Bridle Trails State Park. Nearly 500 acres of mixed forest sit right in the middle of the neighborhood, on the line between Bellevue and Kirkland, with miles of trails open to hikers, joggers, and equestrians. It's one of the few urban state parks in Washington where you can still hear more birds than traffic.

Having a park like that as your backyard shapes everything: the density of the neighborhood, the lot sizes, the feel of the streets. Buyers who prioritize walkable green space and privacy without giving up city proximity consistently put Bridle Trails at the top of their list.

## Bridle Trails Real Estate: What to Expect

Homes in Bridle Trails range from mid century ramblers on generous lots to newer custom builds and updated contemporaries. Because the neighborhood developed over several decades, the housing stock is genuinely varied, you're not looking at a cookie cutter streetscape. Lot sizes here tend to run larger than in more densely developed parts of Bellevue, which is a big part of the appeal.

Properties with direct trail access or views into the park command a premium, and rightfully so. But even homes a few blocks removed benefit from the neighborhood's reputation for quality, quiet, and location. Inventory in Bridle Trails tends to move, well priced homes rarely sit long, particularly in spring and early summer.

If you're selling in Bridle Trails, the lifestyle story sells itself. Buyers coming from Seattle or relocating to the Eastside for work respond strongly to the combination of natural surroundings and easy access to both Bellevue and Kirkland.

## Location and Commute

Bridle Trails sits in a genuinely convenient spot on the Eastside. The Microsoft campus in Redmond is a short drive away, and downtown Bellevue is easily accessible via NE 8th Street or 116th Avenue NE. For Amazon employees and others commuting to Seattle, the SR 520 connection keeps you well positioned.

Kirkland's waterfront and restaurant scene on Lake Washington is close enough to be a regular destination rather than a special occasion. Shopping in nearby Overlake, Kirkland, and Redmond covers everyday needs without requiring a highway trip.

## Schools Serving Bridle Trails

Bridle Trails is split between two school districts. Much of the Bellevue side is in the Bellevue School District, with Cherry Crest Elementary right in the neighborhood, while the Kirkland side falls in the Lake Washington School District. Both consistently rank among the stronger districts on the Eastside. Families moving to the area with school age children should verify current attendance boundaries directly with the district, as boundaries can shift, but the district's reputation for strong academics and extracurricular programming is well established and a consistent draw for buyers in this area.

## The Community Feel

Bridle Trails has the kind of neighborhood identity that's increasingly hard to manufacture. People actually know their neighbors here. You see it in the way folks use the park, running into the same faces on the trails, kids biking in the street, a general sense that people chose this neighborhood with intention rather than just landing in it.

The equestrian heritage is still alive too. Some properties retain horse facilities, and you'll occasionally spot riders heading toward the park trails. It gives the neighborhood a genuinely unique character that you won't find in newer master planned communities further east.

## Is Bridle Trails Right for You?

If you want walkable urban amenities at every corner, Bridle Trails probably isn't your neighborhood, downtown Bellevue or downtown Kirkland would suit you better. But if you want space, trees, a sense of privacy, strong schools, and the ability to be in the middle of the Eastside's best job market without feeling like you live in a suburb that could be anywhere, Bridle Trails deserves a serious look.

It's the kind of place where people buy expecting to stay five years and end up staying fifteen.

## Thinking About Buying or Selling in Bridle Trails?

I've worked with buyers and sellers throughout Bridle Trails and the surrounding Bellevue neighborhoods, and I know how different these streets feel compared to the rest of the Eastside market. If you're curious about what homes are actually selling for right now, or you're wondering what your property might be worth in this market, let's have a real conversation. Reach out to me directly, I'm happy to walk you through what I'm seeing on the ground.

## Common Questions

### What is Bridle Trails known for in Bellevue?

Bridle Trails is known for its wooded, residential character, larger lot sizes, and direct proximity to Bridle Trails State Park, a nearly 500 acre forest preserve in the heart of the Eastside. It has an equestrian heritage and attracts buyers looking for privacy and green space without leaving Bellevue.

### What school district serves Bridle Trails?

Bridle Trails is split between the Bellevue School District, which covers much of the Bellevue side, and the Lake Washington School District, which covers the Kirkland side. Both are highly regarded districts on the Eastside. Buyers should confirm specific school assignments with the district directly, as attendance boundaries can change.

### How is the Bridle Trails real estate market?

Bridle Trails tends to be a competitive market with limited inventory. Homes are varied in style and age, with generous lot sizes compared to much of Bellevue. Well priced homes typically move quickly, especially those with trail access or park proximity.

### How far is Bridle Trails from Microsoft and downtown Bellevue?

Bridle Trails is conveniently positioned between Bellevue and Redmond, making it a short drive to the Microsoft campus and to downtown Bellevue. It's a well located neighborhood for tech workers on the Eastside.

### Are there equestrian properties available in Bridle Trails?

Yes, some properties in Bridle Trails retain horse facilities and equestrian use, reflecting the neighborhood's historic character. The adjacent state park includes trails open to equestrians, making it a genuinely rare find this close to urban Bellevue.

# Cost of Living in Bellevue WA: What to Actually Expect

> Thinking about relocating to Bellevue? Here is an honest breakdown of what housing, groceries, taxes, and daily expenses actually look like.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 9, 2026
Topic: Relocation
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/cost-of-living-in-bellevue-what-to-expect/

People moving here from other parts of the country often have one of two reactions when they start pricing things out. Either they already knew Bellevue was expensive and are mentally prepared, or they did not quite believe it until they started looking at actual apartments and grocery receipts. This guide tries to give you a realistic picture rather than a rosy one.

## Housing Is the Big Number

There is no way around it. Housing is where Bellevue separates itself from most of the country, and even from most of the Pacific Northwest. As of August 2026, the median single family sale price in Bellevue was about $1.8 million according to NWMLS data, with areas like West Bellevue and parts of the Bridle Trails corridor running significantly higher. East Bellevue and parts closer to Factoria tend to come in closer to the lower end of that range, but that is still a high floor.

Condos and townhomes fill some of the gap. There is a real condo market in downtown Bellevue and along the Spring District area, and prices there can range from the mid $500s for a smaller one bedroom up into the seven figures for newer high rise units. Townhomes in the $800k to $1.1 million range are relatively common in the central and south Bellevue areas.

Renting is not cheap either. A one bedroom apartment in a newer building downtown will typically run around $3,000 per month or more; RentCafe put the average downtown one bedroom at about $3,070 in August 2026. Two bedrooms in most parts of Bellevue run $2,800 to $3,500, sometimes more in recently constructed buildings. If you are relocating and renting first while you figure out neighborhoods, budget accordingly.

## Washington Has No State Income Tax

This is genuinely meaningful if you are coming from California, Oregon, New York, or most other states. Washington does not currently tax wage income. A new 9.9 percent tax on income above $1 million was signed in March 2026, but it does not start until 2028, faces a legal challenge, and would not touch most households. For a household earning $200,000 or more, that can represent a substantial difference in take home pay compared to what you were used to.

The tradeoff is that Washington funds itself largely through sales tax, and Bellevue's combined state and local sales tax rate is 10.3 percent. You will feel that at the register, especially on big purchases. There is also a 7 percent capital gains tax on long term gains from stocks and other assets above an inflation adjusted standard deduction ($278,000 for 2025), plus an extra 2.9 percent on gains above $1 million, though real estate sales are excluded from that tax.

Property taxes in Bellevue are not particularly low. On a $1.5 million home, annual property taxes are likely to run somewhere around $11,000 to $12,000, depending on the specific parcel and any applicable exemptions. Bellevue's most common levy rate in 2025 was about $7.33 per $1,000 of assessed value. That is worth factoring into your monthly budget if you are comparing the true cost of ownership against renting.

## Day to Day Expenses

Groceries in the Bellevue area run noticeably higher than the national average. QFC and Safeway are the most common conventional supermarkets. Whole Foods has a presence in the area. Trader Joe's locations in Bellevue and Redmond tend to be a bit more accessible on price. H Mart in downtown Bellevue is excellent and often more affordable for produce, meat, and pantry staples, particularly if you cook Asian cuisine regularly.

Dining out is expensive. A sit down dinner for two at a mid range restaurant in downtown Bellevue or around Bellevue Square will easily run $80 to $120 before tip. The Bravern area and some of the newer restaurant openings around the Spring District skew even higher. You can eat well for less if you explore Factoria, parts of the Eastgate area, or the strip malls along Bel Red Road, which have a lot of good independent and ethnic restaurants at friendlier prices.

Utilities are relatively reasonable by the standards of a high cost city. Puget Sound Energy provides electricity in Bellevue, and electricity bills for a typical single family home tend to run $100 to $180 per month depending on the season and the size of the home. Natural gas adds another $50 to $150 in winter months. Water and sewer are set by the city and are not unusually high.

Childcare costs are a real factor for families with young kids. Full time daycare in Bellevue can run $2,000 to $2,500 per month per child at licensed centers. In home nannies are higher. This is one of the areas that surprises people the most if they are moving from a lower cost region.

## Getting Around and What It Costs

Most people in Bellevue own a car, and most households own two. The city is built around driving, and while that is slowly changing with the East Link light rail extension bringing rail access to Bellevue and Redmond, for now a car is close to essential for most daily routines outside of downtown.

Gas prices in Washington have recently run about $1 per gallon above the national average (AAA, September 2026). Parking downtown is metered and not cheap, though it is more manageable than downtown Seattle. If you work in Seattle and are commuting across the lake, tolls on SR 520 add up over a month, with the weekday peak toll at $4.90 per trip with a Good To Go pass, less off peak, and $2 more per trip if you pay by mail.

The new light rail link changes the calculus somewhat for people working near downtown Seattle or near a station. If your office is close to a station on both ends, it is genuinely convenient and eliminates the toll and the bridge traffic stress. For everyone else, the commute math still usually involves a car at some point.

## What Your Dollar Actually Gets You Compared to Nearby Cities

Redmond and Kirkland both sit close to Bellevue in overall cost, though Kirkland has certain pockets, particularly near the waterfront, that are just as expensive as anything in Bellevue. Sammamish tends to run slightly lower on housing prices and has larger lots on average, with the tradeoff being more distance from major employment centers and less walkable infrastructure. Issaquah is more affordable still, and feels more like a small town, which suits some people perfectly and drives others a little stir crazy.

Bothell and Woodinville come in meaningfully lower on housing, and for families who are willing to accept a longer commute or who work on the north end of the Eastside, those areas offer a real value difference without feeling dramatically different in terms of quality of life.

The short version: Bellevue prices reflect its centrality. You are paying for proximity to major employers like Microsoft, Amazon's Eastside offices, and a growing list of tech companies that have put down roots here. If your job is in Bellevue or close to it, the cost often makes more sense than it looks on paper. If you are commuting to Seattle every day and just want more space, somewhere further out might pencil out better.

## A Realistic Household Budget Snapshot

This is a rough illustration, not financial advice. A dual income household earning a combined $300,000 per year in Bellevue, owning a home in the $1.4 million range with a conventional down payment, might look something like this on a monthly basis:

* Mortgage payment (principal and interest at current rates): approximately $7,000 to $8,000

* Property taxes and homeowner's insurance: approximately $1,000 to $1,300

* Groceries for a family of four: approximately $1,000 to $1,400

* Childcare if applicable: $2,000 to $4,500 depending on number and age of kids

* Transportation including gas, insurance, and tolls: $800 to $1,200

* Dining out and entertainment: highly variable, but $600 to $1,200 is common

* Utilities: $300 to $500

That is a significant monthly outflow, and it does not leave enormous room after taxes even at $300,000 in household income. People make it work, often because income growth in the tech sector outpaces the cost of living increases over time, but it is worth being clear eyed about the numbers before you move.

## Common Questions

### Is Bellevue more expensive than Seattle?

For housing, yes, generally. Median home prices in Bellevue have consistently run higher than in Seattle proper over the past several years. Day to day expenses like groceries and dining are comparable. Seattle has higher parking costs in some areas, but Bellevue has its own premiums, especially in downtown and the west side neighborhoods.

### Does Washington's lack of income tax make Bellevue more affordable than it looks?

For high earners, yes, meaningfully so. Someone earning $250,000 in California might take home significantly less than the same salary in Washington after state income taxes. The flip side is a roughly 10 percent sales tax and property taxes that are not particularly low. The income tax advantage is real, but it does not fully offset housing costs for most people.

### What are property taxes like on a typical Bellevue home?

On a home assessed around $1.5 million, expect annual property taxes somewhere around $11,000 to $12,000, based on Bellevue's most common 2025 levy rate of about $7.33 per $1,000. Rates vary by parcel and can shift with levy changes, so it is worth pulling the actual tax record for any specific property you are considering rather than estimating.

### How much does childcare cost in Bellevue?

Full time licensed daycare typically runs $2,000 to $2,500 per month per child, sometimes more for infant care. Nanny or au pair arrangements vary widely. This is one of the expenses that catches people off guard if they are relocating from lower cost areas.

### Are there more affordable areas close to Bellevue worth considering?

Sammamish and parts of Redmond come in slightly lower on housing. Issaquah is more noticeably affordable and has a different feel, smaller and quieter. Bothell and Woodinville offer real price differences, particularly on larger single family homes with more land. The tradeoff in each case is usually commute time or distance from the dense amenities that make Bellevue convenient.
