# Moving to Bellevue from California: What to Actually Expect

> Thinking about relocating from California to Bellevue, WA? Here's what actually changes, from taxes to weather to housing costs, explained plainly.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 31, 2026
Topic: Relocation
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/moving-to-bellevue-from-california-a-practical-guide/

Every few weeks I talk to someone who's made the move from California, or is seriously considering it. The reasons vary: a job at Microsoft or Amazon, remote work flexibility, family in the area, or just the sense that they've been priced out of wherever they're living. Whatever brought them here, they tend to arrive with the same set of questions. This is my attempt to answer them honestly.

## The Tax Picture Is Real, But It's More Complicated Than People Think

Washington has no state income tax on wages today. (A 9.9 percent tax on income above $1 million was signed in March 2026, but it does not start until 2028 and faces a legal challenge.) For someone coming from California, where the top marginal rate can hit 13.3%, that's a significant change. On a $200,000 salary, the difference is meaningful enough that it factors into a lot of relocation decisions, and employers here know it too.

What you give up is a relatively low sales tax rate. Washington's combined state and local sales tax in Bellevue is 10.3%. California's base rate is lower, though it adds up depending on the county. Property taxes in Washington are lower than California in some ways and comparable in others, but the assessment structure is different enough that you shouldn't assume either direction without running actual numbers on a specific home.

The other thing California transplants sometimes miss: Washington has a 7 percent capital gains tax on long term gains from certain assets above an inflation adjusted standard deduction ($278,000 for 2025), with an extra 2.9 percent on gains above $1 million starting with 2025. It passed in 2021 and was upheld by the state Supreme Court in 2023. It doesn't apply to real estate sales, but if you're selling stock or other assets as part of your move, worth knowing before you assume it's a fully no income tax state in every dimension.

## What Your Housing Budget Actually Gets You Here

If you're coming from San Francisco, San Jose, or most of Los Angeles, Bellevue will feel expensive but not shocking. If you're coming from Sacramento, Fresno, or the Inland Empire, the sticker prices here will feel significant.

The Eastside (Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish) has seen sustained demand because of the tech employment base. A single family home in Bellevue proper typically starts well above a million dollars. That's a real number, not a rounding error.

What you're getting for that: larger lots than you'd see in comparable Bay Area pricing, newer construction in many pockets, excellent public schools, and generally lower density than urban California neighborhoods at similar price points. The tradeoff is that you are still spending a lot of money, and the Seattle area has had meaningful price appreciation over the past decade, so the "affordable alternative to California" framing only goes so far.

Condos and townhomes fill out the lower end of the market. Areas like Factoria, Crossroads, and parts of northeast Bellevue tend to offer more entry points than the West Bellevue neighborhoods closer to Downtown.

## The Neighborhoods Within Bellevue Feel Pretty Different From Each Other

Bellevue is not uniform. Downtown Bellevue has become a genuinely walkable urban core with high rise condos, the Bellevue Collection shopping district, restaurants along Bellevue Way, and the Lincoln Square towers. It feels more city, like than most people expect before they visit.

Medina, Clyde Hill, and West Bellevue sit just west of Downtown and are some of the most expensive residential real estate in the state. These are established, quiet, and very much single family home territory.

The Eastgate and Factoria areas are more suburban in feel, closer to I 90, and offer a mix of older ranches, townhomes, and some newer construction. Families who want good schools without the highest possible price point often land here.

Crossroads is a neighborhood worth knowing about if you want genuine cultural diversity and more accessible pricing. The area around Crossroads Mall has an international food scene that regulars take seriously, and the housing tends to be more affordable relative to the rest of Bellevue.

Somerset and Newport Hills, in the southeast part of Bellevue, offer hillside homes with views in some cases, proximity to Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park, and a slightly slower pace than the urban core.

## Commute and Getting Around

This is where California transplants sometimes have the most adjusting to do, though not necessarily in the direction they expect. The Seattle metro does not have the freeway capacity to match its growth. I 405 running north, south through Bellevue gets congested in ways that can genuinely surprise people. Trips that look like 20 minutes on a map at 2pm can take 45 to 50 minutes at 5pm.

The good news: the East Link light rail extension connecting Redmond, Bellevue, and downtown Seattle was a significant infrastructure addition, and for people working in South Lake Union or downtown Seattle, it changes the calculus considerably. If your job is in Redmond, Microsoft's campus has its own transit infrastructure and many employees bike the Sammamish River Trail in warmer months.

Within Bellevue itself, getting around without a car is doable in some areas, particularly near Downtown, and much harder in others. It's not the Bay Area in terms of transit density, but it's improved.

## The Weather Is Not What People Fear, But It Is Real

Californians often brace for brutal winters. What they actually get is grey. October through March tends to be overcast, drizzly, and mild rather than cold and snowy. Snow in Bellevue is infrequent enough that the city occasionally shuts down when it does happen, which is its own cultural adjustment.

The summers are genuinely exceptional. June through September is often clear, dry, and comfortable in the 70s. The first summer almost always converts people. The question is whether they can stay converted through February.

Seasonal Affective Disorder is a real thing here, and people talk about it openly. If you've relied on sunlight for mood regulation and have never lived through a long Pacific Northwest winter, it's worth going in clear eyed. Light therapy lamps are not a quirky wellness trend here, they're just a thing people use.

## The Tech Economy Shapes Everything

Microsoft is headquartered in Redmond, a few miles from Bellevue. Amazon's main presence is in Seattle, but has significant operations throughout the region. There's a dense ecosystem of tech companies, startups, and supporting industries that makes the Eastside employment market feel different from most metros.

This also shapes the community in ways that aren't just economic. A significant portion of the population came here from somewhere else, which means it's relatively easy to meet people who are also new. There's also a large South Asian and East Asian professional community, particularly in Bellevue and Redmond, that shows up in everything from the restaurant landscape to the schools.

If you're not in tech, the area still functions fine. Healthcare, construction, retail, and service industries all exist and employ a lot of people. But the baseline salaries and housing prices have been shaped substantially by the tech sector, so it's worth factoring that into your housing budget expectations regardless of what you do.

## Schools and Why They Matter Even If You Don't Have Kids Yet

The Bellevue School District consistently ranks among the strongest in the state. This is not just perception; the test scores and graduation outcomes back it up. For families with kids, it's often the primary reason they end up on the Eastside rather than Seattle proper.

It also matters for resale value. Homes in top rated school districts hold value differently than comparable homes elsewhere. If you're buying and thinking about your exit at some point, the school district your home falls in does affect your buyer pool later.

## Practical Things People Wish They'd Known Earlier

Car tabs cost more here than most places. Sound Transit's regional motor vehicle excise tax (1.1 percent of your vehicle's depreciated value), combined with other state and local fees, produces registration fees that regularly surprise new residents.

Home inspection matters more than in some markets. A meaningful portion of the housing stock in parts of Bellevue was built in the 1970s and 1980s, and deferred maintenance can be hidden under renovation. Don't skip it to compete on an offer.

The offer process here has historically been competitive in a way that requires some strategy. Multiple offers and escalation clauses are common in the spring market. If you're used to making lowball offers in a slower California market, the approach needs to adjust.

Most Californians also underestimate how much of daily life here happens outdoors in ways that require gear rather than just showing up. Trail running, kayaking, skiing at Snoqualmie Pass (about 45 minutes from Bellevue on I 90), hiking in the Cascades. The outdoor access is a legitimate quality of life asset, and people who engage with it tend to adapt to the weather much better than people who don't.

## Common Questions

### Is Bellevue actually more affordable than the Bay Area for housing?

For comparable properties, Bellevue tends to be less expensive than San Francisco or San Jose, but the gap is smaller than people expect and has narrowed over the past decade. If you're comparing to Sacramento or San Diego, Bellevue can actually feel more expensive in many segments. The income tax savings help the affordability equation, but they don't close the gap on their own.

### How hard is it to get into the Bellevue School District?

If you live within the district boundaries, your kids attend BSD schools. The district covers most of Bellevue proper along with some surrounding areas. The thing to verify when buying is which specific school your address feeds into, since individual school quality within the district does vary even if the district overall is strong.

### Do I need to worry about earthquakes moving from California?

The Pacific Northwest sits on the Cascadia Subduction Zone, which is capable of producing very large earthquakes. This is a real risk that is discussed seriously in emergency planning circles, though major seismic events are infrequent. If you've lived in California, you already understand earthquake risk. Washington's building codes have improved significantly, but it's worth understanding the regional geology before assuming you're moving somewhere geologically calmer.

### What's the rental market like if I want to rent before buying?

Renting for six to twelve months before buying is genuinely smart in this market if you're not certain which area fits your lifestyle. Bellevue has a solid apartment and rental home inventory, particularly near Downtown and in neighborhoods like Crossroads. Rents are high by national standards but give you time to understand which neighborhoods actually suit how you live, which is worth the cost of waiting.

### Will I feel culture shock moving from California to Bellevue?

Probably less than you'd expect. Bellevue is a diverse, internationally connected city with a lot of transplants. The cultural adjustment is more about weather rhythms and pace than anything political or social. People here tend to be outdoors oriented, and there's a strong coffee shop culture that makes the grey months more bearable. The biggest shock for most Californians is just how dark and overcast the winters are.

# Bellevue School District Guide for Home Buyers

> A practical guide to Bellevue School District for home buyers, covering boundaries, school quality, what the data means, and how BSD shapes the market.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 4, 2026
Topic: Schools and family
Area: Bellevue, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/bellevue-school-district-guide-for-home-buyers/

## Why BSD Comes Up in Almost Every Conversation

If you're buying a home in Bellevue or the surrounding area, the Bellevue School District comes up fast. Sometimes it's the first question, before we've even talked about price range or commute. That's not surprising given BSD's reputation, but I want to give you a more honest picture than the usual ranking site summary, because the way BSD shapes the housing market is more nuanced than "it's a great district, buy here."

Let me walk through what's actually useful to know.

## What BSD Actually Covers

Bellevue School District doesn't map cleanly onto the city of Bellevue. It covers most of Bellevue plus Clyde Hill, Medina, Hunts Point, Yarrow Point, and Beaux Arts, along with portions of Issaquah, Kirkland, Newcastle, and Redmond. This surprises a lot of buyers who assume a Bellevue address automatically means BSD. It doesn't.

The reverse is also true: some homes with Redmond or Kirkland mailing addresses fall inside BSD boundaries. So the only reliable way to confirm which district and which school serve a specific property is to use the BSD boundary tool on the district's website and enter the actual address. Don't go by neighborhood name, don't go by the listing description, and don't go by what the neighbors say. Check the address directly.

## How the Schools Are Organized

BSD runs a standard K through 5 elementary, 6 through 8 middle, and 9 through 12 high school structure. There are four comprehensive high schools: Bellevue, Interlake, Newport, and Sammamish. Skyline High School, which buyers sometimes lump in, is in the Issaquah School District. Each serves a defined geographic zone, and which high school your address feeds into matters to a lot of families.

Beyond the neighborhood schools, BSD has a handful of choice and specialty programs that draw applicants from across the district. International School is probably the most well known. It serves grades 6 through 12 with its own rigorous curriculum that includes years of French, and admission is by lottery for students who live in the district, so it is not guaranteed by address. Interlake offers the International Baccalaureate program and is the high school home of the district's advanced learning program, which draws qualifying students from across the district. These programs are worth knowing about if you have specific educational goals for your kids, but they're separate from your neighborhood assignment and shouldn't be the primary reason you buy in a particular zone.

## Are All the Schools Equally Strong?

BSD as a whole performs well on state and national benchmarks, but no, all the schools are not identical. There are real differences between elementary schools in particular, and those differences get discussed extensively in local parent communities.

Test scores, class sizes, and principal stability vary. The schools that consistently draw the most attention from buyers tend to be in the south Bellevue and Somerset areas, and some of the Sammamish feeders. But I'd push back on the idea that you should stretch your budget significantly just to land in one elementary school zone over another. Elementary attendance areas have shifted over time as the district has adjusted for enrollment changes. The school your neighbor's kid attended five years ago may not be the school your child attends.

Middle and high school boundaries are more stable, and those arguably matter more for longer term planning.

## How BSD Affects Home Prices

BSD is one reason Bellevue carries a premium over some neighboring cities. But within BSD, there are meaningful price differences tied to school zone. Homes that feed into Newport High School have historically commanded strong interest. Homes in the Interlake and Bellevue High zones vary more depending on location and housing stock.

What I see play out regularly is buyers paying more than they expected for a home partly because of the school assignment, then realizing a few years later that the school was fine either way. The premium is real. Whether it's worth it depends on how strongly you weight school assignment relative to other factors like lot size, commute, or the home itself.

It's also worth knowing that BSD covers enough geography that you can often find a solid home in the district at a range of price points. The expensive assumption is that only the most sought after addresses inside BSD count. That's not really true.

## Open Enrollment and Boundary Exceptions

BSD does allow some flexibility through open enrollment, which lets families apply to schools outside their attendance area if space is available. This is not guaranteed and depends on capacity year to year. If you're buying with the intention of open enrolling your child somewhere other than the neighborhood school, understand that this plan can change. Build your decision around where your address actually sends your kids, not where you hope to transfer them.

## A Few Things That Don't Show Up in the Rankings

Commute to school is worth thinking about practically. BSD is geographically spread out, and if your elementary school is more than a mile or two from home, you're either driving or figuring out the bus schedule. The district does provide bus service, but not universally to every student at every school, and the routes and eligibility rules are worth reviewing directly with the district before you assume transportation is handled.

Also, the district has invested heavily in facilities in recent years following bond measures, so the physical condition of buildings is generally good across BSD. That's not always the case in every district in the region, and it matters for day to day experience even if it doesn't show up in test score tables.

## What to Actually Do Before You Make an Offer

Look up the specific address on the BSD boundary locator. Confirm the elementary, middle, and high school assignments. If you have strong feelings about a particular school, drive by it, look up recent GreatSchools or Niche profiles with some skepticism about what those scores actually measure, and if possible talk to parents in the neighborhood. That last one tells you more than any ranking.

If you're cross shopping BSD against Lake Washington School District or Issaquah School District, all three are strong, and the honest answer is that for most families the differences matter less than proximity to work, the home itself, and what you can realistically afford. BSD has the strongest name recognition in the region, but that name recognition is partly why Bellevue costs what it costs.

## Common Questions

### Does a Bellevue mailing address always mean Bellevue School District?

No, and this is one of the most common misconceptions buyers run into. City limits and school district boundaries don't match up. Some Bellevue addresses fall in Lake Washington School District or even Issaquah School District. The only reliable way to confirm is to enter the specific property address into the BSD boundary locator on the district's official website.

### What are the four high schools in BSD and does it matter which one a home feeds into?

The four comprehensive high schools are Bellevue, Interlake, Newport, and Sammamish. Skyline is an Issaquah School District school. It does matter to many buyers, and Newport in particular tends to draw the most attention from families. That attention is reflected in home prices in that zone. Whether the differences in outcomes between the high schools justify the price premium is something each family has to decide for themselves, but they're all functioning well resourced schools.

### Can I choose a different school within BSD than my address is assigned to?

BSD does have an open enrollment process, but spaces are limited and availability changes year to year. It's not something you can count on when you're planning a purchase. If a specific school is a priority, buy in that attendance area rather than assuming you'll transfer in later.

### How do BSD schools compare to Lake Washington School District?

Both are well regarded and competitive with each other on most measures. BSD has stronger name recognition, which is a real factor in home pricing. Lake Washington SD covers Kirkland, Redmond, and parts of Sammamish, and its schools perform at a similar level in most categories. Buyers who need to be closer to the 520 corridor or who find better value in Kirkland or Redmond sometimes end up in LWSD and are generally satisfied with it.

### Does BSD provide bus transportation to all students?

Not universally. Eligibility for bus service is based on distance from school and grade level, and routes can change. If daily transportation logistics matter to your family, contact the district directly before closing on a home rather than assuming the bus will cover your address.

### How stable are school attendance boundaries in BSD?

Boundaries do shift, particularly at the elementary level, as enrollment patterns change across the district. High school boundaries have been more stable historically. If you're making a long term plan based on a specific school assignment, it's worth knowing that the assignment your address carries today may not be permanent, especially at the elementary level.

# Redmond Ridge: What Buyers Should Actually Know

> Thinking about Redmond Ridge in Redmond, WA? Here is what the housing stock, commute, and community feel are really like before you schedule a tour.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 19, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Redmond, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/redmond-ridge-homes-for-sale-community-guide/

A lot of buyers first hear about Redmond Ridge from a coworker who lives there and won't stop talking about it. That tracks. It's the kind of place people feel genuinely good about landing in, partly because it was built with some intention rather than just platted and sold as fast as possible. But before you start browsing listings, it's worth understanding what Redmond Ridge actually is, because it surprises some buyers in ways that affect the decision.

## The Short Version of What Redmond Ridge Is

Redmond Ridge is a master planned community built out mostly in the late 1990s through the 2000s, sitting on the east side of Redmond near the Union Hill Road corridor. It's not technically inside the City of Redmond proper, it's in unincorporated King County, which matters more than people expect (more on that in a minute). The community was developed by Quadrant Homes along with several other builders in phases, so the housing stock is relatively consistent in age and quality, with single family homes, townhomes, and some attached product spread across the ridgeline.

It's a planned community in the truest sense. There are parks built into the layout, trails that connect the neighborhoods, a community center, and commercial space at Redmond Ridge East. It doesn't have the organic, grew over decades feel of somewhere like Rose Hill or Bridle Trails. Whether that's a feature or a limitation depends on what you're looking for.

## The Location Math

The address says Redmond, but Redmond Ridge sits further east and uphill from downtown Redmond than the name implies. Getting to the Microsoft Redmond campus or downtown Bellevue means dropping down off the ridge and navigating SR 202 or Union Hill Road to connect to either SR 520 or I 90. That commute is real. On a good day it might be 20 minutes to Microsoft. On a bad day, especially during school pickup traffic on Union Hill, it can stretch considerably. People who work in Bellevue or downtown Seattle should honestly map their specific commute at rush hour before falling in love with a house here.

That said, for people working at companies along the SR 202 corridor or in Redmond's Overlake area, the location is genuinely fine. And remote workers or those with flexible hours largely report that it's a non issue.

## Unincorporated King County: Why That Matters

Because Redmond Ridge sits in unincorporated King County rather than inside Redmond city limits, a few practical things differ from what buyers expect. Permitting goes through King County rather than the City of Redmond. Some services are county managed rather than city managed. Property tax structures can differ slightly. For most buyers this doesn't come up day to day, but if you're thinking about additions, ADUs, or anything requiring permits, it's worth knowing who you're dealing with before you buy.

There is also an HOA covering Redmond Ridge, which handles the community center, trails, and common area maintenance. HOA dues are something to verify per listing since they vary by subneighborhood within the larger development.

## What the Housing Stock Looks Like

Most of the single family homes were built between roughly 1997 and 2010, which means you're looking at homes that are old enough to need some updating but young enough to avoid the bigger structural and systems concerns you'd find in 1960s or 1970s construction. Typical footprints run from around 1,800 to 3,500 square feet, with most homes on the larger side compared to what that price point would get you in closer in Redmond neighborhoods.

Lots tend to be smaller than what you'd find in somewhere like Sammamish Plateau's older developments, though some of the eastern sections have more generous setbacks and views. The construction style is generally Pacific Northwest traditional, lots of Craftsman influenced detailing, two car garages, and layouts built around the family use patterns of the early 2000s. Open kitchen to family room, formal living and dining that sometimes end up underused, primary suites upstairs.

Townhomes and attached homes exist throughout Redmond Ridge and Redmond Ridge East, and those tend to price meaningfully lower, making them an entry point for buyers who want the community amenities but can't stretch to detached pricing.

## Schools

Redmond Ridge feeds into the Lake Washington School District, which is consistently one of the stronger districts in the region. Louisa May Alcott Elementary is the neighborhood school physically located in the Redmond Ridge area, and it gets good marks from families there. That said, school boundaries in LWSD shift over time and assignments depend on your specific address, so always confirm your street using the LWSD school locator at lwsd.org before making decisions based on a particular school. Middle and high school pathways run through the LWSD system, which also serves Redmond, Kirkland, and parts of Sammamish. Buyers coming from outside the area often don't realize how well regarded LWSD is compared to some neighboring districts, so that's a genuine positive here.

## Trails, Parks, and Daily Life

This is where Redmond Ridge earns a lot of its reputation. The trail network built into the community is genuinely good, with paved and unpaved paths connecting the neighborhoods, looping through forested sections, and linking to the larger Redmond Ridge Open Space. Families with kids and people with dogs tend to love this about living there. You can get out of the house on foot or bike and actually go somewhere without immediately hitting traffic.

The Redmond Ridge Community Center at Cedar Park has tennis and volleyball courts, meeting space, an outdoor amphitheater, and is used for community events. The broader park system includes more than 14 parks and miles of trails maintained by the ROA. Redmond Ridge East has a QFC, some restaurants, and everyday commercial needs. It's not a walkscore neighborhood in the urban sense, you'll drive for most errands and restaurants, but the internal trail and park infrastructure is genuinely above average for a suburban development.

## Who Tends to Do Well Here and Who Doesn't

Redmond Ridge works well for families who want newer construction quality, a lot of trail access, good schools, and a neighborhood with some cohesion. It also works for buyers pricing themselves out of closer in Redmond or Kirkland who still want a functional commute to the Eastside tech corridor.

It tends to disappoint buyers who want walkability to restaurants and coffee, buyers who want an older home with character and a larger lot, and anyone whose daily commute involves a lot of time on the west side of the lake. The location is genuinely east of everything. If you're doing a Seattle commute regularly, factor that drive honestly.

It also doesn't suit buyers who strongly dislike HOA living. The HOA here is active and the rules are real. That's not a criticism, it's just a relevant fact about what you're signing up for.

## Pricing Context

Redmond Ridge generally prices below the comparable square footage you'd find in Kirkland or central Redmond, and below the comparable lot size you'd find in older Sammamish. That gap exists because of the location premium you give up by being further east. Whether that tradeoff makes sense depends on your priorities. If square footage, newer construction, and trail access matter more than proximity, the value here is real. If commute time and urban walkability are the priority, the discount exists for a reason.

## Common Questions

### Is Redmond Ridge actually in Redmond?

It uses a Redmond mailing address, but Redmond Ridge sits in unincorporated King County rather than inside Redmond city limits. For day to day life this usually doesn't matter much, but it affects permitting, some services, and occasionally property tax details. Worth knowing before you buy.

### What HOA fees look like in Redmond Ridge?

HOA dues vary depending on which subneighborhood within Redmond Ridge you're buying in, so you'll want to verify the specific amount for any home you're seriously considering. The HOA covers common areas, the community center, parks, and trail maintenance, so you're generally getting something for the cost, but it's a real ongoing expense to factor in.

### How does Redmond Ridge compare to the Sammamish Plateau?

They're similar in some ways: both are planned communities with good schools, newer construction, and trail access. Sammamish Plateau tends to have more variety in lot size and older stock mixed in from the 1990s. Redmond Ridge has a more cohesive community feel with its own center and commercial node. Sammamish is generally a longer drive from the Microsoft and Overlake corridors than Redmond Ridge, though both require some commute planning.

### What is the community center like and is it worth using?

The Redmond Ridge Community Center at Cedar Park has tennis and volleyball courts, meeting rooms, a large fireplace, an outdoor amphitheater, and space for community events. The broader ROA park and trail system is what most residents get the most day to day use out of. It's genuinely used and maintained, not one of those facilities that's nice on paper and empty in practice.

### Are there resale concerns with master planned communities that buyers should think about?

The main thing to think about is that because Redmond Ridge was built out in a concentrated period, a lot of homes hit certain age related maintenance thresholds around the same time, roofs, exterior paint, appliances. When you're buying a home here, look carefully at what has been updated and what hasn't, because deferred maintenance on 2000s construction isn't always obvious from a first walkthrough. A good inspection matters here just as much as anywhere else.

# Dog Parks in Redmond, WA: A Local's Guide

> A real look at Redmond's best dog parks and off leash areas, what they're actually like, where they're located, and what to know before you go.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 21, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Redmond, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/dog-parks-in-redmond-wa-a-local-s-list/

People moving to Redmond with dogs ask about this more than you'd think. Not just "are there dog parks" but "are they actually good" and "which one is worth driving to." The honest answer is Redmond does pretty well on this front, partly because of how much green space the city has managed to hold onto even as it's grown. Here's what I know about the main options.

## Marymoor Park Off Leash Area

This is the big one. Marymoor's off leash area in Redmond is one of the largest in the region, and it's genuinely impressive. You're looking at roughly 40 acres where dogs can run free, including a stretch along the Sammamish River where most dogs end up wading in at some point. If your dog loves water, they'll love Marymoor.

The space is mostly open field with some wooded edges. It gets crowded on weekends, especially on sunny afternoons, so if you have a dog that gets overwhelmed by large groups of other dogs, a Tuesday morning is a very different experience than a Saturday at 2pm. The area has gated entry points, but it's a big open space rather than a small enclosed run, so good recall matters.

Parking at Marymoor costs $1 per vehicle per day, or $100 for a 12 month parking permit. It's not free, but it's cheap, so the annual permit only pays off if you go very often.

## Idylwood Park

Idylwood sits on the western edge of Redmond along the shores of Lake Sammamish. It's not a dedicated off leash area the way Marymoor is, but dogs are welcome on leash throughout the park, though dogs aren't allowed on the designated swim beach, so plan on a leashed walk rather than a swim. The park itself is well maintained and less hectic than Marymoor on a typical weekend.

If you're hoping for true off leash freedom here, you won't find it. But for a leashed walk with great scenery and water nearby, it's worth knowing about.

## Farrel, McWhirter Park

This one surprises people who haven't been. Farrel, McWhirter is a city owned farm park in east Redmond on NE Redmond Road, with trails through second growth forest and open fields. Dogs are allowed on leash on the trails, and the network gives you enough variety that a regular walk here doesn't get stale the way a small neighborhood loop does.

There are farm animals on the property, which is worth mentioning if your dog has strong opinions about goats. The park doesn't have an off leash area, and dogs aren't allowed in the barnyard. Still, it's a good leashed walking option if you're on the east side of Redmond and don't want to drive all the way to Marymoor every time.

## Grass Lawn Park

Grass Lawn is a well used community park in west Redmond on 148th Avenue NE, near the Bellevue border. Dogs are welcome on leash. There's no dedicated off leash zone here, but it's a large, well maintained park with plenty of open space. Families use it heavily, so it's a place where a dog that's calm around kids fits in easily. One with a tendency to jump on strangers might find it a bit stimulating.

The park is closer to the Overlake area than to Redmond Town Center, so it's easy to combine a dog walk with errands or coffee on that side of town.

## What Redmond Is Missing

Compared to some cities, Redmond doesn't have a dense network of small neighborhood off leash areas scattered throughout residential zones. Marymoor covers a lot of ground for the whole region, but if you live in East Redmond or up near Education Hill, getting to Marymoor requires a real drive, not a quick walk out your front door. Redmond's own city parks currently have no permanent off leash area, though the city has run seasonal pop up dog parks and plans a permanent dog park at Luke McRedmond Park with an anticipated opening in October 2026. Someone who wants a fenced off leash area within a five minute walk of their house may find Redmond's options thinner than they'd like depending on exactly where they live.

This is something worth thinking about when choosing a specific neighborhood, not just the city overall.

## A Few Practical Notes

* King County requires dogs to be licensed and up to date on rabies vaccination to use off leash areas. Make sure you're current before you go.

* Bring your own bags. Most parks have dispensers but they run out.

* The Sammamish River Trail runs near Marymoor and connects to a long stretch of paved trail. It's leashed only, but great for longer runs with a dog that can handle the pace and the other trail users.

* Summer afternoons at Marymoor can get genuinely hot on the open field sections. Early mornings are better for dogs that overheat.

Redmond's dog friendliness is one of the things that makes it a good fit for people who take their dogs seriously. Marymoor alone would make most dog owners happy. The rest of the parks fill in the leashed, walk side of things reasonably well, even if the off leash network outside of Marymoor is sparser than it looks on a map.

## Common Questions

### Is Marymoor Park off leash area free to use?

The off leash area itself doesn't have an entry fee, but parking at Marymoor costs $1 per vehicle per day, or $100 for a 12 month permit. The permit only pays off if you go very often.

### Are there any fully fenced off leash areas in Redmond outside of Marymoor?

Not permanently, as of now. Redmond's city parks are leashed only, though the city has run seasonal pop up dog parks at Luke McRedmond Park and Hartman Park, and a permanent dog park at Luke McRedmond Park is expected to open around October 2026. Marymoor is really the main dedicated off leash space in the area.

### Can dogs swim at Marymoor?

Yes. There's river access along the Sammamish River within the off leash area and most dogs take advantage of it. It's one of the main reasons people drive to Marymoor specifically.

### Which part of Redmond is closest to Marymoor Park?

Marymoor sits at the south end of Redmond near the Redmond Town Center area, so neighborhoods in that part of the city have the easiest access. If you're looking at homes in East Redmond or Redmond Ridge, you're looking at more of a drive to get there.

### Do I need proof of vaccination to use the off leash area at Marymoor?

King County requires dogs using off leash areas to be licensed and vaccinated for rabies. You're not asked for paperwork every visit, but the rules are enforced and it's worth making sure you're current before you go.

# Redmond vs. Sammamish: An Honest Eastside Comparison

> Redmond and Sammamish are both popular Eastside suburbs, but they suit different buyers. Here is what actually differs between the two.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 28, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Redmond, Sammamish, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/redmond-vs-sammamish-comparing-two-eastside-suburbs/

This question comes up a lot, usually from buyers who have narrowed their search to the Eastside and are trying to figure out where to plant a flag. Both cities are well regarded, both have good schools, and both have seen serious price appreciation over the past decade. But they are genuinely different places to live, and the differences are not just cosmetic.

## What Redmond Actually Feels Like

Redmond has a real downtown, which matters more than people realize until they have lived somewhere without one. There are actual restaurants, coffee shops, a farmers market, and the Sammamish River Trail running right through the middle of things. Downtown Redmond is walkable in a way that most Eastside cities cannot honestly claim. If you want to walk somewhere on a Tuesday evening without getting in a car, Redmond gives you that option. Sammamish does not.

Redmond is also where Microsoft is headquartered, and the employment presence there shapes the city in real ways: housing demand, commute patterns, the general density of tech workers in every coffee shop. If you or your partner works at Microsoft or somewhere nearby in the Overlake corridor, Redmond is the obvious choice on commute logic alone.

The housing stock in Redmond is more varied. You will find older ramblers and split levels from the 1970s and 1980s alongside newer townhomes and condos. Lot sizes tend to be smaller than Sammamish, especially closer to downtown. The tradeoff is that you are buying into a more established, walkable urban grid rather than a quieter cul de sac neighborhood.

## What Sammamish Actually Feels Like

Sammamish is almost entirely a car dependent suburb, and there is no point pretending otherwise. There is no real downtown. Most of the commercial activity is spread across strip style centers anchored by grocery stores like QFC. If that sounds like a criticism, it is also just an accurate description of a place that a lot of families genuinely love, because the tradeoff is space, quiet, and neighborhoods that feel intentionally residential rather than transitional.

The housing in Sammamish is mostly newer, a lot of it built in the 1990s through the 2010s, which means you get larger floor plans, more consistent finishes, and bigger lots on average. Many neighborhoods sit on the plateau with views of the Cascades or the Olympics on a clear day. Pine Lake, Beaver Lake, and the area around Sahalee are the kinds of places where buyers specifically ask to stay within a few blocks when they find the right street. That neighborhood loyalty is real.

Sammamish consistently ranks among the safest cities in Washington, which is something parents with young kids mention often. Sammamish is split between school districts: roughly the north end is Lake Washington School District, most of the south is Issaquah School District, and a small eastern area is Snoqualmie Valley, so the district and specific schools depend on where exactly you land.

## The Commute Question

This is where the two cities diverge most sharply for a lot of buyers. Redmond sits right at the edge of SR 520 access and is directly connected to the Microsoft and Overlake tech corridor. Light rail reached Redmond Technology Station in 2024 and downtown Redmond in May 2025, and since the 2 Line opened across Lake Washington in March 2026, downtown Redmond has a direct train link to Bellevue and Seattle that skips I 405 and SR 520 traffic entirely. That is not a small thing.

Sammamish has no light rail and no freeway running through it. Getting off the plateau during peak hours means sitting on Sahalee Way toward SR 202, East Lake Sammamish Parkway, or the roads down to I 90, depending on which direction you are heading. Commutes to Seattle or Bellevue from Sammamish can be genuinely painful during rush hour, and that is one of the honest downsides people figure out after they move there. If you work from home most of the week, it matters less. If you commute daily, factor it in seriously.

## Price Differences and What You Get for the Money

Both cities are expensive. That said, Sammamish homes skew larger and newer, so the overall median sale price there tends to run higher. Per Redfin, the August 2026 median sale price was about $1.49 million in Sammamish versus about $1.34 million in Redmond, though price per square foot comparisons swing a lot by neighborhood and home type.

Redmond offers more entry points if budget is a constraint, partly because of the townhome and condo inventory near downtown. Those do not exist in Sammamish in any meaningful way. So if someone's ceiling is somewhere in the lower range for the Eastside, Redmond has options that Sammamish simply does not.

## Schools

Redmond is served almost entirely by Lake Washington School District, while Sammamish is split between Lake Washington in the north and Issaquah School District in most of the south, with a small area in Snoqualmie Valley. Both main districts are consistently strong, so this is one area where the comparison is genuinely close. Elementary school assignments differ by address, and families with specific school preferences should look up boundaries before committing to a neighborhood rather than assuming the city name tells the whole story. The overall district performance is high in both cities.

## Who Each City Actually Suits

Redmond tends to appeal to buyers who want walkability, a shorter commute to the tech corridor, and do not need a large lot to be happy. It also suits buyers who want the option of not owning a car for daily errands, which is increasingly possible with the light rail connection.

Sammamish tends to appeal to buyers who want more space, newer construction, quieter residential streets, and are comfortable being car dependent in exchange for those things. It suits families who prioritize yard size, neighborhood feel, and do not have a daily commute tying them to a specific corridor.

Neither is the wrong answer. But they are genuinely different answers, and buyers who try to compare them purely on price per square foot or school ratings usually end up missing the part that will actually determine whether they are happy there two years later.

## Common Questions

### Does Sammamish have its own city amenities like a community center or recreation programs?

Sammamish has invested in parks and recreation over the years, including Sammamish Commons and several well maintained trail systems. However, the city is relatively young, incorporated in 1999, so some of the civic infrastructure that older cities have built over decades is still developing. King County parks also serve the area.

### Is the light rail in Redmond actually useful for everyday commuting?

The Redmond Technology Station connects to the East Link line, which runs to downtown Bellevue and then into Seattle. For someone commuting to Capitol Hill, South Lake Union, or downtown Seattle, it is a genuinely viable option that avoids SR 520 traffic entirely. It is less useful if your destination is Kirkland, Renton, or somewhere off the line.

### Which city has more new construction available?

Sammamish historically had more land available for large subdivisions, so much of its housing stock is newer. Redmond's new construction tends to be denser, mostly townhomes and multifamily near downtown or the Overlake area, rather than large single family subdivisions.

### How do property taxes compare between Redmond and Sammamish?

Both are in King County, so the framework is similar. Exact rates vary by levy district and specific address. Because Sammamish homes tend to be higher assessed value on average, the dollar amount in property taxes often ends up higher there even if the rate is comparable. Worth checking specific addresses with the King County Assessor site when you are evaluating offers.

### Are there meaningful differences in lot sizes between the two cities?

Yes. Sammamish neighborhoods, particularly those built in the 1990s and 2000s, commonly sit on lots of 7,000 to 12,000 square feet or larger. Redmond lots closer to downtown can be notably smaller, especially for newer townhomes and small lot homes. If outdoor space matters to you, this is worth paying attention to when filtering listings.

# Downtown Redmond Homes and Condos Neighborhood Guide

> Thinking about buying or selling in Downtown Redmond WA? Jack Macdonald shares what living here actually looks like, from condos to commutes.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 13, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Redmond, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/downtown-redmond-condos-and-homes-neighborhood-guide/

## What Downtown Redmond Actually Feels Like

I have been driving through Downtown Redmond for a long time, and the change over the past decade is hard to overstate. What used to feel like a quiet suburban core has grown into a walkable, genuinely livable neighborhood with real density and real energy. And yet it has not lost the thing that made it worth paying attention to in the first place: it still feels like a place people actually live, not just a backdrop for coffee shops and fitness studios.

If you are thinking about buying a condo or home in Downtown Redmond, or if you are a current owner wondering what your property is worth right now, this guide is meant to give you a grounded look at the neighborhood. Not a sales pitch. Just what I know from being here.

## The Housing Mix in Downtown Redmond

Downtown Redmond is primarily a condo and townhome market, which sets it apart from the single family neighborhoods you find further east toward Redmond Ridge or south toward Sammamish. If you are coming from a house and considering a move into the urban core, that shift in housing type is real and worth thinking through carefully.

The condo buildings here range from older mid rise construction to newer developments with modern finishes, rooftop decks, and underground parking. Some buildings sit right on Redmond Way or Cleveland Street, which puts you a short walk from dining and not far from the Redmond Saturday Market on Willows Road NE, which runs Saturdays from May through October. Others are tucked a few blocks back, which trades some convenience for a bit more quiet.

Townhomes do exist in and just around Downtown Redmond, and they tend to attract buyers who want the walkability of the urban core without giving up a garage or a small outdoor space. Inventory on those moves quickly, and well priced units rarely sit long.

## Living Here Day to Day

One of the things I always tell buyers considering Downtown Redmond is to think about what they actually do on a weekday morning versus a Saturday. On a weekday, the proximity to the Redmond Transit Center and the SR 520 corridor matters a lot. Microsoft's main campus is a short drive or a quick 2 Line light rail ride from the Downtown Redmond station. Amazon and other tech employers in the broader Eastside corridor are also well connected from here.

On a Saturday, you are a short walk from Marymoor Park, which is one of the best parks in the region by almost any measure. Whether you have a dog, a bike, or you just want to watch a concert on the lawn, Marymoor draws people from all over the Eastside. Having that in your backyard is not something you fully appreciate until you live here.

The Redmond Central Connector, part of the Eastrail network, runs through downtown and ties into the Sammamish River Trail, which leads toward the Burke Gilman Trail in Bothell, for cyclists and walkers. That trail is a real amenity, not a checkbox. I have talked to buyers who made it a deciding factor.

## Schools and Families in Downtown Redmond

Downtown Redmond falls within the Lake Washington School District, which is consistently one of the more respected districts on the Eastside. Families with school aged children should confirm current attendance boundaries directly with the district, since boundaries can shift with new development, but the district reputation holds across most of the neighborhood. I would rather send you to verify the current map than give you a number that turns out to be stale.

## What the Market Looks Like Right Now

Downtown Redmond condos tend to move in a fairly tight price band relative to the broader Eastside market, though that band has shifted upward meaningfully over the past several years. Location within the urban core, floor level, parking situation, and HOA health all affect value more than buyers sometimes expect coming from the single family side of the market.

If you are a seller, the condo market here rewards preparation. Professional photography matters more in a multi unit building where your listing competes directly with other units in the same complex. Pricing built on actual recent comparable sales, not optimism, is what gets you to closing without a price reduction. That is the approach we take with every listing.

If you are a buyer, the most important thing I can tell you is to understand HOA financials before you fall in love with a unit. Reserves, pending assessments, rental caps, and pet policies all shape the long term cost of ownership in ways that are easy to overlook in a competitive market.

## Ready to Talk About Downtown Redmond?

I grew up on the Eastside. I know Downtown Redmond not as a data set but as a place I have watched change over decades. If you are thinking about buying here, I can tell you which buildings I would look at first and why. If you are thinking about selling, I can tell you what your unit is likely worth and how to position it well.

Reach out directly. I return calls and I answer questions without the runaround. That is how I work, and it is how most of my clients find me in the first place.

## Common Questions

### Is Downtown Redmond a good place to buy a condo?

Downtown Redmond offers genuine walkability, proximity to major employers like Microsoft, and access to Marymoor Park, the Sammamish River Trail, and the Redmond Central Connector. For buyers who want an urban lifestyle on the Eastside without being in Bellevue or Seattle, it is one of the stronger options in the region. The key is understanding the specific building you are buying into, including HOA health and financials, not just the neighborhood overall.

### What is the commute like from Downtown Redmond to Seattle or Bellevue?

Downtown Redmond is well connected via SR 520 and the Redmond Transit Center. Access to the Microsoft campus is particularly close. Commutes to Bellevue and Seattle vary by time of day, so I always encourage buyers to test drive the route during their actual commute hours before committing, rather than relying on average estimates.

### What school district covers Downtown Redmond?

Downtown Redmond falls within the Lake Washington School District, which is one of the more respected districts on the Eastside. Specific school assignments depend on your address and current attendance boundaries, so I recommend confirming directly with the district once you have a property in mind.

### How do I find out what a Downtown Redmond condo is worth?

Condo values in Downtown Redmond depend on floor level, views, parking, building age, and HOA financials among other factors. The best starting point is a conversation with a local agent who can pull recent comparable sales in your specific building or nearby buildings. Feel free to reach out to Jack Macdonald directly for a no pressure market analysis.

# Education Hill Homes for Sale: What Buyers Should Know

> Thinking about buying a home on Education Hill in Redmond WA? Local agent Jack Macdonald shares what makes this neighborhood worth a closer look.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 12, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Redmond, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/education-hill-homes-for-sale-what-buyers-should-know/

## Education Hill in Redmond: A Neighborhood That Earns Its Reputation

Education Hill sits in the heart of Redmond, and if you have spent any time looking at homes in the Eastside, you have probably heard the name come up more than once. There is a reason for that. This is a neighborhood where families tend to stay, where neighbors actually know each other, and where the streets feel lived in rather than staged. That is not a coincidence. It is the product of good schools, walkable parks, and a location that makes everyday life genuinely easier.

I have been working the Eastside market for a long time, and Education Hill is one of those places I can talk about with some specificity, not just general enthusiasm.

## What the Streets Actually Feel Like

Education Hill rises up from the flats of Redmond with views that catch you off guard if you are not expecting them. The terrain gives the neighborhood a distinct sense of place. The residential streets off 166th Ave NE and the blocks surrounding Hartman Park have a quieter residential feel that does not always match what buyers expect when they hear Redmond. Most people associate Redmond with tech campuses and new construction. Education Hill is something else. It is older tree cover, established lots, and a mix of ramblers, split levels, and updated Craftsman style homes that reflect decades of real use.

Hartman Park is one of the anchors here. It is a 40 acre park with baseball and turf fields, tennis and pickleball courts, trails, and the Redmond Pool, and it draws families from across the area. If you have kids who play any kind of organized sport, you will probably spend time there regardless of where you live in Redmond. Living within walking distance of it is a genuine quality of life upgrade, not a marketing line.

## Schools and Why They Drive Demand

The neighborhood name is not accidental. Education Hill is served by the Lake Washington School District, which consistently draws strong reviews from families across the Eastside. I am careful not to quote ratings that shift year to year, but what I can tell you is that the schools in this area come up in almost every conversation I have with buyers considering Redmond. Parents ask about them early, and the answers tend to reinforce the interest rather than complicate it.

That reputation for strong public schools is one of the primary reasons homes on Education Hill hold their value well and tend to move quickly when priced right. Buyers know what they are getting, and they are willing to compete for it.

## What the Market Looks Like for Buyers

Homes on Education Hill range widely depending on size, age, and condition. You will find original construction from the seventies and eighties alongside homes that have been substantially updated or rebuilt. Lot sizes tend to be generous by Eastside standards, which matters to buyers who want outdoor space without going all the way out to Sammamish or Woodinville.

Inventory here moves. When a well priced home comes up in this neighborhood, it does not sit. Buyers who are serious need to be prepared: financing lined up, priorities clear, and someone in their corner who understands the neighborhood well enough to help them read a listing correctly before they walk through the door.

That is the part of this job I take seriously. Knowing whether a home is priced to reflect the lot or the finishes or the school boundary it sits in requires more than a spreadsheet. It requires knowing the street.

## Getting to Work from Education Hill

Redmond's location on the Eastside means commuters have real options. Access to SR 520 puts downtown Bellevue and Seattle within reach, and the local Microsoft and Amazon campuses are close enough that many residents can avoid the freeway entirely on their worst days. The Eastside's broader infrastructure continues to evolve, and Redmond is well positioned within it.

## Is Education Hill Right for You

If you are a family prioritizing schools and park access, this neighborhood deserves a serious look. If you are a buyer who values established neighborhoods over brand new construction, you will find more character here than in many of the newer developments going up elsewhere on the Eastside. And if you are a homeowner thinking about selling, the demand for this area is real and consistent, which matters when it comes to timing and strategy.

I grew up on the Eastside and have watched these neighborhoods change over decades. Education Hill has held onto what makes it work while the areas around it have shifted considerably. That kind of stability does not happen by accident.

If you are thinking about buying or selling on Education Hill and want to talk through what the market looks like right now, reach out to me directly. I would rather have a real conversation about your specific situation than send you a generic report. That is how this works best.

## Common Questions

### What makes Education Hill in Redmond a popular neighborhood for families?

Education Hill is served by the Lake Washington School District, which has a strong reputation across the Eastside. The neighborhood is also home to Hartman Park, generous lot sizes relative to other Eastside areas, and a quieter residential feel that appeals to families who want space without moving far from Redmond's core.

### How competitive is the real estate market on Education Hill?

Well priced homes on Education Hill tend to move quickly. Demand is driven by school district access and the neighborhood's established character. Buyers should come prepared with financing in order and a clear sense of priorities before they start touring.

### What types of homes are available on Education Hill in Redmond?

The housing stock on Education Hill is a mix of original construction from the seventies and eighties, updated ramblers and split levels, and some substantially renovated or rebuilt homes. Lot sizes tend to be larger than in many newer Eastside developments, which is part of what draws buyers to the area.

### How does Education Hill compare to other Redmond neighborhoods?

Education Hill has more established tree cover, older lots, and a quieter residential feel than some of the newer developments in Redmond. It sits at a slightly elevated position in the city, which gives parts of the neighborhood some views. It tends to appeal to buyers who want neighborhood character and school district access over brand new finishes.

# Lake Washington School District Choice and Tech Schools Explained

> How admission really works for choice schools and tech programs in Lake Washington School District, explained clearly for Redmond area families.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 9, 2026
Topic: Schools and family
Area: Redmond, Kirkland, Sammamish, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/choice-schools-and-tech-schools-in-lake-washington-school-district-how-admission-works/

One of the first questions I hear from families moving to Redmond or anywhere else in the Lake Washington School District is some version of: "We heard there are special schools you can apply to. How does that actually work?" It comes up constantly, and the honest answer is that the system is genuinely good but genuinely confusing if you don't know where to start.

Lake Washington School District (LWSD) runs what most districts don't: a real network of choice schools and specialized programs that go beyond your assigned neighborhood school. These aren't private schools or charters. They're public, tuition free, and open to any student who lives within the district. But getting in isn't automatic, and the timelines matter more than most families realize until they've already missed something.

## What "Choice School" Actually Means Here

In LWSD, a choice school is a public school with a specific instructional focus or philosophy that families opt into rather than being assigned to by address. You apply, and if there are more applicants than seats, admission is determined by lottery. Siblings of currently enrolled students typically get priority at the entry grade level, which is worth knowing if you have more than one child you're thinking about enrolling.

The district's choice options have shifted over the years, so it's worth going directly to the LWSD website to confirm what's currently available for each grade band. That said, the programs that have been consistently part of the choice landscape include environmental and STEM focused options, a Spanish and English dual language program at the elementary level, and the flagship STEM program at the high school level.

## The STEM School: What It Is and Who It's For

The most talked about piece of this is Tesla STEM High School, the district's science, technology, engineering and mathematics choice high school located in Redmond. It draws families from across the district, not just from one corner of it.

Tesla STEM isn't a vocational program in the traditional sense. The curriculum integrates science, technology, engineering and mathematics into a college prep framework using problem based learning. Students still take standard core courses. The difference is in how those courses connect to applied STEM projects and research, and in the culture of the school, which tends to attract students who are genuinely interested in building and making things rather than just consuming technology.

Admission to Tesla STEM is competitive, but not in the way a private school is competitive. There's no entrance exam or portfolio review for the lottery itself. You apply during the choice school enrollment window, and if demand exceeds capacity, a lottery is held. Where things get more selective is in specific pathways or courses within the school, some of which have prerequisites or teacher recommendations attached.

At the middle school level, LWSD also offers several choice schools with distinct instructional approaches, including options focused on environmental education, international studies, and arts integrated learning. None of these carry the same STEM only focus as Tesla at the high school level, but families should check the district's current choice schools page for the full list of what is available at each grade band, since programs do change.

## The Enrollment Calendar Is the Thing Most Families Miss

Choice school applications in LWSD typically open in early November for enrollment the following school year, with applications due around December 1. Lotteries are generally held in January, with families notified shortly after. That window is short, usually about a month, and it's easy to miss if you move to the area after it's closed.

If you're relocating to Redmond or Kirkland and your move happens to fall outside that window, your child's options for the current year may be limited to the neighborhood school. The choice school waitlists do move sometimes, but you shouldn't count on it. Families who are serious about a particular program tend to plan their move timing around the enrollment calendar, which sounds extreme until you realize how much these programs matter to some kids.

The district holds informational nights for choice schools, and I'd genuinely encourage families to attend rather than rely entirely on the website. The principals and program coordinators do a good job of explaining what the day to day experience actually looks like, which helps you figure out whether the fit is real or just appealing on paper.

## Neighborhood School vs. Choice School: The Real Tradeoff

Something worth saying directly: the neighborhood schools in LWSD are strong. This district consistently ranks among the top performing in Washington state, and a kid who goes to their assigned school is not getting a lesser education by default. The choice schools serve a specific purpose for families who want a particular environment or instructional approach, not for families who think the alternative is inferior.

The practical tradeoff with choice schools is transportation. Parents and guardians of students who attend choice schools are responsible for arranging their own transportation. The district does offer limited shuttle bus service to some choice schools in some cases, but it is not guaranteed and may involve a fee and its own lottery. Families should contact the specific choice school they are interested in to ask about what transportation options currently exist. For families in, say, the Sammamish area applying to a school in Redmond or Kirkland, the logistics are real and worth thinking through before the lottery, not after.

## What This Means When You're Choosing Where to Live

Some families deliberately choose a neighborhood based on its proximity to a choice school they're targeting. That's a reasonable strategy, but it comes with a caveat: admission isn't guaranteed. I've worked with buyers who planned their entire search around a specific program, didn't get the lottery slot, and then weren't wild about their neighborhood school. It's worth having a backup position on where you'd be happy if the choice school doesn't work out.

On the other side, there are buyers who assume their assigned school will be the thing that matters most, then discover their kid qualifies for or is passionate about a program across town. According to the district's own map, LWSD covers 76 square miles and serves the cities of Kirkland and Redmond, as well as about half of Sammamish, so "across town" can mean a real commute.

If schools are central to your housing search and you're narrowing down areas, it's worth a direct conversation with the district's enrollment office rather than relying on third party school rating sites. Those sites often lag behind changes in program availability, and they don't capture the culture and environment of a school, which is often what families are really trying to evaluate.

## A Few Practical Notes Before You Apply

You must be a resident of the Lake Washington School District to participate in choice school enrollment. The district boundaries don't perfectly match city limits, so if you're near the edges of Redmond, Kirkland, or Sammamish, it's worth verifying your address falls within LWSD and not a neighboring district before you plan around it.

Siblings of currently enrolled choice school students typically receive enrollment priority at the entry grade level. This is significant for families with more than one child: getting one kid into a program can meaningfully improve the odds for a younger sibling down the road. That said, sibling priority policies can vary by school, so it's worth confirming the specific policy with whichever program you're interested in.

Finally, the landscape of which specific schools carry which programs does change. New programs get added, some get restructured, and grade configurations shift. The district's official enrollment page is the right source, not what a neighbor told you worked three years ago.

## Common Questions

### Do you have to live in a specific neighborhood to apply to a choice school in LWSD?

No. Any student who lives within the Lake Washington School District boundaries can apply to any choice school, regardless of which neighborhood they live in. The lottery is open districtwide. The main thing to verify is that your home address actually falls within LWSD, since the district boundaries don't always align neatly with city limits.

### Is there an academic requirement to get into the STEM school?

For the lottery itself, no. Admission to Tesla STEM High School goes through the same choice school enrollment process as other choice schools, and a lottery determines placement when there are more applicants than seats. However, once a student is enrolled, some specific courses or pathways within the school may have prerequisites or teacher recommendations attached.

### What happens if we move to the area after the choice school enrollment window closes?

Your options for that school year may be limited to your assigned neighborhood school. Choice school waitlists exist and do move occasionally, but there's no guarantee. Families relocating with a strong interest in a specific program often try to time their move so they're enrolled in the district before the enrollment window opens, which typically happens in early November with applications due around December 1.

### Does the district provide transportation to choice schools?

Generally, parents and guardians are responsible for arranging their own transportation to choice schools. The district does offer limited shuttle bus service to some choice schools in some cases, but availability is not guaranteed and details vary by school and year. Contact the specific choice school you are interested in for current transportation information.

### If one of my kids gets into a choice school, does that help my younger child get in later?

Yes, sibling priority is a real factor in LWSD choice school enrollment. Siblings of currently enrolled students typically receive enrollment preference at the entry grade level during the application process, which improves the odds considerably compared to applying without any existing connection to the school. The specifics can vary by program, so it's worth confirming the sibling policy directly with the school you're interested in.

Prices are softer than a year ago, which is worth knowing when you write an offer.
