# Buying on the Sammamish Plateau: What to Know First

> A real local guide to Sammamish Plateau homes, neighborhoods, commute realities, schools, and tradeoffs from an agent who grew up in the area.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 21, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Sammamish, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/sammamish-plateau-homes-for-sale-neighborhood-guide/

A lot of buyers come to me asking about the Sammamish Plateau after hearing it has good schools, newer homes, and more space than you'd get closer to Bellevue. All of that is generally true. But the Plateau is also a specific kind of place, and it works better for some people than others. This guide is meant to give you an honest picture so you can decide if it fits what you're looking for.

## What "the Plateau" Actually Means

Sammamish sits on an elevated shelf of land east of Lake Sammamish, bordered roughly by Redmond to the north and Issaquah to the south. When people say "the Plateau," they usually mean the incorporated city of Sammamish, which became its own city in 1999. Most of the housing there was built between the mid 1980s and the 2010s, with a big wave of development happening in the 1990s and 2000s as the tech industry expanded eastward.

The result is a city that feels cohesive in some ways and sprawling in others. There's no real downtown, no main street with restaurants and coffee shops within walking distance of most neighborhoods. The commercial areas are concentrated along Issaquah, Pine Lake Road, around the Sammamish Town Center (which is still somewhat in development as a destination), and near the edges of the city where it connects to Redmond and Issaquah. If you picture a walkable urban neighborhood, the Plateau is not that.

## The Housing Stock: What You're Actually Looking At

Most homes on the Plateau are single family houses on lots ranging from around 5,000 square feet up to a quarter acre or more, depending on the neighborhood and when it was built. Earlier subdivisions from the late 1980s and early 1990s tend to have more modest lots and simpler exteriors. Homes built in the late 1990s and 2000s often run larger, with two car garages, formal dining rooms, and the kind of floor plan that was standard for that era: living room, family room, kitchen that opens to the back, primary suite upstairs.

You'll also find newer construction, particularly in the northern part of the city near Redmond, where infill developments and some planned communities have added townhomes and paired homes that attract buyers who want less maintenance without leaving the area entirely.

Lot sizes do matter here because they vary more than people expect. Some neighborhoods back up to wetlands or greenbelt, which gives you privacy but also limits what you can do with the yard. Others are tightly packed enough that you can hear your neighbors through the fence. Worth paying attention to when you're comparing listings.

## Neighborhoods Within Sammamish Worth Knowing

The Plateau covers a lot of ground, and not all of it feels the same.

**Trossachs and Klahanie** are two of the more established neighborhoods in the southern end of the city. Klahanie has a community association, trails, parks, and a shopping center with groceries and restaurants, which makes it feel more self contained than a lot of the Plateau. Trossachs sits nearby and tends to attract buyers who want larger lots and a slightly quieter setting. These areas feed into the Issaquah School District rather than Lake Washington School District, which matters to some buyers and not at all to others.

**Pine Lake** is a mid Plateau area centered around Pine Lake itself, with some homes that back to the water or are close enough to use the park there. It's a mix of older and newer construction and tends to be a bit more affordable than some of the newer build neighborhoods.

**Newer communities** in the northern part of the city sit closer to Redmond. These developments from the 2000s and 2010s have more contemporary finishes and tend to be priced higher. The tradeoff is that you're farther from the southern retail clusters and closer to the Redmond commute corridors.

**Inglewood Hill Road area** is worth mentioning for buyers who want something that feels a bit more rural. There are larger parcels out there, some with acreage, and it's a different feel from the dense subdivisions closer to the city center.

## The Schools Question

Schools drive a lot of the demand on the Plateau, so it's worth being precise about this rather than just saying the schools are good.

Sammamish is split mainly between two districts. The northern part is in the Lake Washington School District, whose high school on the Plateau is Eastlake High School. Much of the southern part, including Klahanie and Trossachs, is in the Issaquah School District, which includes Skyline High School in Sammamish. A small area on the east edge is in the Snoqualmie Valley School District. All of them have strong reputations in the region. Either way, you're in solid district territory, but the specific school your kids would attend depends on the address, and it's worth confirming that before you fall in love with a particular house.

## Commuting Off the Plateau

This is the part of the Sammamish conversation that deserves the most honest treatment. Getting on and off the Plateau is genuinely difficult during peak hours, and it has been for years.

The main routes down are 228th Avenue NE toward Redmond, SE 8th Street and similar corridors toward Bellevue, and the various ways down into Issaquah toward I 90. None of them are fast at 7:30 in the morning. The roads that exit the Plateau funnel a lot of traffic down fairly limited arterials, and there's no light rail or meaningful transit option that changes that picture right now.

If you're commuting to Redmond, Microsoft's campus is relatively close in distance, but the actual drive time is highly variable. If you're going to Bellevue or Seattle, add meaningful time, and plan around it. Remote or hybrid work has made the Plateau more livable for people who were previously grinding that commute five days a week. If you're back in the office full time, be honest with yourself about whether the drive fits your life.

## What People Trade Off to Live Here

Buyers who choose the Plateau are usually making a conscious decision to prioritize space, schools, newer construction, and a quieter residential environment over walkability, urban access, and commute convenience. That's a legitimate set of priorities for a lot of families. The neighborhoods are generally safe, the parks are well maintained, and there's a strong sense of community in many of the established subdivisions.

The things you give up: you will drive everywhere. Groceries, coffee, dinner, kids' activities, all of it involves getting in the car. The Town Center has been developing slowly and has added some options, but it's not a substitute for real urban walkability. And if you value proximity to Seattle for weekend life as much as weekday work, the Plateau puts some distance between you and that.

Price is the other honest variable. The Plateau commands a premium because of the schools and the housing quality, but pricing has moved around since the 2022 peak, so lean on recent comparable sales rather than headlines. Compared to Bellevue or Kirkland, you generally get more house for the money. Compared to Issaquah just to the south, the gap is smaller, and it varies a lot by neighborhood and home.

## A Few Practical Details That Actually Matter

The Plateau gets real weather in winter. Snow doesn't happen constantly, but when it does, getting off the hill gets complicated quickly. Worth thinking about if you have any kind of regular obligation that can't flex.

HOA situations vary significantly by neighborhood. Klahanie has an active one. Some neighborhoods have minimal or no HOA involvement. If HOA fees or rules matter to you in either direction, check each community individually rather than assuming.

Lots with wetland buffers can complicate additions or outbuildings. If you're buying with plans to expand, confirm the setbacks before you commit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Sammamish a good place to buy if I'm not in tech?

Yes. The city skews toward tech employment because of proximity to Microsoft and Amazon's Eastside offices, but the neighborhoods themselves are just neighborhoods. Plenty of residents commute to healthcare, trades, education, and other industries. The commute math is the same regardless of your employer; it's more about direction and distance than industry.

### How different are the northern and southern ends of the city?

More different than people expect. The northern end near Redmond runs newer on average, tends to be priced a bit higher, and has better access to Redmond's amenities. The southern end around Klahanie and Trossachs has a more established feel, larger trees, and connects more naturally toward Issaquah and I 90. School district boundaries also split along roughly this north, south line. If you have a strong preference for one district over the other, let that narrow your search geographically first.

### Are there condos or attached homes on the Plateau?

Not many. The Plateau is overwhelmingly single family detached housing. There are some townhome developments, particularly in newer pockets near the Redmond border, and a small number of condo communities, but this is not a place with a deep inventory of attached product. If you need that price point or that format, Issaquah, Redmond, or Bellevue will give you more options.

### What's the wildfire or natural hazard situation?

The Plateau itself is less exposed than more rural areas to the east, but it's not without risk. Some neighborhoods near forested edges or open space carry more fire exposure than dense subdivisions. Flooding isn't a widespread concern on the elevated portions of the Plateau, but properties near wetlands or creek corridors can have drainage issues. Worth a standard inspection and a look at any wetland designation on the parcel before closing.

### Do homes here tend to have good resale history?

Generally yes. The combination of school district quality and housing type has supported consistent demand over time. That said, the Plateau was not immune to the broader correction that hit the Eastside in 2022 and into 2023, and some buyers who purchased at peak 2021 and early 2022 prices are sitting on paper losses if they needed to sell quickly. Longer holds have done well historically, but short term timing risk is real here as it is anywhere.

## Common Questions

### Is Sammamish a good place to buy if I'm not in tech?

Yes. The city skews toward tech employment because of proximity to Microsoft and Amazon's Eastside offices, but the neighborhoods themselves are just neighborhoods. Plenty of residents commute to healthcare, trades, education, and other industries. The commute math is the same regardless of your employer; it's more about direction and distance than industry.

### How different are the northern and southern ends of the city?

More different than people expect. The northern end near Redmond runs newer on average, tends to be priced a bit higher, and has better access to Redmond's amenities. The southern end around Klahanie and Trossachs has a more established feel, larger trees, and connects more naturally toward Issaquah and I 90. School district boundaries also split along roughly this north, south line, so if you have a strong preference for Lake Washington versus Issaquah School District, let that narrow your geography first.

### Are there condos or attached homes on the Sammamish Plateau?

Not many. The Plateau is overwhelmingly single family detached housing. There are some townhome developments, particularly in newer pockets near the Redmond border, but inventory of attached product is limited. If that format or price point matters, Issaquah, Redmond, or Bellevue will give you more to choose from.

### What natural hazards should I think about in Sammamish?

The Plateau is less exposed than more rural areas to the east, but properties near forested edges carry more fire exposure, and parcels near wetlands or creek corridors can have drainage issues. A standard inspection plus a look at any wetland designation on the parcel is a reasonable starting point before closing.

### Do Sammamish homes hold their value well over time?

Historically yes, supported by school district quality and consistent demand from Eastside tech employment. That said, the Plateau followed the broader Eastside correction in 2022 and 2023, and buyers who purchased at peak 2021 or early 2022 prices took paper losses if they needed to sell quickly. Longer holds have generally done well, but short term timing risk is real.

# Klahanie Homes for Sale: A Real Buyers Guide

> Thinking about buying in Klahanie, Sammamish? Here is what the neighborhood actually looks like, who it suits, and what to expect from the housing market.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: August 13, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Sammamish, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/klahanie-homes-for-sale-community-guide/

## What Klahanie Actually Is

Klahanie is a planned community that sits in the southern part of what is now Sammamish, though for most of its history it was technically unincorporated King County. It was annexed by Sammamish on January 1, 2016, which matters less day to day than you might think, but it does explain why longtime residents sometimes still say "Issaquah" when they describe where they live. The Issaquah School District serves Klahanie regardless of the city boundary, so for families that is the practical thing to know.

The community was built out largely between the mid 1980s and the mid 1990s, so you are dealing with homes that are roughly 30 to 40 years old. That means you are past the newness premium, but also that things like roofs, HVAC systems, and kitchen finishes are going to be in various states depending on how each owner maintained the home. It is a range. Some homes have been well kept and nicely updated. Others have not been touched since Clinton was president.

## The Layout and How the Neighborhood Feels

Klahanie is organized around a central amenity core that includes the Klahanie HOA's two pools, tennis courts, and park areas. The trails connect through much of the neighborhood, and the bigger Issaquah Alps trail systems are a short drive away, which is genuinely one of the better things about living here. You can get on a real trail without getting in a car.

Most of the streets curve through wooded lots, and depending on where exactly a home sits, you can feel like you have a lot of privacy even on a relatively modest lot. Tree coverage is a real feature here, not just a marketing line. The tradeoff is that some homes deal with moss, gutter issues, and shade that limits what you can do with a yard. Worth thinking about if you have gardening in mind.

The neighborhood is mostly single family homes, though it also includes a meaningful number of townhomes, condos, and apartments. The dominant housing type is detached homes on lots ranging from roughly 5,000 to 10,000 square feet, sometimes larger on the more forested streets. You are not going to find a lot of the smaller lot density that newer Sammamish developments have brought in.

## Who Tends to Buy Here

Klahanie draws a lot of families because of the school district and the community infrastructure. The pools and courts give kids something to do close to home, and the trail access appeals to adults who want outdoor activity without a long drive. It also attracts people relocating from outside the area who are looking for a more established neighborhood feel rather than a brand new subdivision where every house looks the same and the trees are still saplings.

It is a reasonable commute corridor for people working in Bellevue, Redmond, or Seattle, though I would not call any of those drives trivial. Issaquah Fall City Road and Issaquah Pine Lake Road are the main arteries getting you out of the neighborhood, and at peak times they earn their reputation. Heading down into Issaquah to get on I 90 is how most people head west. If you are commuting to South Lake Union daily in a car, budget your time honestly.

## What the Homes Are Like

Most homes in Klahanie run between 1,800 and 3,500 square feet, with the larger homes on the more wooded streets further from the main entry points. Architecture is typical Pacific Northwest builder product from that era: lots of vaulted ceilings, skylights, two car garages, and layouts that feel a little formal by today's standards. Separate living and dining rooms that nobody uses for their original purpose anymore. Open concept was not the norm when these were built.

Basements are relatively common, which is not always the case in this part of the state. Full walkout basements exist on some of the sloped lots, which adds usable square footage without always being reflected prominently in listing data, so it is worth paying attention to actual finished square footage versus what automated estimates show.

Updates that add real value here tend to be kitchen and primary bath renovations, modernized electrical panels, and newer roofs. Composite decks have largely replaced the original wood ones that were rotting by the 2010s. If a home still has the original single pane windows, that is a negotiating point worth raising.

## The HOA and What It Covers

Klahanie has a homeowners association, and most homes in the community fall under it. The HOA maintains the common areas, the pool facilities, the trails, and the parks. Monthly fees are moderate compared to some newer master planned communities, though you should always verify current amounts directly because they adjust over time.

The rules are not unusually restrictive, but there are standards around things like exterior paint colors, fence styles, and keeping properties maintained. If you are someone who wants to paint your house a bold color or run a home based business with regular customer traffic, read the CC&Rs before you close.

## Schools

The Issaquah School District has a strong reputation and is one of the primary reasons families target this area specifically. Elementary school assignments within Klahanie depend on your exact address, so if a particular school matters to you, confirm the boundary before you go under contract rather than assuming. Challenger Elementary sits right in Klahanie on SE Klahanie Boulevard, but boundary lines have shifted over the years, so check the Issaquah School District's school locator for the exact address.

Challenger Elementary feeds Beaver Lake Middle School and then Skyline High School, but confirm the assignment for any specific address. These are consistently well regarded schools with strong extracurricular programs, which is a real draw for families who are relocating from competitive school districts elsewhere in the country.

## What You Pay and What You Get

Klahanie is not the cheapest way into the Sammamish or Issaquah market, but it also is not the most expensive. You are generally paying for an established neighborhood with real amenities and good schools, not for brand new finishes or a premium view. Homes that have been updated and maintained well command a notable premium over those that have not, which is more pronounced here than in newer subdivisions where everything starts at the same baseline.

Buyers sometimes find better value per square foot here than in some of the newer Sammamish neighborhoods further north, where land costs pushed prices up sharply. The offset is that you are buying an older home, so you need to go in with realistic expectations about what a preinspection will find and what deferred maintenance might look like.

Demand has historically been steady because the fundamentals are solid. Good schools, trail access, an actual community infrastructure, and a location that works for a lot of different commute directions. That does not mean homes sell instantly in every market condition, but it does mean Klahanie tends to hold value reasonably well relative to other areas in the same price bracket.

## Things Worth Knowing Before You Look

Some streets in Klahanie back up to or sit near SE Klahanie Boulevard, which carries more traffic than it might look like from the inside of the neighborhood. Street noise varies significantly by location. Worth driving the specific block at different times of day before you decide.

The forested lots are beautiful but they come with maintenance. Moss on roofs, debris in gutters, and trees that need regular attention are part of owning here. If you are used to a more manicured suburban setting, the ongoing yard work reality is different.

Finally, the trail system is a genuine asset. Klahanie has its own network of trails, and Grand Ridge Park, Tiger Mountain, and Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park are all a short drive away. If outdoor access is important to your quality of life, this neighborhood delivers on that in a real way.

## Common Questions

### Is Klahanie in Sammamish or Issaquah?

Klahanie is part of the City of Sammamish, which annexed the area effective January 1, 2016. However, it is served by the Issaquah School District, which is why many residents still associate it with Issaquah. For school purposes, think Issaquah. For city services, it is Sammamish, though many addresses still show Issaquah with the 98029 ZIP code.

### What is the Klahanie HOA like?

Klahanie has an active homeowners association that manages shared amenities including pools, tennis courts, parks, and trails. Fees are moderate compared to newer master planned communities, and the rules are reasonable but do cover things like exterior colors and property upkeep. Always read the CC&Rs before closing if HOA rules matter to your lifestyle.

### How are the schools in Klahanie?

Klahanie is served by the Issaquah School District, which has a strong overall reputation. Elementary school assignments depend on your specific address since boundaries have changed over the years, so confirm your school boundary before going under contract. Challenger Elementary, which is in Klahanie, feeds Beaver Lake Middle School and Skyline High School, but confirm the assignment for your exact address.

### What do homes in Klahanie typically look like?

Most are single family homes built between the late 1980s and early 2000s, ranging from roughly 1,800 to 3,500 square feet. Expect traditional Pacific Northwest builder layouts with vaulted ceilings, two car garages, and somewhat formal floor plans. Basements are relatively common. Condition and updates vary widely by home.

### How is the commute from Klahanie?

It is manageable but not effortless. Most residents take Issaquah Fall City Road or Issaquah Pine Lake Road down to I 90 in Issaquah to reach Bellevue or Seattle. At peak commute times those roads and the I 90 on ramps get backed up. If you are commuting to Bellevue or the Eastside, it is a reasonable drive. Commuting to downtown Seattle daily in a car takes patience.

### Are there trails and parks near Klahanie?

Yes, this is one of the real advantages of the neighborhood. Klahanie has an internal trail network, and Grand Ridge Park, Tiger Mountain State Forest, and Cougar Mountain Regional Wildland Park are all a short drive away.

# What Woodinville Living Is Really Like

> Thinking about moving to Woodinville, WA? Here is what daily life actually looks like, from the commute trade offs to the housing stock and local feel.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 7, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: Woodinville, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/what-woodinville-living-is-really-like/

People usually discover Woodinville one of two ways. Either they stumbled into wine country on a Saturday afternoon and started thinking, "I could live here," or they got priced out of Kirkland and Redmond and started looking east. Both groups end up in the same place, but they arrive with pretty different expectations. It's worth sorting out which version of Woodinville you're actually buying into.

## It Is Not Quite a Suburb and Not Quite Rural

Woodinville sits in that in between zone that is hard to categorize. You're not in a dense suburb with gridded streets and retail on every corner. You're also not out in the country. What you get is a town that still has a small city feel in some pockets, open space and horse properties a few miles in any direction, and a genuinely low rise downtown that fills up on weekends but stays pretty quiet through the week.

For some people that's exactly the appeal. You can have a third of an acre, a real backyard, and a neighborhood where your kids ride bikes without it feeling like a traffic experiment. For others, the lack of walkable density gets old fast. There's no serious main street with everyday retail the way Kirkland has, and running errands usually means getting in the car. That's just the reality of the place.

## The Wine Thing Is Real, But It's Mostly a Weekend Draw

Woodinville has more than 130 wineries and tasting rooms spread across the Hollywood District and surrounding areas. That sounds like a lot, and it is. On a sunny weekend in September it feels like the whole Eastside has descended on a few blocks near the Hollywood Schoolhouse.

If you live there, you quickly find your favorites and stop going on peak weekends. Locals tend to use the tasting rooms more like neighborhood hangouts than tourist attractions, which is a different experience than what visitors see. It's a genuinely nice thing to have nearby, especially if you entertain. But it doesn't shape your daily life the way people imagine before they move there.

## What the Housing Stock Actually Looks Like

Most of the established neighborhoods in Woodinville were built out through the 1980s and 1990s. You'll find a lot of two story colonials and split levels on lots that range from a quarter acre to well over an acre depending on where you are. Hollywood Hill, which sits up on a ridge north of downtown above the Sammamish River valley, has some of the larger lots and more spread out properties. Closer to the core of town around NE 145th Street and the NE 175th corridor, things get tighter.

Newer construction exists but it's not as abundant here as it is in, say, Sammamish or Issaquah. The parcels that were easy to develop got developed a while ago. What new construction does exist tends to come in as infill or small subdivisions tucked into areas that used to be larger single lots. Prices for those newer builds have generally tracked with the rest of the Eastside market, which means they're not cheap.

One thing worth knowing: if you're looking at properties farther out toward the Snohomish County line, some areas have well water and septic rather than city utilities. That's not necessarily a dealbreaker, but it comes with its own maintenance considerations and can affect financing depending on the lender.

## The Commute Conversation

This is where Woodinville asks you to make a real trade. There is no direct freeway access the way you'd have living right off I 405 in Bellevue or Kirkland. Getting to Redmond or Bellevue typically means taking SR 202 to Redmond and then connecting from there, or cutting through Bothell on SR 522 toward I 405.

In light traffic it's manageable. In the morning rush headed toward Redmond or Bellevue, it can stretch significantly. The people who make this work best are usually those who have some flexibility in their hours, work hybrid schedules, or have found a route that doesn't require them to hit the worst of it every day. Microsoft's Redmond campus is actually a reasonable drive from much of Woodinville, which is one reason you see a lot of tech workers who've made the trade off and decided the space and quiet are worth it.

There is bus service, and Sound Transit's Stride S3 Bus Rapid Transit line is currently under construction along SR 522 and NE 145th Street, running between Shoreline and Bothell with connecting service options toward Woodinville. As of fall 2026 the line is under active construction and Sound Transit's official schedule targets a 2028 opening. That should improve connectivity over time, but right now, if you're commuting to downtown Seattle or South Lake Union five days a week without driving, Woodinville makes your life noticeably harder than living closer in.

## Schools and Families

Woodinville falls in the Northshore School District, which covers a large swath of the area including Bothell and Kenmore. Woodinville High School has a solid reputation and the district overall performs well. For families, this is generally one of the boxes that gets checked without a lot of stress. Elementary school boundaries shift over time and specific feeder patterns matter depending on where in Woodinville you're buying, so it's always worth verifying current assignments through the district's school locator rather than assuming.

## What People Don't Expect Until They Live There

A few things come up consistently from people who've moved to Woodinville from denser Eastside cities.

The first is that it's dark. Not in a bad way necessarily, but if you're coming from a neighborhood with streetlights and a lit up commercial corridor nearby, the shift is noticeable. Some parts of the area, especially up on the hill or along the rural residential roads, get genuinely dark at night. Some people love this immediately. Others feel isolated by it for the first winter.

The second is the seasonal swing in activity. Summer and early fall in Woodinville are genuinely great. The weather cooperates, the tasting rooms are hopping, the Sammamish River Trail and the grounds around Chateau Ste. Michelle are well used and beautiful. Winter is quieter in a way that can feel peaceful or a bit flat depending on your temperament.

The third thing is that property maintenance takes more time when you have a larger lot. People who move from a townhouse or a smaller city lot sometimes underestimate what it takes to keep up with a third of an acre or more of yard, especially in a climate where things grow aggressively from April through October.

## How It Compares to Bothell and Kenmore

Bothell and Kenmore share a school district with Woodinville and sit nearby on the map, but they feel different in practice. Bothell, especially around Canyon Park and the downtown Bothell corridor, has more density and retail options. It also has better access to I 405, which matters a lot for commute purposes. Kenmore sits right on Lake Washington and has a waterfront character that Woodinville doesn't have.

Woodinville tends to have slightly larger lots on average and a quieter feel. If you're trying to decide between these areas, the honest question is whether you prioritize commute access and walkable retail on one hand, or space, quiet, and the wine country environment on the other. They're genuinely different trade offs rather than one clearly better option.

## Common Questions

### Is Woodinville actually walkable for daily errands?

Mostly no. There is a small commercial core near downtown Woodinville, and you can walk to a few things if you live close to it. But for the majority of the city, a car is necessary for groceries, pharmacy runs, and most day to day errands. If walkability is a priority for you, Woodinville will probably disappoint compared to Kirkland or Redmond.

### What are property sizes like compared to closer in Eastside cities?

Generally larger. Lots of a quarter acre to half an acre are common in established neighborhoods, and some areas, particularly up on Hollywood Hill and farther from the town center, have significantly larger parcels. This is one of the main reasons people choose Woodinville when they want more outdoor space and privacy without moving far from the Eastside job market.

### How does the Woodinville real estate market move compared to neighboring cities?

Woodinville tends to track closely with the broader Eastside market since it draws from the same buyer pool, primarily tech workers and families priced out of Kirkland or Redmond. It does not see quite the same intensity of competition on individual listings as some closer in cities, partly because the commute trade off eliminates some buyers. Larger or more rural properties can also sit longer than comparable homes in more connected locations.

### Are there good trails and outdoor recreation close by?

Yes, this is one of Woodinville's genuine strengths. The Sammamish River Trail runs through the area and connects toward Redmond to the south and Bothell to the west, making it a popular cycling and running route. The Chateau Ste. Michelle grounds add to the green, open feel of the area. The Tolt Pipeline Trail is also accessible for longer hikes and runs. If outdoor access is part of what you're looking for, Woodinville delivers pretty well on that.

### What should I know about utilities if I buy farther out from the town center?

Some properties in the more rural or semirural edges of Woodinville use well water and septic systems rather than city water and sewer. This is worth asking about specifically during your search. Well and septic properties can be perfectly functional, but they require more active maintenance and some lenders have additional requirements when financing them. Getting an inspection that includes the septic system and a water quality test for the well is standard practice and worth doing carefully.

# Northshore School District: What Buyers in Bothell and Woodinville Should Know

> A practical guide to Northshore School District for home buyers in Bothell and Woodinville, covering schools, boundaries, and what to watch for.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 5, 2026
Topic: Schools and family
Area: Bothell, Woodinville, Kenmore, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/northshore-school-district-guide-for-home-buyers-in-bothell-and-woodinville/

One of the first questions I get from families buying in Bothell or Woodinville is some version of: "What's the school situation here?" And it's worth a real answer, because Northshore School District is the kind of district where the details actually matter. The overall ratings are strong, but which school your kids attend depends entirely on where you buy, and those boundaries don't always line up the way people expect.

## The Short Version on Northshore

Northshore School District covers a large footprint across Bothell, Woodinville, Kenmore, and parts of Kirkland and Redmond. It's consistently one of the higher performing districts in King and Snohomish counties, and that reputation is one reason homes in these areas hold value the way they do. But "Northshore" isn't one school experience. It's a collection of schools with meaningfully different enrollment sizes, program offerings, and community feels depending on where you land.

The district runs 20 elementary schools, six middle schools, and four high schools. Most buyers I work with are primarily thinking about high school, but the elementary and middle school assignments matter too, especially if you're buying a house you plan to stay in for ten or more years.

## High Schools: The Four You'll Encounter

Northshore's four high schools are Bothell High, Inglemoor High, Woodinville High, and North Creek High. If you're buying in this area and you care about schools, these are worth understanding individually, not just as a group.

**Bothell High School** is one of the larger high schools in the district and draws from much of central and western Bothell. It has strong athletics and a broad range of programs. Families who have gone there tend to be proud of it, and it consistently posts solid graduation and college enrollment numbers.

**Inglemoor High School** sits in Kenmore but serves parts of Bothell. It's known for having strong academic programs and tends to draw a lot of attention from families who are comparison shopping between Northshore and Lake Washington School District to the south. If you're buying on the Bothell side near the Kenmore border, you may end up here.

**Woodinville High School** serves much of the Woodinville area and has a reputation for strong academics and a tight knit community feel given the more suburban, lower density nature of that part of the district. The school consistently performs well, and families in Woodinville tend to be very engaged.

**North Creek High School** is the newest of the four, opened in 2017 to relieve overcrowding across the district. It serves the Mill Creek adjacent areas and parts of Bothell north of the main corridors. Because it's newer, some buyers ask whether it's "as good" as the others. From what I've seen, it's well regarded and fully established at this point. The newer facilities are a real plus.

## The Boundary Question Nobody Thinks to Ask Until It's Too Late

Here's the thing about school boundaries in Northshore: they can shift. The district has adjusted boundaries multiple times over the years, especially around North Creek as enrollment balanced out after it opened. Buying a home assuming your kids will attend a specific school is a reasonable goal, but you should verify the current boundary directly with the district before you close, not just rely on what a listing says or what a neighbor tells you.

The Northshore School District website has an Address Look Up Tool where you can enter an address and get the current assignment. Use it. And if you're buying new construction in a growing area, ask explicitly whether the school assignment is locked in or subject to change as the development fills out.

I've seen buyers fall in love with a house partly because of the assumed school assignment, only to discover after moving in that the boundary had shifted in the most recent redistricting cycle. It's not common, but it happens enough that it's worth the two minutes to check.

## Programs That Cross Boundaries

Northshore has a few specialized programs that draw students from across the district rather than just from a specific attendance zone. The most notable is the district's highly capable cohort program, which groups advanced learners together at designated schools. If your child qualifies for highly capable services, their school placement may not follow the standard neighborhood assignment.

There are also choice transfer options within the district, though those come with no transportation guarantee and are approved on a space available basis. Families sometimes pursue transfers to a specific elementary school for a particular program or teacher reputation, but it's not something you can count on when making a buying decision.

## How Schools Affect Price in This Area

Northshore's reputation does get priced into homes, especially at the elementary level where parents feel the most day to day connection to the school their kid attends. I've seen streets just one or two blocks apart carry noticeably different interest levels based on which elementary school they feed into, even when the homes themselves are nearly identical.

Woodinville in particular tends to price at a slight premium compared to equivalent homes in parts of Bothell, and the school district perception is one factor in that, alongside the lower density feel and larger lots. It's not the only factor, but it's real.

If you're buying primarily for school access and you're working with a tight budget, it's worth looking carefully at where you land in the boundary map rather than assuming any address in Bothell or Woodinville gets you the same school outcome.

## What the District Doesn't Control

A district's quality can tell you a lot, but it doesn't tell you everything about whether a school is the right fit for your specific kid. Class sizes, the individual principal, extracurricular offerings, and the parent community at a given school can vary quite a bit even within a strong district. If school fit is a major priority for your family, visiting the actual school before you buy is worth doing, not just reading the ratings.

GreatSchools ratings are a starting point, but they weight test scores heavily and don't capture things like how a school handles kids who learn differently, the strength of its arts or technical programs, or how the staff communicates with families. Talk to parents in the neighborhood if you get the chance. That's usually more useful than any ranking.

## Snohomish vs. King County and the District Overlap

Northshore straddles the King and Snohomish county line, which is one of the things that makes it a little unusual. Parts of Bothell are in King County, parts are in Snohomish County, and the school district assignment doesn't follow that county line at all. This matters practically because property taxes, county services, and some administrative things differ by county even if the school is the same. Buyers sometimes assume the county determines the school district or vice versa. They're independent of each other.

If you're buying in the canyon road corridors or the areas north of SR 522, pay attention to which county the property sits in. It affects your tax bill more than your school assignment does.

## A Few Things Worth Verifying Before You Buy

* Confirm the school assignment directly through the Northshore district's Address Look Up Tool, not through the listing agent or Zillow.

* If highly capable or special education programs matter to your family, call the district's student services office and ask specifically how placement works, since it often doesn't follow neighborhood boundaries.

* For new construction, ask the builder whether boundary decisions for that development have been finalized with the district.

* Check when the last boundary adjustment happened in the area you're considering and whether another is being discussed.

Northshore is a genuinely good district and that's not just a talking point. But it's a big, diverse district with meaningful differences between schools and areas, and the families who research it carefully before buying tend to end up happier with their choice than those who assume it all works out the same regardless of address.

## Common Questions

### Does the whole city of Bothell fall under Northshore School District?

Most of Bothell is served by Northshore, but not all of it. A small portion of Bothell falls within the Edmonds School District, particularly in areas near the western edges of the city. Always verify the specific address rather than assuming the city name equals the district.

### Which high school serves most of Woodinville?

The majority of Woodinville feeds into Woodinville High School, but parts of the area closer to the Bothell border may be assigned to Bothell High or North Creek High. Use the district's Address Look Up Tool to confirm before making a decision based on a specific school.

### Is North Creek High School newer and does that affect its quality?

North Creek opened in 2017 and was built specifically to reduce overcrowding across the district. Being newer means the facilities are excellent. In terms of academic performance and community feel, it's considered on par with the other Northshore high schools at this point, though it has had less time to build traditions and alumni networks.

### Can I request a transfer to a different school within Northshore?

Northshore does have an intradistrict transfer process, but approvals are based on available space and are not guaranteed. If a specific school is critical to your decision, buying within that school's attendance boundary is the only reliable way to secure that assignment.

### How do Northshore home values compare to Lake Washington School District homes nearby?

Both districts are well regarded and both carry a premium compared to surrounding areas. Lake Washington tends to get slightly more attention from buyers focused on the Kirkland and Redmond markets, while Northshore is the primary driver in Bothell and Woodinville pricing. The gap between the two in terms of actual school outcomes is smaller than the difference in perception sometimes suggests.

About the author: Jack Macdonald grew up in Bellevue and helps buyers and sellers across Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish, Issaquah, Woodinville, and Bothell with Macdonald Group of Compass. Phone 425.941.6998. Website https://jackmacdonaldre.com/

## What this means if you're selling

At 3.2 months of supply, buyers have some choice but not a lot. Homes that are prepared and priced right still move; homes priced on hope tend to sit. Sellers averaged 98.5% of list price. ## What this means if you're buying

At 3.2 months of supply you have some room to look. That's more choice than a year ago, but well priced homes in the best locations draw competition. Homes averaged 98.5% of list price, so there is usually a little room to negotiate, but not much on the best homes. Prices are softer than a year ago, which is worth knowing when you write an offer.

# North Bend WA: What Living and Buying Here Is Really Like

> Thinking about buying in North Bend, WA? Here is what the housing market, commute, lifestyle, and tradeoffs actually look like from someone who knows the area.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 14, 2026
Topic: Neighborhood guides
Area: North Bend, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/north-bend-wa-what-living-and-buying-here-is-really-like/

People ask me about North Bend pretty regularly, and it usually comes from one of two places: either someone got priced out of somewhere closer in and is now doing the math on whether the commute is worth it, or they have been out there hiking or camping and thought, wait, could I actually live here? Those are pretty different starting points, and they lead to pretty different conversations.

So here is what I actually tell people.

## The drive into Bellevue or Seattle is the first thing to get honest about

North Bend sits at the base of the Cascades, about 30 miles east of Seattle on I 90. On a good day with no traffic, you can be in Bellevue in 30 to 35 minutes. But that version of the commute does not exist at 8 in the morning on a Tuesday. During peak hours, it regularly runs 45 minutes to over an hour each way, sometimes more when there is an incident on I 90 or snow on the pass affects traffic patterns even on the lower highway.

That is not a reason not to move there, but it is a real thing to sit with before you commit. People who make it work usually have some flexibility, remote work a few days a week, a partner who works locally, or a job that does not require traditional 9 to 5 hours. People who underestimate the commute and have no flexibility tend to burn out on it within a year or two.

There is no light rail serving North Bend, and there is no realistic near term prospect of it reaching there. King County Metro runs some bus service connecting North Bend to Issaquah and points west, but it is limited and not practical for everyone. You are largely driving.

## What the housing stock actually looks like

North Bend is a mix of things that do not always exist together this close to a major metro. You have neighborhoods with relatively affordable single family homes on standard subdivision lots, some larger parcels and horse properties out toward the edges of town, and a handful of newer construction developments that have gone up over the last decade as demand pushed east.

The older parts of town, closer to North Bend Way and downtown, have smaller homes from the 1970s to 1990s, some with a lot of character and some that need updating. The newer developments around areas like Edgewick Road and farther out toward Mount Si have more of the standard Pacific Northwest suburban look, larger square footage, open floor plans, two or three car garages.

If you want acreage, this area opens that up in a way that Issaquah or Sammamish simply cannot match at the same price. A half acre to a full acre lot is not unusual here. True rural parcels with several acres exist too, though those come with their own considerations around septic systems, well water, and fire risk zones.

Prices have come up significantly over the past several years, though they are still meaningfully lower than Issaquah or Sammamish for comparable square footage. The market has moved considerably, so I would encourage you to ask me for current figures before drawing any conclusions. Anything with significant acreage or mountain views commands a premium.

## The Mount Si shadow effect

This sounds like a small thing but it matters more than people expect. North Bend sits right up against the Cascade foothills, and certain parts of town, especially those tucked closer to Mount Si itself, see significantly less direct sunlight in winter. The mountains to the east and south block the low winter sun earlier in the afternoon than you might experience even 10 miles west. If you are someone who feels the Pacific Northwest winters hard, this is worth paying attention to when you look at specific lots and orientations. Not every part of North Bend is equally affected, but it is worth asking about for any property you get serious about.

## What the town itself offers day to day

North Bend has grown a lot but it is still a small town in feel and function. There is a downtown strip with restaurants, a couple of coffee shops, and some local businesses. Si View Community Center is a genuinely good local recreation facility with a pool, gymnasium, and programs run by the Si View Metropolitan Park District. North Bend Premium Outlets is right there if that matters to you.

For grocery runs, there is a QFC right in town on North Bend Way, and residents also plan shopping around trips closer to Issaquah for more variety. It is not a hardship, but it is a different rhythm than living in a more urban suburb where everything is five minutes away.

The outdoor access is legitimately exceptional. Mount Si trail, Little Si, Rattlesnake Ledge, the Iron Horse Trail, Twin Falls, the Snoqualmie River corridor, all within a short drive or even a walk from some neighborhoods. For people who structure their weekends around being outside, this is not a compromise, it is the whole point. That lifestyle pull is real and I have seen it drive purchasing decisions that might look unusual on paper but make total sense for the person making them.

## Schools and families

North Bend falls in the Snoqualmie Valley School District, which serves a wide area including Snoqualmie, Fall City, and surrounding communities. The district has a generally solid reputation and a strong community following. Mount Si High School is the high school that North Bend students feed into and has a good track record academically and in activities.

Families considering the area should look at where the specific elementary school boundaries fall for any given property, since the district covers a large geography and the experience can vary by school and by how rural the location is. Check the district's school locator for the exact address you are considering.

## Who tends to be happy here and who is not

The people who love North Bend tend to share a few things. They value space and quiet over convenience. They are okay with driving as a normal part of life. They spend meaningful time outdoors, not just occasionally but as a regular habit. And they have made peace with the fact that a spontaneous weeknight dinner in Capitol Hill is not happening.

The people who struggle with it usually underestimated how isolated it can feel in winter, overestimated how often they would get used to the commute, or had a life that required more access to the city than they realized. It is a real enough pattern that it is worth being honest with yourself about upfront.

One more practical thing: snow. North Bend gets meaningful snowfall most winters, and I 90 through the pass affects conditions in and around town even when Seattle sees nothing. If you are not experienced driving in snow or do not have an all wheel drive or four wheel drive vehicle, that is something to think about seriously before buying there.

## Is it a good investment?

It has appreciated well over the past decade alongside the broader Eastside market, and the relative affordability compared to areas closer in has kept demand real. But I would not buy in North Bend purely as a financial move. The people who do best there are the ones who genuinely want to be there, and that tends to take care of the investment side over time anyway. If you are buying it because you love the lifestyle and the location pencils out, that is a solid foundation. If you are buying it reluctantly hoping to move closer in a few years, the commute will probably wear you down before the appreciation pays off.

## Common Questions

### Does North Bend flood? I have heard the Snoqualmie River can be an issue.

Yes, flooding is a real consideration in parts of North Bend. The Snoqualmie River watershed does flood, and certain lower lying areas near the river or its tributaries have meaningful flood risk. The City of North Bend notes that a significant portion of its land area sits within the 100 year floodplain of the Snoqualmie River forks or local creeks. Before getting serious about any property there, check the FEMA flood map for that specific address and ask specifically about flood insurance requirements. Some properties carry required flood insurance that adds to monthly carrying costs and can complicate financing. A good inspector and your lender can help you understand what you are looking at for a specific address.

### Are there properties with acreage available in North Bend or is it mostly subdivisions now?

Both exist. There are established subdivisions with standard suburban lots, and there are also properties with half an acre, a full acre, or larger parcels, especially as you get farther from the downtown core toward the edges of the valley. True hobby farm or horse property setups exist in the surrounding area. The tradeoff is that more rural properties often mean well water and septic systems instead of city utilities, which adds inspection and maintenance considerations.

### How does winter driving affect life in North Bend compared to closer in suburbs?

Noticeably more. North Bend sits at a higher elevation and right at the base of the Cascades, so it sees more snow events than Issaquah or Bellevue. I 90 over Snoqualmie Pass frequently has chain requirements or closures in winter, and even lower elevation driving around town can be icy when the rest of the Eastside is just wet. Most longtime residents drive all wheel or four wheel drive vehicles. If you are not comfortable in winter conditions, this is worth taking seriously before committing to a property that far east.

### What is the difference between buying in North Bend versus Snoqualmie right next door?

They are close but feel different. Snoqualmie has a newer planned community area around Snoqualmie Ridge that is more polished and suburban in feel, with newer construction and a private golf club. North Bend has a more established small town character and a wider range of housing ages and styles. Prices are generally similar between the two, though Snoqualmie Ridge tends to have newer homes at higher price points. Which appeals to you comes down to whether you prefer a newer planned neighborhood or an older town with more variety.

### Is there anything walkable in North Bend or do you need a car for everything?

You need a car for most of daily life. That said, the downtown area along North Bend Way is reasonably compact and you can walk between a handful of restaurants, coffee shops, and small businesses if you are already there. The trail system is legitimately accessible on foot from certain neighborhoods, which matters to a lot of buyers. But for groceries, services, and most errands, you are driving. This is a car dependent town and the lifestyle works around that.

# Eastside Market Update: October 2026

> Eastside housing market for July to September 2026: median sale price, homes sold and days on market in Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah, North Bend, Fall City, with links to each city's full report.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 12, 2026
Topic: Market reports
Area: Eastside, Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah, North Bend, Fall City, Washington

Here's where the Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah, North Bend and Fall City housing markets stand for July to September 2026. Every number below is for single family homes over a rolling 3 month window, from the Redfin Data Center.

Bellevue's median single family sale price was $1.84 million for July to September 2026, up 2.3% from the same months last year. 266 single family homes sold (15.6% fewer than a year ago), and the median home spent 20 days on the market.

* Homes sold: 266 (last year: 315)

* Median days on market: 20

* Average sale to list price: 97.4%

* Months of supply: 3.1

## Issaquah

* Homes sold: 61 (last year: 69)

* Median days on market: 15

* Average sale to list price: 97.8%

* Months of supply: 2.9

[Full Issaquah market report](https://jackmacdonaldre.com/market-reports/issaquah/), with the trend chart and what it means if you're buying or selling.

North Bend's median single family sale price was $1.30 million for July to September 2026, down 1.6% from the same months last year. 34 single family homes sold (15.0% fewer than a year ago), and the median home spent 22 days on the market. North Bend is a small market, so a few sales can move these numbers a lot.

* Median sale price: $1,299,482 (same months last year: $1,319,998)

## Common Questions

### What are median home prices on the Eastside right now?

For single family homes sold July to September 2026, according to Redfin Data Center figures: Bellevue $1,841,766; Redmond $1,541,885; Kirkland $1,374,452; Issaquah $1,635,598; North Bend $1,299,482; Fall City $732,208.

# How Much House Can You Afford on the Eastside in 2026

> A realistic look at Eastside WA affordability in 2026: what income, down payment, and rates actually mean for your buying power in Bellevue, Kirkland, and beyond.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 14, 2026
Topic: Buying
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/how-much-house-can-you-afford-on-the-eastside-in-2026/

The question I hear most from buyers who are new to the Eastside isn't about neighborhoods or schools. It's a quieter, more personal one: *can I actually afford to buy here?* The honest answer is that it depends on a few specific numbers, and getting clear on those before you start touring homes will save you a lot of frustration.

## What Lenders Look At First

The standard starting point is your debt to income ratio. Lenders typically want your total monthly debt payments, including your future mortgage, to stay under 43 to 45 percent of your gross monthly income. Some loan programs allow a bit higher, but 43 percent is a reasonable ceiling to plan around.

So if your household brings in $20,000 per month before taxes, your maximum monthly debt load in a lender's eyes is somewhere around $8,600. After accounting for a car payment, student loans, or credit cards, the room left for a mortgage payment is often smaller than buyers expect.

The other number lenders weigh heavily is your credit score. A score above 740 typically gets you the best rate tiers. Below 680, you will still find financing, but the rate premium adds up meaningfully over a 30 year loan.

## What Rates Are Actually Doing to Your Buying Power

Rates matter enormously on the Eastside because the loan amounts here are large. The difference between a 6.5 percent rate and a 7.5 percent rate on a $900,000 loan is roughly $600 per month in payment. That same $600 per month, if you ran the math backwards, represents about $80,000 to $90,000 in purchasing power. Which means a buyer who qualified for $1.1 million when rates were 6 percent might genuinely only reach $950,000 to $1,000,000 at 7.5 percent, even if their income hasn't changed at all.

In early 2025, 30 year fixed rates were hovering in the high 6s to low 7s for conventional loans. Where they land through 2026 is genuinely uncertain, but planning around a 7 percent rate is a reasonable conservative assumption right now. If rates improve, your position improves. Build your budget around today's rates, not optimistic projections.

## What Prices Look Like Across the Eastside

The Eastside is not one market. Bellevue proper, especially west of I 405 near downtown, runs significantly higher than areas like Bothell, Kenmore, or parts of Issaquah. Here's a rough sense of where median single family prices have been landing by area:

* **Bellevue (west side, closer to downtown):** Median prices regularly exceed $1.5 million. Entry level detached homes are scarce below $1.2 million.

* **Kirkland:** Prices vary sharply by location. Totem Lake and Kingsgate are more accessible than Houghton or Bridle Trails, which push well above $1.5 million for anything updated.

* **Redmond:** The tech employment concentration keeps demand steady. Detached homes in good school zones frequently sit in the $1.1 to $1.5 million range.

* **Sammamish:** Large lots and newer construction attract families, but prices have followed demand. Most detached homes run $1.2 million and up.

* **Issaquah and Maple Valley:** Maple Valley offers real price relief, with an August 2026 NWMLS median house price around $755,000. Issaquah runs higher, with a median house price around $1.4 million that month. Commute tradeoffs are real in both.

* **Bothell and Woodinville:** Bothell is one of the better entry points on the Eastside perimeter, with an August 2026 NWMLS median house price around $1.1 million. Woodinville runs higher, closer to $1.4 million, reflecting its larger lots.

These are general ranges, not current listings, and they shift with inventory and season. But they give you a realistic frame for where your number needs to land.

## How Down Payment Affects the Equation

On the Eastside, the down payment conversation is more complicated than just hitting 20 percent. A 20 percent down payment on a $1.2 million home is $240,000. That is a significant amount of liquid capital, and a lot of buyers, including well paid tech workers who are relatively new to the area, don't have that sitting in a checking account.

There are legitimate options below 20 percent. Conventional loans allow as little as 3 percent down on primary residences for first time buyers and certain programs (5 percent for most other buyers), though you will pay private mortgage insurance until you reach 20 percent equity. Jumbo loans, which kick in above the conforming loan limit ($1,063,750 for a single family home in King County for 2026, though this adjusts annually), have stricter requirements. Many jumbo lenders want 20 percent down and stronger reserves.

One pattern I see regularly: buyers come in with a solid income but limited down payment. They can qualify for the payment, but the loan program options narrow. If you are in that position, talking to a lender before you start touring is worth doing, not to get preapproved necessarily, but just to understand what programs you actually qualify for.

## A Realistic Income to Price Benchmark

A rough rule of thumb is that most buyers stay comfortable borrowing between 3 and 4 times their gross annual household income. At 4 times, payments get tight and there is less room for property taxes, maintenance, or anything unexpected.

On the Eastside, property taxes on a $1.2 million home typically run somewhere between $9,000 and $13,000 per year depending on the city and school district levies (Bellevue's most common 2025 rate was about $7.33 per $1,000 of assessed value, or roughly $8,800 on a $1.2 million home). That is roughly $750 to $1,100 per month on top of your mortgage principal and interest. Add homeowner's insurance and potentially HOA fees if you are buying in a planned community, and the gap between what a lender approves and what feels manageable in daily life becomes clearer.

A household income of around $250,000 to $300,000 per year puts buyers in realistic territory for the $1 million to $1.3 million range with a meaningful down payment. At $200,000 household income, the math is tight at those prices, and Bothell, Maple Valley, or condos and townhomes closer in become more sensible anchors for a search.

## The Condo Option Worth Taking Seriously

Condos on the Eastside get overlooked by buyers who have their heart set on a detached home, but they are worth understanding as a real entry point. In Bellevue's downtown core and along the 116th corridor, condos can be found in the $500,000 to $900,000 range depending on size and building. Kirkland's waterfront and downtown areas have condos too, though pricing there reflects the location premium.

The tradeoff is HOA fees, which in newer high rise buildings with amenities can run $800 per month and often well over $1,000. That eats into affordability in a way that doesn't show up in the purchase price. Run the full monthly cost number before assuming a condo is automatically more affordable than a townhome or small detached house in a more suburban location.

## What Actually Makes the Eastside Worth the Price to Most Buyers

I want to be direct about this because it matters for how you think about the affordability question. The Eastside carries a price premium for real reasons: the concentration of tech employment, the quality of public schools in districts like Bellevue, Lake Washington, and Issaquah, the access to outdoor recreation without leaving the metro area, and comparatively low crime rates in most of these cities.

For buyers who work at Microsoft, Amazon, Google, or one of the dozens of mid size tech companies clustered around the SR 520 and I 405 corridors, paying a premium to live close to work is a reasonable tradeoff. For buyers who could work remotely from anywhere, or whose employer is in Seattle rather than on the Eastside, the calculus is worth examining honestly before stretching your budget here instead of somewhere cheaper.

## The Number to Know Before You Start

Before you look at a single listing, I'd encourage you to figure out three specific numbers: your maximum monthly payment including taxes and insurance, your available down payment, and your total liquid reserves after closing (lenders want to see 3 to 6 months of mortgage payments in the bank after you close, especially on jumbo loans). Those three numbers, run through a lender, will give you a purchase price ceiling that means something, rather than a Zillow estimate that doesn't account for your actual financial picture.

The Eastside is expensive. It has been for years, and nothing on the horizon suggests a dramatic reversal. But knowing your real number, not a hopeful guess, is how buyers here avoid spending six months touring homes they cannot actually buy.

## Common Questions

### What counts as a jumbo loan on the Eastside and why does it matter?

A jumbo loan is any mortgage above the conforming loan limit, which in King County is $1,063,750 for a single family home in 2026 (this adjusts annually, so confirm the current limit with your lender). Because many Eastside purchases need a loan above that amount, a lot of buyers end up in jumbo loan territory without realizing it. Keep in mind the limit applies to the loan, not the price, so with 20 percent down you can stay conforming on a purchase up to roughly $1.33 million. Jumbo loans typically require a 20 percent down payment, stronger credit scores, and more cash reserves than conventional conforming loans. This is a meaningful practical difference, not just paperwork.

### Are there first time buyer programs that work at Eastside price points?

Most first time buyer assistance programs have income caps, and some (like ARCH's East King County program) also cap the purchase price, which makes them harder to use in Bellevue or Kirkland, where median home prices exceed $1 million. The Washington State Housing Finance Commission does offer programs, but you'll want to check their current limits against actual Eastside prices. Condos, townhomes, and lower priced areas are where those programs are most usable, which is another reason buyers on a tighter budget look there first.

### How much should I have in reserves after closing on an Eastside home?

Beyond your down payment and closing costs, most lenders on jumbo loans want to see 6 to 12 months of mortgage payments in liquid assets after closing. On a $1.2 million purchase, that can mean keeping $60,000 to $100,000 in accessible accounts even after you've closed. This surprises buyers who have spent everything they had on the down payment and are otherwise well qualified on income.

### Does it make more financial sense to buy in Bothell vs Bellevue if I can stretch to either?

It depends on where you work and what you actually use day to day. If your office is in Redmond or Bellevue, living in Bothell adds meaningful commute time, especially on I 405 during peak hours. But you can often get significantly more house, a larger lot, and newer construction in Bothell for a price that is $200,000 to $400,000 less than a comparable Bellevue home. For families who are less tied to proximity to Bellevue's urban core, Bothell often delivers more for the dollar.

### How much do property taxes vary across Eastside cities?

Meaningfully. Effective property tax rates across King County cities tend to cluster between roughly 0.75 and 1.1 percent of assessed value (Bellevue sits near the low end, at about $7.33 per $1,000 in 2025), but the specific rate in your area depends on the city, the school district levies in effect, and any special levies voters have approved. The difference between a 0.85 percent rate and a 1.1 percent rate on a $1.2 million home is about $3,000 per year, which is roughly $250 per month. It is worth asking your agent or lender to pull the actual tax history on any home you are seriously considering.
