# First Time Home Buying on the Eastside: A Real Step by Step Guide

> A practical, honest guide to buying your first home on the Eastside of Seattle, from financing basics to closing day, written by a local Bellevue area agent.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 11, 2026
Topic: Buying
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/first-time-home-buying-on-the-eastside-step-by-step/

Most people who are buying their first home on the Eastside come in thinking the process is more straightforward than it turns out to be. Not because it's impossibly complicated, but because there are a lot of moving pieces that nobody explains clearly until you're already in the middle of them. This guide tries to fix that.

## Before You Look at a Single Listing

The first thing worth saying is that browsing Zillow before you've talked to a lender is the wrong order of operations. It's very easy to fall in love with a house in Kirkland or Sammamish and then discover your actual budget is 15 or 20 percent lower than what that house costs. That's a lousy way to start.

Getting preapproved early does a few things. It tells you what you can actually borrow, which shapes everything else. It also tells you where your credit stands and whether anything needs to be cleaned up before you make an offer. On the Eastside, where good homes in the $700k to $1.1M range often see multiple offers within days of listing, sellers take preapproval seriously. An offer without one rarely gets a second look.

One thing first time buyers sometimes confuse: prequalification is not the same as preapproval. Prequalification is basically a rough estimate based on what you tell the lender. Preapproval means the lender has actually verified your income, assets, and credit. Get the real thing.

## What Kind of Loan Actually Makes Sense Here

The Eastside's price ranges put a lot of homes above conventional conforming loan limits, which means you may end up looking at jumbo financing. Jumbo loans have their own underwriting rules, and they typically require a larger down payment, often 20 percent, and stronger reserves in the bank after closing. If your budget is putting you into Bellevue, Redmond, or Kirkland proper, it's worth asking your lender specifically how jumbo loans work and whether that's where you'll land.

For buyers who do fall within conforming limits, conventional loans with 5 or 10 percent down are common. FHA loans are an option too, though the loan limits and mortgage insurance structure make them less common at higher price points. Washington State Housing Finance Commission also runs some down payment assistance programs worth looking into if you're genuinely stretching to make the numbers work.

One honest note: a 3 percent down loan sounds attractive, but in a market where sellers sometimes choose between multiple offers, a buyer putting down 20 percent signals financial strength in a way that matters. It's not always decisive, but it's not nothing either.

## Figuring Out Where on the Eastside You Actually Want to Live

This is where local knowledge matters more than most people realize. The Eastside is not a monolith. Bellevue and Kirkland have older housing stock in many areas, smaller lots, and more walkable pockets near downtown cores. Sammamish and Issaquah tend to have newer construction, bigger lots, longer drives to get anywhere, and very different day to day rhythms. Woodinville and Bothell skew larger lots, more space, and a longer commute if you're heading into Seattle or downtown Bellevue regularly.

The commute question is real. If you're working in Seattle and trying to cross the lake, I 90 and SR 520 are not interchangeable. SR 520 tolls add up. The traffic patterns at different times of day are different. Where you land on the Eastside genuinely affects your commute in ways that a map doesn't show you.

School districts matter too, and on the Eastside the lines are drawn in ways that don't always follow intuition. Bellevue School District, Lake Washington School District, and Issaquah School District all have strong reputations, but specific schools within those districts vary. A house two blocks from another house can be in a different school boundary. If schools are a priority, verify the exact address against district maps before you get attached to a property.

## Making an Offer in a Competitive Market

On the Eastside, the market for well priced homes in desirable areas tends to move fast. A home listed on a Thursday often has offers due by Monday. That's not universal, and it varies by price point and neighborhood, but you should expect that pace on anything priced reasonably in a strong location.

What makes an offer competitive beyond price? Earnest money is one lever. A larger earnest money deposit signals commitment. Inspection timing matters too: some buyers waive inspection contingencies entirely in hot markets, which is a significant risk, while others shorten the inspection period to 5 days rather than 10 to show flexibility without fully giving up protection. Escalation clauses, where your offer automatically increases up to a ceiling if there are competing offers, are common here and worth understanding before you need to use one.

The financing contingency is another thing sellers pay attention to. If your financing is very solid and you have a strong preapproval, there's sometimes room to shorten or modify that contingency window, though you should never waive it without understanding exactly what you're giving up.

## The Inspection: What to Actually Do With It

This is an area where first time buyers sometimes overcorrect in both directions. Some people treat every item on an inspection report as a reason to cancel. Others are so afraid of losing the deal that they ignore things they shouldn't.

Most Eastside homes, especially anything built before the late 1990s, will have inspection findings. Some are genuinely important: the condition of the roof, evidence of water intrusion, the age and condition of the furnace and water heater, the electrical panel type. Others are routine maintenance items that every older home has and that shouldn't be alarming.

The inspection period is your window to get real information and make a real decision. Use it. Hire an inspector who will let you walk the house with them. Ask questions. And then think clearly about what you're looking at: is this a problem that affects your safety or the home's integrity, or is this routine wear?

## Closing Costs: The Number People Forget to Budget For

First time buyers often budget carefully for the down payment and then get surprised by closing costs. On the Eastside, closing costs for a buyer typically run somewhere in the range of 1.5 to 3 percent of the purchase price, depending on loan type, lender fees, and how the deal is structured. On a $900,000 home, that's $13,500 to $27,000 on top of your down payment. You need that money liquid and ready.

What's included? Loan origination fees, appraisal, title insurance, escrow fees, prepaid homeowners insurance, prepaid property taxes, and sometimes points if you're buying down your interest rate. Your lender is required to give you a Loan Estimate early in the process that breaks all of this down. Read it carefully and ask about anything that isn't clear.

## Between Mutual Acceptance and Closing

Once a seller accepts your offer, you're in what's called the mutual acceptance period, typically 30 days in Washington though it can vary. During this time, your lender is doing their full underwriting, the title company is researching the property's ownership history, and you're completing your inspection.

A few things to be careful about during this stretch: do not make any large purchases on credit, do not change jobs if you can avoid it, and do not move money around between accounts in ways that will be hard to document. Lenders reverify your financial situation right before closing, and changes that affect your debt to income ratio or deposit history can create last minute problems.

You'll also do a final walkthrough of the home, typically in the day or two before closing. This is to confirm the property is in the agreed upon condition, not a time to negotiate new items. If something has changed since inspection, that's the time to flag it.

## A Few Things Nobody Tells You Until After

Property taxes on the Eastside are meaningful. King County has one of the higher effective tax rates in Washington, and on a home priced above $800,000, you should factor that into your monthly carrying cost honestly. Your lender's estimate will include this, but make sure you're looking at the actual current assessed value, not what the seller paid several years ago.

HOA dues are common in newer Eastside developments and planned communities, particularly in Sammamish and parts of Issaquah and Redmond. They can range from modest to surprisingly high. Always find out what the dues are, what they cover, and what the reserve fund looks like. A low due is less meaningful if the association is underfunded and a special assessment is coming.

Finally: the Eastside has a lot of new construction, and buying new is a different process than resale. Builder contracts are not the same as standard purchase and sale agreements, and builders generally don't negotiate the same way private sellers do. If you're considering new construction, it deserves its own research rather than assuming the process is identical.

## Common Questions

### How much do I actually need saved before buying a home on the Eastside?

At minimum, you need your down payment plus closing costs plus some cushion left over. Closing costs for buyers in Washington typically run 1.5 to 3 percent of the purchase price, so on a $900,000 home you might need $13,000 to $27,000 beyond your down payment. Lenders also want to see reserves after closing, meaning money still in the bank, so plan for that as well. The exact number depends on your loan type and purchase price, but anyone telling you that you only need the down payment is leaving out a significant chunk.

### Do I need 20 percent down to buy on the Eastside?

No, but it helps in competitive situations. Conventional loans allow as little as 3 percent down for qualifying first time buyers, and FHA allows 3.5 percent. That said, many Eastside homes fall into jumbo loan territory, which typically requires 20 percent. And in multiple offer situations, a larger down payment does signal financial strength to sellers. If 20 percent is not realistic right now, that doesn't disqualify you, but you should understand how your offer might be perceived in a competitive situation.

### How long does it usually take from starting the process to closing?

Getting your financing in order and finding a house can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on how competitive the areas you're targeting are and how quickly you find something that fits. Once you have a signed purchase agreement, closing in Washington typically takes around 30 days. In practice, budget two to four months from serious start to keys in hand, and longer if you're in a price range where inventory is limited.

### What's the biggest mistake first time buyers make on the Eastside specifically?

Underestimating how fast things move. A lot of first time buyers want to take their time making decisions, which is completely understandable for a purchase this large. But on well priced homes in areas like Kirkland, Redmond, or central Bellevue, you may have two or three days to decide and submit a competitive offer. The buyers who succeed are the ones who have done enough homework ahead of time that they can move confidently when the right place shows up, not the ones who are still figuring out their financing or criteria when the listing goes live.

### Is it worth waiving the inspection contingency to win an offer?

This is genuinely a risk management question, not a yes or no. Waiving inspection entirely means you're agreeing to take the home in whatever condition it's in, and if something significant comes up, you own it. That said, many buyers in competitive Eastside markets do take this step, particularly on newer homes or when they've done a preinspection before offering. A middle path is shortening the inspection period rather than eliminating it, which shows sellers you're serious without fully giving up your ability to know what you're buying.

# Selling an Inherited Home on the Eastside: Where to Start

> Inherited a house in Bellevue or on the Eastside? Who can sign, protecting the home, belongings, fix up or sell as is, and the tax questions to ask first.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 21, 2026
Topic: Selling
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/selling-an-inherited-home-on-the-eastside-where-to-start/

The call usually starts the same way. Someone's parent has passed, there's a house in Bellevue or Kirkland or out in the valley full of forty years of life, and three siblings in three different states are wondering what they're supposed to do first. Nobody wants to make a mistake, and nobody wants it to drag on for a year.

There is no single right order for every family, but there is a sensible one. Here is how I'd walk through it if it were my own family.

## Figure out who is allowed to sell the house

Before you pick an agent, a price or a listing date, you need to know who has the legal authority to sign. That depends on how the house was held when the owner died.

If the home goes through probate, the court appoints a personal representative, the person most people call the executor. In Washington, when the court grants that person nonintervention powers, they can sell estate property without going back to the judge for an order (RCW 11.68.090). That makes the sale itself work a lot like a normal one.

If the house was in a living trust, the trustee usually handles it. And if the owner recorded a transfer on death deed, the home passes to the named beneficiary outside of probate entirely. Your estate attorney will tell you which of these applies. Getting that answer first saves weeks later, because a buyer's title company will ask exactly the same question.

## Protect the house while it sits

An empty house needs more attention than people expect. Keep the power, heat and water on so pipes don't freeze in a cold snap. Have someone check on it every week or two, bring in the mail and make sure it looks lived in.

Call the homeowner's insurance company too. Many policies treat a vacant home differently than an occupied one, and you want to know where you stand before something happens, not after.

## Pick one point person for the family

The sales that go smoothly almost always have one person who talks to the attorney, the agent and the vendors, then shares updates with everyone else. That doesn't mean one sibling makes every call. It means decisions get made in one place, in writing, with everyone seeing the same numbers.

When I work with a family, I send the same updates, comps and offers to every heir who wants them. Nobody should feel like they're finding out secondhand.

## Sort out the belongings before you list

This is usually the hardest part, and not because of the work. Start with what family members want to keep, and give people a real deadline so it doesn't stall. Photograph anything sentimental that nobody has room for.

After that, an estate sale company can sell furniture and household items, donations can take a lot of what's left, and a clean out crew can handle the rest in a day or two. The order matters: estate sale first, then donations, then the final haul. I'm happy to connect families with people my clients have liked.

## Decide: fix it up or sell it as is

There are two honest paths here, and either can be the right one.

Selling as is is simpler and faster. Fewer decisions, no contractors, and buyers know what they are getting. Prepping first takes more time and money up front, usually paint, yard work, deep cleaning and small repairs, and it often brings a stronger price.

The way to decide is with real numbers. I walk the house and price both options: what it could sell for today, and what it could sell for after a short list of fixes, with conservative costs for each. Then the family chooses based on money, time and how much energy everyone has left.

Two different homes, shown to illustrate the choice.

## Know the basic tax questions to ask

I'm not a CPA, and this is where you want one. But these are the questions families end up asking, so it helps to know them going in.

The IRS generally sets the tax basis of inherited property at its fair market value on the date of death. That is why many CPAs ask for a value as of that date. Washington's real estate excise tax does not apply to inheriting a home, but it does apply when an heir sells to an outside buyer, according to the Washington rule on inheritance transfers. Your CPA can tell you what all of that means for your situation.

If your CPA wants a sense of the market around the date of death, I can pull what similar homes nearby sold for around that time. Some will still want a formal appraisal, and that is their call.

## Price it off what actually sold

Inherited homes are often priced emotionally in both directions. Some families want to hold out for what the house meant to them, and some just want it gone. The fix for both is the same: look at what similar homes near you actually sold for in the last few months, then adjust for condition. I show every heir the comps behind the number, so the price is something the whole family can agree on.

From there, the sale itself runs much like any other: photos, showings, offers, inspection and closing. The main differences are who signs and how many people need to stay in the loop. For family members who live out of state, signing can usually be arranged so nobody has to fly in.

Sources: [RCW 11.68.090](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=11.68.090), [Washington rule on inheritance and excise tax](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/washington/WAC-458-61A-202), [IRS: Gifts and inheritances](https://www.irs.gov/faqs/interest-dividends-other-types-of-income/gifts-inheritances/gifts-inheritances), [King County Law Library on transfer on death deeds](https://kcll.org/from-the-director-october-2023/). General information only, not legal or tax advice. For the full rundown, see [how I help with inherited and estate homes](https://jackmacdonaldre.com/inherited-homes/).

## Common Questions

### Can we list an inherited house before probate is finished?

Often yes. Once the court appoints a personal representative and grants nonintervention powers, they can usually sell without waiting for the estate to close. Your estate attorney will confirm the timing for your situation.

### Do all the heirs have to sign?

It depends on how the house is held. If a personal representative or trustee has authority, they typically sign for the estate or trust. If the heirs own the house directly, each owner usually signs. Your attorney and the title company will confirm who needs to sign.

### What happens to the stuff left in the house?

Family keeps what they want first, then an estate sale company, donations and a final clean out handle the rest. Doing it in that order usually gets the house ready to list fastest.

### Should we sell an inherited house as is?

Sometimes. Selling as is is simpler and faster, while a short list of fixes often brings a stronger price. The best way to decide is to price both options with real numbers before choosing.

About the author: Jack Macdonald grew up in Bellevue and helps buyers and sellers across Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish, Issaquah, Woodinville, and Bothell with Macdonald Group of Compass. Phone 425.941.6998. Website https://jackmacdonaldre.com/

# How to Price Your Home Right on the Eastside

> Pricing your Eastside home correctly from day one matters more than most sellers realize. Here is how to think through it clearly before you list.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 16, 2026
Topic: Selling
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/how-to-price-your-eastside-home-in-today-s-market/

## The number you pick on day one matters more than anything else you do

Sellers spend weeks on paint colors, staging, and landscaping. That stuff matters. But the single biggest lever you have as a seller is the price you put on the home when it hits the market. Get that right and everything else gets easier. Get it wrong and you are fighting uphill from the moment you go live.

Pricing on the Eastside is not a simple exercise. You are dealing with a market where Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish, Issaquah, Woodinville, and Bothell all behave differently, sometimes block by block. A price that would be aggressive in one zip code might be conservative in a neighborhood two miles away. That granularity is where the real work happens.

## What a real pricing analysis actually looks at

Most sellers have heard of comparables, the recent sold homes that form the foundation of any pricing conversation. But pulling comps is not just grabbing the three highest sales in your zip code and averaging them. The honest version is more selective and more demanding.

The comps that matter most are homes that a buyer would genuinely have considered alongside yours. Same general location, similar square footage, similar lot size, similar condition and finish level, and sold recently enough that the data is still relevant. On the Eastside right now, I give the most weight to sales from the last 60 to 90 days. Anything older than that starts to reflect a different market moment.

Within that pool of comps you have to make adjustments. A home with a three car garage is worth more than one with a two car garage on the same street. A south facing backyard matters in some neighborhoods. A busy arterial behind the fence matters almost everywhere. These are not big abstract numbers. They are specific line items that you can defend in a negotiation.

Active listings also belong in the conversation. They tell you what your competition looks like to buyers right now, not six months ago. If there are three similar homes sitting unsold at a price point, that is a signal worth paying attention to before you decide where to list.

## Why the Eastside is not one market

One thing that trips sellers up is treating the Eastside as a single uniform place. It is not. Bellevue has consistently strong buyer demand and relatively tight supply, particularly in neighborhoods close to downtown. Kirkland Waterfront carries a premium that nonwaterfront Kirkland does not. Sammamish tends to attract families who want newer construction and larger lots and are willing to accept the driving that comes with it. Woodinville and Bothell offer more value per square foot but serve a buyer pool that is often more price sensitive than Bellevue buyers.

What this means practically is that a pricing strategy that works in one of these cities can fall flat in another. The psychology of the buyer shifts, the pool of competing homes shifts, and the acceptable price per square foot shifts. You have to know which version of the Eastside market you are actually in.

## The case against overpricing

Almost every seller I talk to initially wants to list high and see what happens. The logic feels reasonable. You can always come down. Leaving money on the table is worse than trying. I understand the instinct, but the data on this is pretty consistent and not in favor of that strategy.

Homes on the Eastside typically get the most buyer attention in the first seven to ten days on market. That is when the buyers who have been actively searching and are genuinely ready to move jump on a new listing. If the price is off, those buyers skip it, or they come, feel like it is overpriced, and leave without writing an offer. Once a listing sits past that first week or two, something changes in how buyers perceive it. They start to wonder what is wrong with it. The days on market number follows the listing everywhere, and buyers and their agents notice it.

Price reductions attract less attention than new listings do. By the time you cut the price to where it should have started, some of the best buyers have moved on to other homes. You often end up selling for less than you would have if you had priced correctly from the beginning.

I have seen this play out enough times that I am direct about it with sellers even when the conversation is uncomfortable. The goal is the best net result, not the most optimistic starting number.

## When pricing below market value makes sense

There are situations where deliberately pricing below recent comps is the right call. In a competitive seller's market with limited inventory and motivated buyers, a sharp price can generate enough competing offers that the home sells well above where it started. This is not a trick. It only works when the conditions genuinely support it, meaning enough buyers are actively looking, inventory is low enough that your home stands out, and the home itself is prepared and presented well enough to create urgency.

It is a strategy, and like any strategy it requires honest assessment of current conditions rather than wishful thinking. When the market is softer and buyer traffic is lighter, this approach can backfire. You price low hoping for multiple offers and get one offer at the low price with no competition to push it up.

## What condition and presentation actually do to price

Pricing is not just about the comps. It also has to account honestly for the condition of your home relative to what sold. If the best comparable sale was a fully updated kitchen with quartz counters and new appliances, and your kitchen has not been touched since 2003, those homes are not equivalent. Buyers will make that adjustment whether or not you do.

This is one reason I think getting the home right before listing is worth serious attention. A home that shows well, photographs well, and has addressed obvious deferred maintenance will defend its price better than one that is priced the same but gives buyers reasons to discount. Buyers and their agents are looking for any reason to justify a lower offer. You want to give them fewer of those reasons, not more.

## How interest rates affect where buyers draw the line

Rates matter to pricing in a way that is sometimes underappreciated. When rates move, buyer purchasing power moves with them. A buyer who could comfortably afford a $1.4 million home when rates were at one level may be squeezed at a higher rate environment, not because their income changed but because the monthly payment did.

On the Eastside, where prices are high enough that most buyers are carrying substantial loans, this effect is real. Certain price thresholds become psychological breaking points for buyers. Pricing your home just above one of those thresholds without strong justification can reduce your buyer pool more than you expect.

This is worth factoring into your pricing conversation rather than treating as background noise.

## What to do if you and your agent disagree on price

This happens. Sellers have an emotional and financial stake in their home that is completely legitimate, and it is natural to want a number that reflects everything you have put into the property. Sometimes the market supports that number and sometimes it does not.

My approach is to show the work. I will walk through every comparable sale, explain the adjustments I made, show you the active competition, and tell you exactly where I think the price lands and why. If you disagree with my conclusion, I want to know which part of the analysis you see differently. That is a real conversation. What does not help either of us is picking a number because it feels right or because a neighbor said their house sold for X.

If after that conversation we are still far apart on price, that is important information. It might mean we are not the right fit for each other, and that is okay. Working with a seller who is committed to a price the market will not support is a bad outcome for both sides.

## A few things sellers often underestimate

* The difference in buyer traffic between a home priced at $1,395,000 and one priced at $1,450,000 can be significant even if the gap feels small to the seller.

* Seasonal timing affects pricing too. What a home can realistically achieve in March is often different from what it can achieve in November, even if the underlying market has not changed much.

* Buyer agents talk to each other. If your home gets a reputation as overpriced, that perception spreads faster than you might think.

* A price that generates no showings in the first ten days is sending you a clear signal. Waiting longer rarely changes the outcome.

Getting the price right is ultimately about being honest with yourself and the market about what the data says. The Eastside is a strong market and a good time to sell is relative, but none of that changes the basic reality that buyers have choices and they are making comparisons. A home priced well for what it is will find its buyer. A home priced for what you wish it were worth is a harder road.

## Common Questions

### How do I know if a comp my agent used is actually comparable to my home?

Ask your agent to walk you through why each sale was included. The useful questions are: Would a buyer who looked at that home also look at mine? Are the lot sizes and locations genuinely similar? Is the finish level and condition close enough that the numbers are meaningful? If a comp is being used because it sold nearby at a high price but the homes are quite different, that is worth pushing back on.

### Does it matter which month I list on the Eastside?

Yes, meaningfully. Spring, roughly late February through May, tends to produce the most buyer activity on the Eastside. Fall has a secondary window, with buyer activity picking back up after Labor Day through October. The summer slowdown is real, and listing in late November or December usually means a smaller buyer pool even if your home is priced well. That does not mean other times of year never work, but timing is a real variable in your pricing and strategy conversation.

### If I get a low offer early, does that mean my price is wrong?

Not necessarily. Some buyers lowball regardless of price as a negotiating tactic. The more useful signal is whether you are getting showings and whether agents who showed the home are giving you feedback that the price feels off. One low offer from one buyer is noise. No offers and no serious traffic after two weeks is data.

### How much does lot size actually affect price on the Eastside?

It depends heavily on the city and neighborhood. In parts of Bellevue and Kirkland where land is scarce, lot size and the potential to build or expand can carry significant weight. In Sammamish, lot sizes vary considerably across neighborhoods, from compact lots in master planned communities to larger parcels on the plateau, so how much weight the market gives to lot size shifts depending on the specific area you are in. Your agent should be able to show you sold comps that illustrate how the local market is actually valuing land in your specific area.

### Should I price my home based on what I need to net, or based on what the market will bear?

The market does not care what you need to net. I say that plainly because sellers sometimes anchor on a number based on what they owe, what they paid, or what they need for the next purchase. Those are real constraints but they are separate from what a buyer will pay. If there is a gap between what the market supports and what you need, it is better to know that before you list than to find out three weeks in after the home has been sitting.

# Why Eastside Homes Don't Sell and What to Fix Before Relisting

> If your Eastside home didn't sell, here's what actually went wrong and what to change before you relist. Practical advice from a local agent.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 13, 2026
Topic: Selling
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/why-eastside-homes-don-t-sell-and-what-to-change-before-relisting/

When a listing expires on the Eastside, the story sellers usually tell themselves is that the market was slow, or the timing was bad, or buyers just weren't serious. Sometimes that's true. More often, the home had a problem that was visible to everyone except the people selling it.

I've watched listings sit in Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, and Sammamish while nearly identical homes nearby went under contract in a week. The difference is almost never location. It's usually one of three things: price, presentation, or both. Here's how to think through each honestly before you put the sign back in the yard.

## Start With the Price, Even If You're Certain It Was Right

The hardest conversation I have with sellers is about price, because everyone has a number they feel entitled to. That number is usually built from what they paid, what they've put in, or what their neighbor got two years ago. None of those things are what the market cares about today.

If your home sat for 30 or more days without an offer, price is the first thing to examine seriously. Not adjust slightly downward to look cooperative. Examine seriously. Pull up the homes that actually sold during your listing period, the ones that closed, not the ones listed at similar prices that also didn't sell. Look at price per square foot, condition, lot size, and location relative to yours. If buyers had comparable options that were cheaper or better, that's the answer.

On the Eastside, the gap between a property that feels slightly overpriced and one that buyers will overlook entirely can be surprisingly small. Buyers here do their homework. Many are moving from out of state with relocation packages and very specific budgets. Others are locals who have been watching the market for months. They know when something is priced 5 to 10 percent above what they'd pay, and they simply move on.

## What Buyers Actually Saw When They Walked Through

If you had showings but no offers, that's its own signal. It means buyers were interested enough to come, but something stopped them from writing. That something is usually one of these things.

### The photos didn't match reality

This goes both directions. If the photos oversold the home, buyers arrived expecting more and left disappointed. If the photos undersold it, you probably didn't get enough showings to begin with. Either way, photos matter more than sellers often want to admit. A significant percentage of buyers have already decided how interested they are before they walk through the door, based entirely on what they saw online.

Professional real estate photography isn't a luxury on the Eastside. It's expected. If your listing used phone photos, or even decent camera photos with bad lighting, that's likely costing you both traffic and credibility.

### The home needed work buyers didn't want to take on

There's a large group of Eastside buyers, especially in the tech sector, who are working long hours and don't want a project. Deferred maintenance reads as risk to them. It's not that they can't afford repairs. It's that they don't want the uncertainty of not knowing what else might be wrong.

A dated kitchen or bathroom isn't necessarily a dealbreaker if the price reflects it. But a roof that looks like it needs replacing, a furnace from 1999, peeling paint, or a crawl space that hasn't been looked at in years, those create doubt. Doubt kills deals.

Before relisting, get a preinspection done. Know what a buyer's inspector will find, and either fix the most significant items or price the home with full transparency about what's there. Sellers who try to hide problems through the inspection process create the worst outcome: a deal that falls apart after two weeks under contract.

### The staging wasn't helping

Empty homes photograph and show poorly. Overly personalized homes are hard for buyers to picture themselves in. Neither extreme works well. If the home was either vacant or filled with very specific personal decor during the listing, that's worth changing before relisting.

Full staging isn't always necessary, but at minimum the home needs to feel clean, uncluttered, and like someone has thought about how it presents. That means editing furniture down, clearing counters, making sure every room has a clear sense of purpose, and addressing anything that smells or feels off the moment someone walks in. First impressions in real estate are genuinely that fast.

## Did the Listing Actually Reach Buyers?

Sometimes the home and the price were fine, and the problem was exposure. Ask for the showing data and marketing details from your previous listing period. How many showings did you get? How many unique online views? Was there an open house? Was the listing shared anywhere beyond the MLS?

The Eastside buyer pool includes a lot of people relocating from other cities and countries, particularly for jobs at Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and the other large employers in the area. Those buyers are often working through relocation services, corporate housing contacts, or real estate agents in other cities who are referring them here. If the marketing for your home only covered the basics, a segment of those buyers may never have seen it.

I'm not saying you need to run a major campaign for every home. But if your prior listing had minimal marketing beyond an MLS entry and a lockbox, that's worth addressing before you relist.

## The Stigma of a Listing That Didn't Sell

Here's something sellers don't always hear directly: when a home relists, buyers notice. The days on market history is visible. Buyers and their agents ask why it didn't sell, and if there's no clear answer, they assume the worst.

This isn't a reason to panic. It's a reason to relist with something actually changed. If the price drops and nothing else is different, buyers who already passed will continue to pass. If the price drops and the photos are new, the home has been refreshed, and there's a clear explanation for why the situation is different now, that resets the psychology somewhat.

The worst version of a relist is a price reduction with the same photos, the same description, and no visible changes. That tells buyers the seller is getting desperate but hasn't done anything to address the underlying issue. That creates lowball offers and difficult negotiations, not the fresh start the seller was hoping for.

## A Few Things Worth Fixing That Sellers Often Skip

Before relisting, walk through your home the way a buyer would, starting at the curb. A lot of sellers spend time and money on interiors while the front yard, driveway, and entry still look neglected. First impressions start before anyone opens the door.

* Power wash the driveway and walkways if they've gone gray or mossy. In the Pacific Northwest this happens fast.

* Refresh the front door. Paint it or replace it if it looks worn. It costs relatively little and shows up immediately in photos.

* Fix anything that's been on the to do list for years. A sticking door, a broken outlet cover, a cracked tile. These are small, but buyers notice them and add them up.

* Have the carpets professionally cleaned or replaced if they've had pets. Smell is the thing that most reliably kills interest, and it's often the thing sellers are least aware of because they've gone nose blind to it.

* Clear out at least a third of everything in closets. Buyers open closets and assess storage. Packed closets signal a lack of space even if the actual square footage is fine.

None of this is complicated. Most of it isn't expensive. But sellers who have lived in a home for years often can't see what a stranger walking through for the first time sees. That's not a criticism. It's just how familiarity works.

## Timing Matters, But Not as Much as Sellers Hope

Sellers often want to believe that relisting at a different time of year will solve the problem. Sometimes that's partially true. Spring is generally the strongest selling season on the Eastside, and a home that struggled in November might get more traffic in April. But timing doesn't fix a pricing or condition problem. It just changes the volume of buyers who encounter that problem.

If the home is properly priced and well presented, it will sell in most months. The Eastside has enough year round buyer activity, driven by corporate relocations and job movement that doesn't follow seasonal patterns, that waiting for spring isn't always the right call. It depends on whether you need to sell now or can genuinely afford to wait.

What I'd caution against is using a seasonal break to avoid making the harder decisions about price or condition. Sitting on a home that needs to be repositioned, hoping the calendar fixes it, usually just adds months to a process that could have been resolved sooner.

## Common Questions

### How long is too long to sit on the market before it becomes a real problem?

It depends on what the market is doing at the time you list. In a fast market, even two weeks without an offer is a signal worth examining. In a slower market, the threshold shifts. The key question to ask your agent is: how long are comparable homes taking to go under contract right now? If your listing is running significantly longer than that without an offer, buyer stigma starts to build, and the longer it continues the harder it becomes to reset. Beyond six to eight weeks, a relist with meaningful changes is usually more effective than continuing the same listing.

### Does relisting with a new agent actually help, or is it just a change for the sake of change?

It depends on why the original listing failed. If the issue was marketing, presentation, or strategy, a different agent with a different approach can make a real difference. If the issue is purely price or condition, changing agents without addressing those things won't move the needle. The agent matters, but they can't override a home that's mispriced or not ready to show.

### Should I get a preinspection before relisting?

I think it's usually worth it. A preinspection lets you know what buyers will find, which means you can decide what to fix, what to disclose clearly, and how to price accordingly. It also builds some credibility with buyers because it signals you're not trying to hide anything. The alternative, being surprised during a buyer's inspection, often leads to renegotiation or a collapsed deal.

### How much should I reduce the price when relisting?

There's no universal number, but a reduction that's too small, say 1 to 2 percent on a home that needed a 7 to 8 percent adjustment, typically doesn't change buyer behavior. Look at what comparable homes actually sold for during your listing period. That gap tells you more than any formula.

### Can I relist immediately after my listing expires, or should I wait?

You can relist right away, but I'd encourage sellers to take a couple of weeks to actually make the changes first. Rushing back to market with only a price drop and nothing else fixed often produces the same result as the first listing. Take the time to get new photos, address the most visible issues, and go back with something genuinely different to show.

About the author: Jack Macdonald grew up in Bellevue and helps buyers and sellers across Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish, Issaquah, Woodinville, and Bothell with Macdonald Group of Compass. Phone 425.941.6998. Website https://jackmacdonaldre.com/

# Preparing Your Eastside Home for Market: A Seller's Guide

> Practical advice for Eastside WA sellers on pricing, preparation, and timing from a local agent who grew up in Bellevue and knows the market well.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: October 2, 2026
Topic: Selling
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/seller-s-guide-preparing-your-eastside-home-for-market/

## What actually moves the needle when you're selling on the Eastside

Sellers ask me all the time what they should do before listing. The honest answer is: it depends on the house, but there are a few things that matter almost everywhere on the Eastside, and a few things people spend money on that don't move the needle much at all.

This isn't a checklist you can print and hand to a contractor. It's more of a framework for thinking through the decisions, because the right prep for a 1988 Sammamish colonial is different from the right prep for a 2002 Kirkland townhome or a mid century Bellevue rambler.

## Start with an honest assessment of the house

Before you call a stager or pick a paint color, walk through the house the way a buyer would. Come in through the front door. Look up at the ceiling. Open the cabinet under the kitchen sink. Flush the toilets. Turn on the faucets.

Buyers notice the things that suggest deferred maintenance more than they notice cosmetic imperfections. A small water stain on a ceiling will get written into every offer you receive, either as a price reduction request or a repair contingency. A fresh coat of paint somewhere else won't offset it.

The goal at this stage is to separate the must fix items from the nice to have items. Some things are worth addressing before you go to market. Others are better left disclosed and priced accordingly.

## The items worth fixing versus the ones worth skipping

Generally worth addressing before listing:

* Anything that will show up on an inspection and give a buyer leverage to renegotiate. Leaky faucets, failed window seals, an aging water heater that's past its expected life, electrical panel issues, wood rot on the exterior.
* Carpet that's clearly at the end of its life. Buyers can smell it and feel it underfoot. Replacement is relatively affordable and the visual change is significant.
* Paint in rooms with dated colors or visible scuffs and marks. Neutral doesn't mean white. It means nothing that a buyer will photograph and send to their friends with a raised eyebrow emoji.
* Landscaping that looks neglected. On the Eastside, where a lot of buyers are coming from tech jobs and don't have a lot of time for yard work, overgrown landscaping reads as future burden. A cleanup, fresh mulch, and some seasonal color near the entry costs a few hundred dollars and photographs well.

Generally not worth doing before listing:

* Full kitchen or bathroom remodels. The ROI on a full kitchen renovation before a sale is almost never there, and you won't choose finishes that appeal to every buyer anyway. Cleaning, decluttering, and making sure everything functions properly is usually more effective than new cabinets.
* Converting a garage or adding square footage. This is a long timeline and a significant spend, and you're unlikely to price it in before you close.
* Highly personalized upgrades. If you're thinking about replacing the counters with something you personally love, think twice. What you love and what photographs well for a broad buyer pool aren't always the same thing.

## Pricing on the Eastside is not a guessing game, but it requires real judgment

I'll be direct about this: pricing is where a lot of sellers lose money, in both directions. Overpricing is the more common mistake, but I've also seen sellers leave value on the table by pricing conservatively in a neighborhood with real demand.

On the Eastside, the price per square foot can vary significantly even within the same city. In Bellevue, a home in the West Bellevue or Medina corridor is priced against a completely different buyer pool than a home in the Newport Hills or Somerset area. In Kirkland, homes near the waterfront or in the Bridle Trails area command premiums that a home a mile east won't get, even if they're otherwise comparable.

The right comp isn't just a similar square footage in a nearby zip code. It's a home with a similar lot, similar school access, similar commute convenience, and a similar renovation level that sold within the last 60 to 90 days. When the market shifts, older comps can mislead you in either direction.

I price homes by looking at what sold, what's currently active and sitting, and what went pending quickly. The homes that sit are often as instructive as the ones that sold fast.

## Staging: when it helps and when it's theater

Staging matters most in two situations: vacant homes and homes with unconventional layouts. A vacant home feels smaller than it is and gives buyers nothing to respond to emotionally. A staged vacant home almost always photographs and shows better than an empty one.

For occupied homes, the biggest staging wins are usually editing rather than adding. Remove half of what's on the kitchen counters. Clear out the garage enough that a buyer can see it's a functional two car garage. Take personal photographs off the main living areas. Let the house be a house rather than someone's home.

Professional staging services on the Eastside vary widely in cost and quality. For most homes in the $1 million to $2 million range, a consultation with a stager followed by selective furniture rental for the main living areas and primary bedroom is usually enough. Full house staging on a larger home can run considerably more and isn't always proportionate to the return.

## Photography and how homes are presented online

Most buyers see your home for the first time on a screen. The listing photos are the first showing. This isn't a place to cut corners.

Professional photography with proper lighting makes a material difference. Wide angle lenses used honestly (not deceptively) show space well. Twilight exterior shots can be compelling for the right home. Video walkthroughs and 3D tours have become more expected, especially for homes in the $1.5 million and above range.

One thing I'd flag: there's a difference between photography that makes a home look its best and photography that sets unrealistic expectations. If a buyer arrives and the home looks nothing like the photos, you've started that relationship with disappointment. Accurate and flattering is the goal, not flattering at the expense of accuracy.

## Timing your Eastside listing

Spring, meaning late February through May, is historically the most active period for Eastside real estate. More buyers are looking, which generally creates more competition for well priced homes. But it also means more competition from other sellers.

Fall, September through early November, is typically a solid secondary window. Buyers who didn't find something in spring are often still active, and inventory tends to drop going into winter, which can work in a seller's favor.

The slowest periods are typically mid December through January and the hottest weeks of August when families are traveling. Listing during those stretches isn't impossible, but you're fishing in a smaller pond.

That said, the right time to list also depends on your house and your situation. A home in a neighborhood with very low turnover can generate strong interest whenever it hits the market, because buyers in that area have been waiting. And sometimes personal timing matters more than market timing.

## Disclosure: don't try to hide things

Washington is a disclosure state, and sellers are required to complete a seller disclosure statement disclosing known material defects. Beyond the legal requirement, there's a practical argument for being thorough: buyers who discover something after closing that you knew about will pursue remedies, and those conversations are far more unpleasant than a price negotiation before closing.

If your home has had water intrusion, a pest issue that was treated, work done without permits, or a neighbor dispute that affects the property, disclose it. A buyer who knows about an issue upfront can make an informed decision. A buyer who finds it during inspection (or worse, after closing) feels misled, and they usually are.

Sellers sometimes worry that disclosing something will kill the deal. In my experience, transparency handled upfront is almost always less damaging than the same information surfacing mid transaction.

## Common Questions

### Should I get a presale inspection before listing my Eastside home?

It's worth considering, especially if the home is older or you haven't done a lot of maintenance tracking. A presale inspection lets you find the issues before a buyer's inspector does, so you can decide how to address them on your own terms rather than under the pressure of a pending deal. The downside is that anything found in a presale inspection generally needs to be disclosed. But in most cases, knowing what's there and getting ahead of it is better than being surprised in the middle of a transaction.

### How much should I expect to spend on preparation before listing?

It varies a lot depending on the home's condition and price point. For a well maintained home that just needs cleaning, paint touch ups, and landscaping cleanup, you might spend $5,000 to $10,000. For a home that needs carpet replacement, exterior paint, and professional staging, you could be looking at $20,000 to $40,000 or more. The question to ask is not how much you're spending but whether the expected return in a higher sale price or faster sale justifies the cost. That math is different for every house.

### Does the school district still matter for Eastside home prices even if I'm selling to buyers without kids?

Yes, and more than most sellers expect. School district assignment affects resale value broadly because even buyers without school age children today know that future buyers will care. Homes in the Lake Washington School District or Bellevue School District tend to hold and often command a premium relative to otherwise similar homes in other districts. It's worth understanding where your home falls before you price it, because that context affects who your buyer pool will be. Confirm your exact district assignment using the district's own school locator, since boundaries can run street by street.

### What's the biggest mistake Eastside sellers make when preparing to list?

Overimproving in the wrong places. I see sellers spend significant money on a kitchen renovation or a bathroom addition when the buyers in that price range would have renovated it themselves to their own taste anyway. The more reliable preparation investments are the ones that remove objections rather than add features: fix the deferred maintenance, freshen the paint, clean everything, and present the house clearly. That approach will get you further than a remodel most of the time.

### Is it worth waiting for spring if my home is ready now?

Maybe, but not always. If you're ready in January, waiting until March buys you a larger buyer pool but also more competing listings. If your home has something specific that makes it appealing year round, like a great floor plan, a coveted school zone, or a location near major employers in Bellevue or Redmond, it may not need the seasonal lift as much. The spring advantage is real but not universal, and sitting on a ready home for two or three months carries its own costs.

# Relocating to the Eastside for a Tech Job: What to Know

> Moving to the Eastside of Seattle for a tech job? Here's what actually matters about neighborhoods, commutes, housing, and tradeoffs before you decide.

Author: Jack Macdonald, REALTOR, Macdonald Group of Compass, Bellevue WA
Published: September 2, 2026
Topic: Relocation
Area: Eastside, Washington
Web page: https://jackmacdonaldre.com/blog/relocating-to-the-eastside-for-a-tech-job-what-to-know/

A lot of people who reach out to me are relocating from out of state, usually for a job at Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, or one of the smaller companies in that orbit. They've done research online, they have a rough sense of prices, and they usually have about a week to see the area before they have to decide. Most of them underestimate how much the Eastside varies from one city to the next, and that gap in understanding leads to decisions they sometimes wish they'd made differently.

So here's what I'd tell you if we were sitting down over coffee before you started your search.

## The Eastside is not one place

When people say "the Eastside," they mean everything east of Lake Washington: Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Sammamish, Issaquah, Woodinville, Bothell, and a handful of smaller areas in between. These places look adjacent on a map but feel meaningfully different to live in. Prices vary. Commute times vary. The age of the housing stock varies. What you give up and what you get changes quite a bit depending on which one you land in.

Microsoft's main campus is in Redmond. Amazon has been expanding in Bellevue aggressively. Google has a large campus in Kirkland, and Meta's Eastside offices are in Redmond and Bellevue. If you know your campus, start your search anchored to it, because traffic on the Eastside can be genuinely bad during peak hours, and the difference between a 10 minute drive and a 40 minute drive matters more than it sounds when you're doing it twice a day.

## What the commute actually looks like

The road situation on the Eastside runs on SR 520, I 90, I 405, and the surface streets that feed them. During rush hour, I 405 between Bellevue and Kirkland or Bellevue and Renton can be slow enough that people who move here specifically to avoid Seattle traffic are surprised. It's not Seattle level, but it's not rural either.

Redmond is the easiest campus to reach from most of the northern Eastside. Kirkland, Redmond, and parts of Bellevue all put you within a reasonable drive of the Microsoft campus, and the East Link light rail extension now connects Redmond Technology Station through Bellevue to Mercer Island and Seattle, which genuinely changes the math for some people who prefer not to drive.

Sammamish and Issaquah are further out and almost entirely car dependent. The tradeoff is more house for your money, newer construction, and quieter streets. If you have a campus in Redmond or Bellevue and you're okay with 25 to 40 minutes in a car each way, they're worth considering. If your job requires being on site daily and you hate driving, probably not.

## How the neighborhoods actually differ

### Bellevue

Bellevue has changed a lot in the last decade. Downtown Bellevue now has real density: high rises, restaurants, a growing walkable core around Bellevue Square and the surrounding blocks. If you're coming from a city and want something that feels more urban than suburb, central Bellevue or areas like West Bellevue near Clyde Hill give you that in ways the rest of the Eastside mostly doesn't. Prices reflect it. Single family homes in Bellevue proper are among the most expensive on the Eastside.

### Kirkland

Kirkland has a downtown right on Lake Washington that feels genuinely walkable, with restaurants and coffee shops along the waterfront. The neighborhoods behind downtown get hilly fast, which affects everything from lot size to how much sun you get. It's a popular landing spot for people at Google given the campus there. Housing ranges from older ramblers to newer construction, and pricing sits below Bellevue but not by a huge margin in the desirable parts.

### Redmond

Redmond is quieter than Bellevue and Kirkland. Redmond Town Center gives it a retail and restaurant core, and the Sammamish River Trail runs through the area, which matters a lot to cyclists and runners. If you're at Microsoft, living in Redmond means you might actually be able to bike to campus. Housing stock is a mix of older neighborhoods close to campus and newer developments further east near the Novelty Hill area. That newer eastern part is farther from everything else but has newer homes.

### Sammamish and Issaquah

These two are the most suburban of the group, in the way that word usually means: larger lots, newer homes, good schools, less walkability, and more driving for everything. Sammamish in particular has grown extremely fast and the infrastructure hasn't always kept pace, so traffic on Sahalee Way or along 228th Avenue can be genuinely frustrating. Issaquah has more of a defined old town core and sits against the Cougar Mountain and Tiger Mountain open space, which is a real draw if you hike or mountain bike. Prices in both cities are lower than Bellevue, which is why families with school age kids often end up there.

### Woodinville and Bothell

These sit in the northern part of the Eastside. Woodinville is known for its wine scene along the Woodinville Wine Country area, which is a fun thing to have near you. Both cities offer more house per dollar than the south and central Eastside. The tradeoff is that if your job is in Bellevue or Redmond, you're adding commute time, and if your job is in Seattle, you're adding more. Bothell straddles the King and Snohomish county line and has a growing downtown that's worth paying attention to.

## Renting first is worth thinking about seriously

If you're moving here without having spent real time in each area, renting for 6 to 12 months before buying is a reasonable choice and one I tell people honestly even though it means they're not buying anything from me right away. The Eastside is expensive enough that a mismatch between where you land and where you actually want to be costs real money to fix. Renting gives you time to figure out which commute you can tolerate, which neighborhoods feel right on a Tuesday night and not just during a Sunday open house, and what your social life actually looks like here.

That said, the rental market on the Eastside is also tight and not cheap, so renting isn't painless either.

## What prices look like and what that means for your search

Per Redfin, the median sale price across all home types was about $1.56 million in Bellevue and $1.49 million in Sammamish in August 2026, with Redmond around $1.34 million and Kirkland around $1.31 million over the summer. Single family homes in the desirable pockets of Bellevue and Kirkland typically sell well above those medians, and Sammamish and Issaquah are where many buyers look for a house with a real yard at a lower price point. Condos in Bellevue's downtown core start lower, though anything reasonably sized is still a significant price point.

Tech compensation packages often look very strong on paper, but a lot of that compensation is in equity that vests over time rather than cash in hand today. Lenders care about your base salary and documented income, so if your total comp includes a large RSU component, have that conversation with a mortgage lender before you set your budget rather than after you've fallen in love with something.

One more thing worth knowing: Washington has no state income tax, which is a real difference if you're coming from California, New York, or other high tax states. It affects how your compensation actually lands in your pocket, which is relevant when you're running numbers on what you can afford.

## Schools, if that applies to you

The Eastside has strong public schools broadly, but there are differences. Bellevue School District and Lake Washington School District (which covers Kirkland and Redmond) both have strong reputations. Issaquah School District is well regarded and draws families specifically for that reason. If schools are a factor in your decision, go beyond the general reputation and look at the specific school boundary for the house you're considering, because boundaries matter more than district level rankings.

## The Pacific Northwest adjustment

This part doesn't always come up in real estate conversations but it should. The weather here is real. From roughly November through March, you will have a lot of gray days with low clouds and frequent rain, not dramatic storms but persistent drizzle and limited sunlight. Most people who grow up here don't notice it much. People relocating from sunnier climates sometimes find the first winter harder than they expected. It's worth thinking about honestly if you're someone who is seriously affected by light and weather.

On the other side: summers here are genuinely spectacular. Long days, low humidity, mountains visible in every direction, and easy access to the water. People who make it through the first winter usually understand pretty quickly why everyone stays.

## Common Questions

### Is it better to live closer to campus or closer to amenities on the Eastside?

It depends on how often you're actually required on site and what you do in your off hours. If you're hybrid and going in two or three days a week, being 20 minutes away instead of 10 is not a big deal. If you're on site every day, proximity to campus pays off quickly in time saved. I'd push back gently on optimizing entirely for commute at the expense of living somewhere you actually enjoy being, especially since Eastside housing is expensive enough that you'll spend a lot of time in and around your home.

### How does the East Link light rail change the equation for Eastside buyers?

The 2 Line now runs from downtown Redmond through Marymoor Village, Redmond Technology, Overlake Village, and Bellevue, then across Lake Washington through Mercer Island and Judkins Park into Seattle, where it continues north toward Lynnwood. For people who work in Seattle but want to live on the Eastside, or vice versa, this is a real option. It also changes how I'd think about living in central Bellevue specifically, since the walkable downtown area around Bellevue Downtown Station becomes more useful if you're using transit regularly. That said, the Eastside is still largely car dependent outside of these corridors.

### Is it realistic to buy a home on the Eastside with a typical tech salary?

For a senior individual contributor or above at a major tech company, yes, the math often works, especially with dual income. For someone earlier in their career, the Eastside is genuinely expensive and may require tradeoffs: a condo instead of a house, a longer commute to reach a lower price point, or renting longer while equity vests. The mistake I see is people anchoring their budget to total compensation including unvested equity before a lender has actually underwritten them.

### How different are property taxes on the Eastside compared to other states?

Washington has no state income tax, which helps. Property taxes vary by city and assessed value but are generally in the range of roughly 0.8 to 1.1 percent of assessed value per year on the Eastside. For a $1.5 million home that's somewhere around $12,000 to $16,000 annually, though I'd encourage you to verify the current rate for any specific property you're seriously considering since it varies.

### What should I actually do first if I'm relocating here and have a month to figure it out?

Spend time in each area at different times of day, not just weekend afternoons. Drive your potential commute during a Tuesday morning if you can. Walk around downtown Kirkland or Bellevue in the evening. Have a real conversation with a lender before you fall in love with a specific price range. And if you're not certain you want to commit to buying yet, give yourself the option of renting for a year. The Eastside is expensive enough that getting it wrong costs real money to fix.
